MR. HOWARD  STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING B.C. FISHERIES DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a question of privilege. Very briefly, my question of privilege is that the Minister of Fisheries misled the house on August 2, and I should like to make reference to Hansard of that day in order to prove my contention. Incidentally, it was not possible for me to raise this question of privilege earlier. This is the first opportunity I have had because it did not come to light until a document was tabled in the house yesterday pursuant to a motion for the production of papers to which I shall refer. I think it is necessary to read a little more than usual in order to illustrate my point.
The hon. member for New Westminster asked the Minister of Fisheries the following question, as reported at page 2945 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I could direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries and ask him for what I hope will be a final progress report on the negotiations with the British Columbia fishing industry?
The minister made the following reply:
Mr. Speaker, as I reported to the house yesterday, negotiations resumed on Wednesday between the two parties involved, the union and the fisheries association of British Columbia. I am pleased to inform the house this morning that the situation has improved greatly in the last 24 hours. In fact, with the indulgence of the house may I be permitted to place on record part of a telegram I received at five o'clock from the union, which reads as follows:
"Reurtel our central strike and policy committee decided upon receipt your telegram bearing in mind urgency expressed regarding resumption operation and failure reach agreement upon scope and terms arbitration that we shall immediately recommend to our membership acceptance of appointment by federal and provincial governments of single arbitrator whose decision shall be final and binding and that the arbitrator shall decide scope and terms of reference after consultation with both parties to the existing dispute."
The minister then went on to say:
A few hours later I received another telegram from the fisheries association which reads in part as follows:
"-the member companies of this association are prepared to accept the decision of a single arbitrator to be appointed by the Hon. H. J. Robichaud and the Hon. L. R. Peterson as final and binding upon the matter or matters which will be agreed to be referred to him."
The only problem which remains, Mr. Speaker, consists of the details of the terms of reference.
Then there are a few other words which are not germane to this particular point. The key points upon which I rest this question of privilege are, one, the fact that the minister read only a portion of the telegram from the fisheries association; and, two, followed the reading of that portion with the words:
The only problem which remains, Mr. Speaker, consists of the details of the terms of reference.
I make this statement especially in view of the fact that the telegram from the united fisheries and allied workers union made reference to the arbitrator deciding the scope of the terms of reference after consultation with the parties to the existing dispute.
I filed a motion for the production of the telegram from the fisheries association of British Columbia which the minister read in part, and it was tabled yesterday. It is dated Vancouver, B.C., August 1, 4.26 p.m., Pacific daylight time. It is addressed to Hon. H. J. Robichaud, M.P., P.C., Minister of Fisheries, Ottawa, Ontario, and reads as follows:
This is a further letter delivered to Mr. R. G. Clements today quote We refer to Mr. Homer Stevens letter addressed to you dated August one 1963, a copy of which you have made available to us. We repeat that the member companies of this association are prepared to accept the decision of a single arbitrator to be appointed by the Honourable H. J. Robichaud and the Honourable L. R. Peterson as final and binding upon the matter or matters which will be agreed to be referred to him.
Then the telegram goes on to say:
It is our understanding that the only matter in dispute which requires reference to arbitration is that of the minimum price to be paid for pink salmon during the 1963 fishing season. If there is any other question in dispute which the union wishes to have referred to the decision of the arbitrator we would appreciate your asking them to inform us through you immediately so that we may consider whether or not we can agree to such question or questions being so submitted. We are unwilling to agree to arbitration of any matter which has not been referred to arbitration by agreement.
Fisheries Association of B.C.
The principle point here is that the association of B.C. indicated in their telegram to the minister that they were only willing to submit to arbitration one single, solitary question, and that was the matter of the minimum price to be paid for pink salmon caught during the 1963 salmon season. If there is any doubt that this was the case,

B.C. Fisheries Dispute
the fisheries association sent another telegram to the minister; and if he did not mislead the house the first time by reading only parts of the telegram, which I contend he did, then he certainly did on another occasion by not relating to the house something which was made even more clear to him by the fisheries association of B.C.
Again this is a sessional paper, No. 64C, which was filed on November 15, and it contains a telegram from the fisheries association of B.C. to the Minister of Fisheries, dated Vancouver, August 2, 1.05 p.m. Pacific daylight time. Mr. Speaker, you will recall that the house sat until 10.56 p.m. that evening, and I suggest this telegram was undoubtedly in the possession of the minister by that time. They say in it, and I only want to quote a part:
That our member companies will agree to arbitration by a single arbitrator to be appointed by the Honourable H. J. Robichaud and the Honourable L. R. Peterson of the minimum price to be paid for pink salmon during the 1963 fishing season and of no other matter whatever.
I submit that when the minister related that information to the house, notwithstanding this second telegram which makes it undoubtedly clear, he misled the house, when he quoted only part of the telegram and when he interpreted that part to say:
The only problem which remains, Mr. Speaker, consists of the details of the terms of reference.
As a result not only was the house placed in the position of not knowing fully what the situation was, but there was an agreement to proceed to arbitration, and that arbitration has not yet been held because the matters to be referred to the arbitrator are still not cleared up; and I submit they are not cleared up primarily because of the information which the minister gave to the house.
I therefore move, based on this question of privilege, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett):
That this house regrets the Minister of Fisheries misled the house on August 2 by failing to advise the house fully of the position of the fisheries association of B.C.

speechtext:
Order. I have to decide whether there is a question of privilege. I would refer to Beauchesne's citation 104, paragraph 5, which reads as follows:
As a motion taken at the time for matters of privilege is thereby given precedence over the prearranged program of public business, the Speaker requires to be satisfied, both, first-
The "first" is my own insertion:
-that there is a prima facie case that a breach of privilege has been committed, and also that the matter is being raised at the earliest opportunity. If he is not so satisfied he may allow the member to make a statement with a view to ascertaining whether or not a prima facie case can be made out.

It seems to me that the long explanation given by the hon. member, working up to the presentation of this motion which he asks the Speaker to accept, is really in the nature of a grievance. I do not believe that the minister, if a misstatement was made, intended to make any misstatement. With regard to the allegation that a false statement was made, I do not believe that has been proved by the facts alleged by the hon. member this morning. In my opinion this is really in the nature of a grievance, and a prima facie question of privilege has not been made out. Therefore in my opinion the motion should not be accepted.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO GOVERNMENT PLANS FOR REMAINDER OF SESSION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO GOVERNMENT PLANS FOR REMAINDER OF SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day I said I would make a statement on the government's plans for the business for the rest of the session. On Monday, I think it was, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam I undertook to say whether there had been any changes in those plans since my statement on this matter on November 4.
On that date I stated that the most urgent business was to complete the consideration of the estimates, and that remains the case. Of the legislation I mentioned then the first three items have been dealt with by the house, the income tax bill, the surcharge on imports bills, and the amendment of the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act.
The house has also been dealing with the next major item on the list, redistribution, about which I will say a word in a minute.

However, I can no longer be hopeful of the house going on before Christmas to the items which were next on my November 4 list, the National Housing Act amendment and the major railway legislation arising out of the MacPherson royal commission, though a resolution to precede that measure is now on the order paper. These matters will probably have to stand over till next session.
The government considers it essential to have the house deal in this session with the following items on the order paper and which have been on the order paper now for some time: first, the amendment to the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act; second, the amendment to the National Centennial Act; third, the resolution and bill respecting C.N.R. finances.
In addition there are the following items on today's order paper which the government desires to have dealt with in the present session: first, the amendment to the Old Age Assistance Act, the Disability Allowance Act and the Blind Persons Act; second, the amendment to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act; third, the amendment to the Small Businesses Loans Act; fourth, the amendment to the Canadian World Exhibition Corporation Act; fifth, a bill to appoint auditors for the national railways. There will also be a measure introduced next week respecting statutory salaries which the government would like to have dealt with.
With respect to redistribution, Mr. Speaker, the government would like to have the resolution and the bill to set up the office of representation commissioner passed during this session. However, it is prepared to hold over the boundaries bill until the next session. Perhaps there could be discussions among the representatives of the parties on the procedure to be followed in respect of that matter, and perhaps some informal discussions in between the sessions concerning it.
Other measures on the order paper which the government would like to have dealt with in this session, and I do not believe these are very contentious items, are first, the Newfoundland savings bank bill; second, the bill approving the Ontario harbour agreement; third, the amendment to the National Harbours Board Act; fourth, the amendment to the Carriage by Air Act; fifth, the bill to amend the Aeronautics Act, which I believe is now in committee. A resolution preceding a measure respecting payment of certain provincial taxes and fees by crown corporations appears on the order paper today which it would be desirable to deal with. There is also a bill respecting what is called the Blue Water bridge at Sarnia which is still to be introduced and which the house might wish to dispose of in this session.
Business of the House
To the best of my knowledge, Mr. Speaker, subject to any emergencies arising, this is all the legislation the government intends to seek to have completed this session. A resolution respecting Indian claims will be put on the order paper, but the government does not expect the house to complete consideration of this measure. I believe there is general agreement to adopt, without debate, the resolutions preceding the bills which have not yet been placed on the order paper-though I think they are on this morning's order paper-on the understanding that the debate would take place on second reading and in committee on the bills in question. If there are any considerations arising out of this statement which require consultation among representatives of the parties, I am sure that can be arranged without delay.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO GOVERNMENT PLANS FOR REMAINDER OF SESSION
speechtext:
I thank the Prime Minister for setting out the menu. All I can say on this, the 105th day of the session, is that his contemplation that so many other matters can be dealt with in a few days, while expressive of a hopeful desire, in the light of the experience during the years I have been in the house would be difficult of attainment before Christmas. There has been excellent progress made. The other day I was glad to hear the Secretary of State, a wise parliamentarian who understands parliament, expressing himself so clearly and definitely that since September there has been no suggestion of obstruction whatsoever, though the fullest debate has taken place; and with that he was in full agreement.
I agree with the Prime Minister that the estimates must be passed, because they cannot be delayed and postponed indefinitely. There are, of course, one or two departments -defence, whose estimates are now being discussed, and agriculture, when the Minister of Agriculture is available-which will require consideration. I think the suggestion made regarding redistribution is a proper one. We shall give every co-operation in the passage of the legislation setting up the representation commissioner and, of course, during the recess we shall be able to meet with representatives of the government and of other groups in the house to discuss this important matter of redistribution legislation.
There is also the question of the resolutions. The Prime Minister referred to this. While preserving and maintaining our rights, and without prejudice to them, we shall not debate these resolutions.
I was surprised, however, that amidst the somewhat unusual collection of legislation mentioned by the right hon. gentleman nothing was said regarding the serious situation which has arisen with respect to foreign

Business of the House
investment in our country. Only yesterday the Minister of Finance, speaking in Chicago, emphasized that Canada needs a large influx of capital. The latest returns given by the dominion bureau of statistics indicates that in the last three months there has been a reduction, on an average, of $100 million per month in foreign investment in Canada.
That is a serious situation and one which I feel deserves the earliest consideration on the part of parliament. I think when one considers what has happened during the last three months in the field of foreign investment, one can only conclude that some of the tinkering which was done in the budget has brought about a reaction in the United States, necessitating the taking of action now in this regard in preference to proceeding with several measures which, I am sure, are of lesser importance.
I think these are all the observations I intend to make at this time. Certainly this situation which was spoken of outside the house yesterday by the Minister of Finance deserves and demands action at the earliest possible date.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO GOVERNMENT PLANS FOR REMAINDER OF SESSION

That might well be the case, but there is no reason why-and it would be the intention of the government to suggest this course-if they cannot be passed within a few days we should not come back after Christmas and see that they do pass, and not allow any desire for a holiday to interfere with our duty.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO GOVERNMENT PLANS FOR REMAINDER OF SESSION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO GOVERNMENT PLANS FOR REMAINDER OF SESSION

speechtext: And an ultimatum.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO GOVERNMENT PLANS FOR REMAINDER OF SESSION
speechtext:
This is a very heavy agenda of legislation, much of which has been added since the right hon. gentleman made his previous statement on November 4.
I think the government has placed the house in a fairly awkward position. Some of this proposed legislation could not have been

introduced earlier. I refer in particular to the measures concerning old age assistance pensions, blind pensions and disabled persons allowances, which had to be left until the federal-provincial conference had concluded. But there are a number of other items which could have been introduced at any time in the last several weeks. The Canadian National Railways auditors legislation, the gold mines assistance legislation, statutory increases, surely these things have not just come up since November 4. It seems to me it is an indication of very poor planning of the business of the house when we find a heavy agenda like this suddenly placed before parliament.
I want to make the position of this party abundantly clear. I think it is essential that most of the legislation which the Prime Minister has announced this morning should be passed this session. There are one or two measures whose urgency is less apparent, but in my opinion most of them should be passed now. As far as we are concerned we are prepared to expedite the passage of the legislation by giving up, as we have already agreed to do, debate on the resolution stage of certain measures. But we are not, of course, prepared to rush the legislation through without giving it proper consideration. As far as we are concerned we are prepared to have a very short Christmas recess of a few days and come back so this legislation can be given the proper and full consideration which it deserves. We shall be most insistent that this session of parliament be not prorogued until at least the legislation having to do with old age pensions, blind pensions, disabled persons allowances, gold mining assistance and other essential matters has been dealt with.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO GOVERNMENT PLANS FOR REMAINDER OF SESSION
speechtext:
We
appreciate the announcement made by the Prime Minister this morning with respect to the program of legislation for the days ahead. I agree with those who have spoken on behalf of the other opposition parties that it does look as though we have a formidable array of legislative items before us.
However, certain discussions have been going on in the usual way and tacit agreement, at least, has been given to certain proposals. I believe it is the desire of every member of the house to proceed as expeditiously as possible in the carrying through of this legislative program. As far as the Social Credit party is concerned we are ready to co-operate to the fullest extent, though reserving our right to criticize and set forth our views with regard to the controversial subjects which may be brought before the house. We intend to exercise that privilege, but to do so with the least possible extension of debate.

As I say, we appreciate this announcement. We will do our best to co-operate, but at the same time we want to express our views with regard to some of the very important issues mentioned this morning, including the increases in various pensions and other matters.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO GOVERNMENT PLANS FOR REMAINDER OF SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister, the government and all other members, we wish to reach Christmas at the same time as everyone else. The announcement made by the Prime Minister this morning as to the legislation to be passed before the Christmas recess is certainly of a kind to interest this house and especially the Canadian people.
However, I wonder why these measures were not introduced earlier in this house, since we have been sitting for almost three months. The resolutions and notices of motion could have been introduced a long time ago, right after the last elections, even at the very beginning of the session on May 16, 1963.
We are all anxious to see the Small Businesses Loans Act extended. We would have liked also to have the resolution introduced concerning the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, but especially regarding the Old Age Assistance Act, the Disabled Persons Act and the Blind Persons Act, so as to increase their monthly allowances to $75.
When the Prime Minister serves us an ultimatum and threatens us to have the house sit between Christmas and New Year's, if necessary, we are willing to return to the house in order that those measures may be passed by parliament as soon as possible.
On the other hand, why wait until Christmas is only a fortnight away to present those resolutions? That is what we are asking ourselves in this corner of the house. At the very last minute the government introduces a whole lot of bills that could have been presented much earlier. We are given a great deal of legislation to consider, with the implication that we are to pass it in haste, without even discussing it, so that the session may end before December 20.
We are ready to co-operate with the government but we would ask the government to co-operate a little more with the opposition and all hon. members and to submit its bills and resolutions earlier so that we may examine them adequately and enact legislation which will benefit the Canadian people as a whole.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with the utmost attention to the speeches made during this debate on national defence. All these speeches, with one or two exceptions-and more particularly with the exception of the speech we have just heard, and which clearly does not deserve any comments-have been serious and well documented; they proved that the essential problem of our national defence is taken seriously.
On the other hand, I feel that many members do not fully realize the magnitude and the necessity of the review which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) has undertaken a few months ago.
Naturally, the minister cannot very well speak himself of what he has accomplished in that field; however, as I have been indirectly connected with that review, I feel that I must inform this house of what is understood by a survey of national defence policy.
May I tell the committee that I feel very happy to have been able to bring my small contribution to that survey. I also wish to stress the fact that my colleague the Minister of National Defence and myself are jointly responsible, and that I accept my share of responsibility for any serious decisions which have already been taken, or which might be taken later.
That survey, which started sometime ago, and which is unprecedented, requires considerable amount of work. The Minister of National Defence had to draw upon his resources of courage, determination and initiative in order to undertake such a review.
Last April, not long after having been appointed Minister of National Defence, he started a series of surveys on the three armed services and throughout the national defence department. I must say that the employees of the department not only offered their cooperation, but were quite enthusiastic, because they realized, as did many others in the country, that it was time to look more closely into our national defence set-up.
Some might ask why we should deem it necessary to proceed with an extensive survey of our national defence system. Well, there were two reasons for it in mind: the first one was that we are living in a new era, where scientific and technical progress controls our way of life. But it is mainly since the first atomic bomb was dropped that we had to undergo those changes, and today's strategy and art of war are very different from what they were before.
It is hardly probable that we should now be called upon to fight a war similar to those in which we took part in 1914 and 1939.

Supply-National Defence
Yet, in spite of those changes in the international and armament fields, there did not seem to be any comparative transformation within the national defence department; we were still preparing to fight a war according to the standards of 1939, or 1914.
Mr. Chairman, some things have changed now, while others have not, which means the necessity for Canada to participate, with the other western countries, in security and collective defence organizations like NATO.
Russia has still the same objective, it is only by having a collective force to face any possible aggression that we will be able to maintain peace.
Now, I heard somebody say yesterday that there was no possible defence against nuclear arms. Probably not. Yet, if we proceed to arm ourselves it is not so much to fight a war, but to safeguard peace. That is the very reason for which we have troops in NATO, that is, to be able to maintain peace in Europe.
If we had to take our forces out of NATO, we would be in the very same position as in 1939, and Russia would again start its aggressive policy against the west European countries as it did a few years ago with regard to east European countries. I would say, Mr. Chairman, that it is our responsibility to contribute to organizations grouping collective defence forces.
We must also make available to that collective force the best we have, the most effective equipment we can find and what we can afford as a country with a population of 19 million people.
The second reason which justified a complete review of the expenditures of the Department of National Defence is that those expenditures were going up at a staggering pace, to the point that if that situation had continued, the expenditures of the Department of National Defence would have exceeded the $2 billion mark by 1970, and that, without having any more assurance that the weapons and equipment available could be adequate to face the conflicts which might arise in the next 10, 15, or 20 years.
Mr. Chairman, I regret that during this debate, some hon. members tried to indulge in petty politics. Surely, the matter of national defence and all the problems involved call for the good will of everyone.
I have listened to the speeches made yesterday and today by members of this house on the estimates of the Department of National Defence. Some of them were very good. Constructive suggestions were made and take my word, they will be given serious consideration.


At the very beginning of his remarks, the Minister of National Defence stated his two-stage plan to cut down expenditures.
As he stated himself, the first phase consisted of a general house cleaning, that is, the expenditures were fully looked into. Attempts were made to avoid duplication, to eliminate wasteful and excessive expenditures and also to cope with uneconomic operations.
Mr. Chairman, I can assure the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) that cuts in expenditures were not made lightly and in a haphazard way and without due consideration. On the contrary, nothing has been cut out before one, two or even three studies have been made into such matters, so as to ensure the general efficiency of our armed forces, both in Canada and in Europe, while curtailing those expenses that could be reduced.
I am convinced that most responsible people will admit that we had tremendous difficulties in deciding to cut certain expenses made by the Department of National Defence. It was not easy to decide to curtail the expenses on such and such an item as, for example, the frigate or aircraft program. It is not easy, moreover, to eliminate radar stations throughout the country.
Since such steps were so difficult to take and so unpopular, I feel it should be recognized that we took them because we thought we were justified in doing so in the common interest.
We are not indifferent to the difficulties that decision might create in the country; we are not indifferent to the fact that people will be laid off. We want to do everything possible to help retrain them. We will, as much as possible, stagger those lay-offs over a period of a few months.
We will work in co-operation with the Departments of Labour and Industry to put these people back to work in industry, if possible. We do not feel some uneconomic stations should be maintained just to keep men at work. In my opinion, we cannot accept that principle. I feel it is a matter of finding for these people another job that will enable them to earn a living.
Mr. Chairman, with regard to the second stage of that plan, the Minister of National Defence has intimated that it would be made public at the beginning of next year. That second stage is related to what we have done already. On the other hand, much research remains to be done before that program is completed and put into force.
That is what we are doing now. We are trying to create a military force that will meet our requirements in Canada as well as in Europe. We want to set up, in the next ten

or 15 years, a well-balanced mobile force equipped with the latest weapons and equipment.
Of course some complain because it took us eight months to formulate a complete plan. Well, I sincerely feel that there are not three members in this house who have any idea of the work involved in the preparation of national defence estimates. And I fail to understand how the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) and the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Martineau) can criticize the government and the Minister of National Defence for not revealing their defence policy.
What is that policy?
Those two hon. members sit on the special defence committee and have been given all the information they requested. There is a reason why we cannot reveal what our defence policy will be.

It was allowed to call anyone. The minister was there and offered to appear before the committee at any time that the committee might want him to do so. Mr. Chairman, a few weeks ago I had the pleasure and the privilege of visiting our troops in Europe, and like most hon. members of the house who had that opportunity I came away with a feeling of pride in both the brigade and the air division. I have been told by General Stockwell of SHAPE, the British general, that our brigade are the best troops, best trained and best disciplined in Europe. They enjoy an excellent reputation among the countries of Europe and they have been given an assignment that shows the confidence that is placed in them. We can all be justly proud of our Canadians overseas.
The same thing can equally be said of the air division. I have also been told that most of the air forces in NATO look up to our air division, and the members of it are doing an exceptionally fine job under conditions that are not always very easy. They should have our support and our appreciation for their work.
I find it very regrettable that one of our Canadian magazine writers who visited our air division thought it necessary to write a most deprecative article. I have often wondered what prompts a writer to turn out that type of article. All I can say here is that I believe the article was uncalled for, unfair, unjust and untrue. I only wish that the people who may have read it could have the opportunity of visiting the air division in Germany to find out for themselves that we can be justly proud of it and that we need not in any way take for granted what this writer has written.
Would the associate minister at least identify the magazine so that we could get some idea what he is talking about?

I would, if it were not for the fact that in doing so I would give more

Mr. Fair weather: I would like to hear it, too.

You come and see me, too. During the course of the debate it has been said that our forces in Europe are ill equipped and they do not have a definite role. Of course this is unfounded. As far as the brigade is concerned the equipment is good, except for one weakness and that is the armoured personnel carrier which we are going to change as soon as it is feasible. So far as the role is concerned, the Canadian brigade has been given a definite role and an important role in the whole set-up of NATO forces in Europe.
So far as the air division is concerned, it too has an important role to play, a role that was accepted by the previous government. Now, Mr. Chairman, we have the same people who gave this role to our air division asking questions about arming our four weapon systems with nuclear warheads.
I can understand the concern of the hon. member for Calgary North who was in favour of them, and who felt there was nothing else to do but to arm the Bomarc, the Voodoo, the CF-104 and the Honest John with nuclear weapons. I can understand that, but I cannot understand the anxiety that was displayed by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre who, during his term of office, even as minister of national defence could not see his way clear to provide nuclear weapons for these four missile systems.

these nuclear weapons, that he should now be exhorting this government to acquire these weapons in a relatively short space of time. He has even accused us of not having fulfilled our duty-

I am sure the hon. member knows quite well that there were several procedures that had to be carried out before the weapons could be acquired. One of those was the basic government-to-government agreement, which was signed on August 16, 1963. Then there were also the technical agreements that had to follow with respect to the Voodoo and Bomarc. These were completed on October 18, 1963. The agreement concerning the CF-104's is expected to be completed shortly.
To answer the question the hon. member asked with regard to the construction of the necessary storage sites and other facilities for nuclear weapons, these facilities for the air division are provided under the infrastructure arrangements and it is expected they will be completed about the spring of 1964. In Canada it was considered prudent not to commence construction of these facilities in so far as the interceptor squadrons are concerned until a nuclear agreement had been signed and the technical agreements completed. Contracts for the construction of these facilities are now being awarded, but they will not be completed until the late summer or fall of 1964. The facilities for the acceptance of these weapons for the Bomarc are available and we anticipate the delivery of the weapons in the very near future. I might add that the authorization for delivery of the weapons must be given by the President personally, and President Kennedy's untimely death has caused some delay.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the hon. member for Calgary North posed questions as to why we phased out the interceptors, the F-86's, before having acquired nuclear weapons for the CF-104's. I am sure both hon. members must know that the conversion of the overseas squadrons to their new role is being undertaken in accordance with SACEUR's plans. There is no alternative to making a conversion of this kind than to discontinue flying the F-86 aircraft because the crews and all the facilities at the bases must be used in converting the crews to their new operational role.
It was earlier expected that the conversion of the R.C.A.F. air division squadrons to CF-104 aircraft would be completed before the end of 1963. Due to technical difficulties with these very complex aircraft it was not possible to train the pilots for the air division

squadrons in their new role at the operational training unit at Cold Lake, Alberta, as quickly as would have been required to meet this schedule. There will, therefore, be a few months delay in getting the last squadron formed in Europe. This will be accomplished early in 1964.
If the hon. member was justified in claiming that we did not do our duty because we were unable to furnish these weapons in a period of eight months, I wonder how he can excuse the procrastination of the previous government, which in that time were not even willing to sign the agreements with the United States for the procurement of these weapons.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister permit another question? The hon. member for Calgary North, I think it was, was also worried about the possibility of holding winter training if we should withdraw from Churchill. I will take only a minute to answer this question, Mr. Chairman. The savings to be accomplished by transfers to other departments of government as distinct from savings due to abandonment of operations are as follows. First, the navy will transfer its housekeeping responsibilities at Fort Pepperrell to the Department of Public Works. Second, the army functions in connection with the northwest highway system are being transferred to the Department of Public Works. Third, the airfields at Resolute Bay, St. Hubert and Torbay are being transferred to the Department of Transport. Fourth, the R.C.A.F. air photographic section, Rockcliffe, is being transferred to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. As the hon. member will appreciate, it is difficult to estimate the exact change in cost to the government in operating and maintenance costs that will result from these transfers, but the total is expected to be in the vicinity of $10 million.
The Minister of National Defence and others of my colleagues, Mr. Chairman, will answer questions as they arise. May I, in conclusion, say that I am very much convinced that the decisions made by the Minister of National Defence are a right step in the right direction at the right time, and that as a result of this review not only will we have a clear and positive national defence policy but we will have more balanced, effective and versatile armed forces.

Mr. Chairman, it would have been very useful at this time if we could have had a general debate on policy, and it is to be earnestly hoped that such a debate will be held before the white paper is published. Because after the white paper is brought down government policy is fixed. So far as the

timetable goes, I am quite sure we will have plenty of time to debate policy before it is published, because I can see the early flowers of spring blooming before we get the white paper here. However, in the meantime I commend to the minister the speech of the hon. member for Victoria, British Columbia, on naval policy. I am sure the minister can find a great deal of help from that speech when he is dealing with naval affairs.
The minister said in his opening remarks that our end objective is to get the best result for each defence dollar spent. I am sure every hon. member of the house and every Canadian agrees with that very worthy objective. However, I think we would have a lot more confidence in what the minister said yesterday if we were assured that the economies he talked about were real, and that they would not impair the efficiency of the services. I have the feeling that perhaps the Minister of Finance ought to be in the committee today, or at least his parliamentary secretary, because these changes and chops in the services were dictated more by the necessity of the Department of Finance, in its recovery from some of the worst mistakes made in the last budget and in its getting ready for the next budget, than from the point of view of military realities. It seems another case of the bright promise of April fading into the false dawn of winter.
I did agree with the minister on one matter, although not for the reasons he gave. I am very pleased to note that he is not proposing to close the military college at Royal Roads. I am much persuaded by the arguments of some former serving officers who suggest that it would be better for the services, for the officers and for the country generally, when it is necessary to give higher education to cadets and officers, to provide it in civilian universities, where the men would live in a civilian atmosphere rather than the narrow atmosphere of serving life. However, I realize that such a course is not possible at this time, because of the great shortage of universities and teachers, and as long as that shortage continues I should hope that such institutions as Royal Roads would be kept open. Indeed, one of the things which is most often overlooked in the discussion of defence expenditures generally is the great value derived from technical training, discipline, and the various courses of education given serving personnel while in the services. I think that is probably the most real dividend that we get from our expenditure on national defence.
I should like to say a few words later about the cuts in the militia. The minister was silent on this particular aspect but I hope he is not contemplating any cut in or curtailment of the training of army cadets, air cadets or

naval cadets. That training is also a most worth-while and necessary branch of military training and it has a value far beyond the short term needs of the moment, which at this particular time appear to one sitting here to be the need to help the Minister of Finance.
The minister said that his was a housekeeping statement. I have been wondering since last night who is going to keep house while the minister is making up his mind. There are many instances where he has not made up his mind, and this gives a rather disquieting feeling to one. I think it is disturbing and feel that we should have further reassurance beyond that given to us by the Associate Minister of National Defence just a few minutes ago. The minister was talking about the reduction of ten auxiliary naval vessels. It seems to me he was trying to come down on both sides of the fence. In one breath he said that the saving was very small, and in the next breath said: "Well, we are doing this to save money". It has always been my understanding that these surface craft and the few helicopters and planes in the navy formed a very small part of the strength of our naval forces, yet added a disproportionately high percentage to the efficiency of the force. In other words, the better served the more efficient are our naval vessels. I think we should have more assurance on this point.
Another matter I should like the minister to assure us on concerns a rumour current today-although a large number of "rumours" have subsequently proved true, as evidenced this week in relation to the Department of National Defence-that there is going to be a further cut in the establishment of our naval vessels. That matter was mentioned on the radio this morning.
There is another matter on which we should have some reassurance. We should know what alternative arrangements, if any, have been made following the decision to close the rescue station at Torbay, Newfoundland. Is the same degree of service to be provided? How are these necessary activities to be continued. Proposals have also been made to close down certain airfields. I think the savings which will follow are purely illusory. We regret the transfer of jurisdiction over the airfields at Resolute Bay, Churchill and, possibly, St. Hubert, though I am mainly concerned about the two in the north. I think this is a mistake. I do not think there will be any real saving and I believe it would be far better to allow those northern airfields to continue to be occupied and run by our armed forces.
There is another so-called economy which the minister has talked about and which causes us on this side of the committee some

I refer to the rebuilding of a merchant navy, a task which would help shipyards all over Canada. Everywhere we go, in the defence committee and elsewhere, we hear talk about the need for mobility, the need to be able to move men and equipment rapidly. Supply-National Defence provide Canada with ten modern merchant vessels which could be easily converted to use in time of war and which could supply our northern stations in summer? Why not do this? It is a positive plan of action and it would save us foreign exchange because we would not have to pay so much out on foreign charters.
The minister spoke of giving those whose jobs will become redundant as much warning as possible. I suggest that his statement with regard to the radar station, leaving it in doubt whether it would be closed or not, is hound to have a most unsettling effect on those directly concerned. If the minister is not yet ready to make an announcement it is unfortunate that the news was allowed to get out. The same applies to the reduction in our naval forces, which he foreshadowed.
The minister based his programs on ability to obtain worth-while economies. I suggest he could have found other fields for economies during the eight months in which he has held office. He could have found some of them by reading parts of the Glassco report. I would be interested to hear him tell the committee what progress was being made in the co-ordination of specialized services within the department. I have in mind the training which is common to those who serve in all arms-vehicle driving and mechanical skills, for example. I believe a much more worth-while saving could be made in this area than may be expected from some of the minister's proposals.
The part of the armed services most severely shaken by the minister's announcement yesterday will be the militia. Out of every ten men now serving in the militia, four are unnecessary-they can get out as quickly as possible. Maybe it works out to nine out of every 20-I did not calculate the percentage too carefully. I would like to remind the minister that the volunteer is the basis of our armed forces. We have never had conscription in time of peace, and even in time of war we have not had more than limited conscription. Frankly, I hope we shall always be able to get enough volunteers to satisfy our requirements for the armed services. We must have a certain facility or knowledge or friendliness with the armed services The minister may quote statistics to show that very few people serve in the militia and then go on to active service. I do not know. Statistics can be used in many ways. But I suggest the fact that we have a good militia and have always had a dedicated and interested militia has made it easier for us to get the soldiers we need for our armed forces on a volunteer basis. I hope that these and related matters will be taken into consideration before these cuts are made. Again, 

as hon. members know, militia has played a central part, in the last few years, in the operations of the emergency measures organization. Has proper consideration been given to the effect the minister's proposals could have on these arrangements, or is the emergency measures organization going to be abandoned? I think we should have a fairly full and detailed explanation of that point from the minister.
It would also be nice if the minister would give us a little of his thinking on future policy. We do not expect him to give the complete policy at this time but he has been fairly free and open at various meetings in expressing his views. I am an avid reader of the Globe and Mail and the Hamilton papers and I have noted that he has made some very interesting disclosures on policy. I should like him to make a few of his random thoughts available to us here in the house, so that we may get some idea of what our future policy is going to be.
In the associate minister's last remarks there was a somewhat disturbing note, because I got the impression that he was speaking of the Honest John and the weapon that will go on the Starfighter in a rather positive sense and more or less saying: You made the arrangements whereby they would be accepted, and therefore we have to accept them. Military history is strewn with discarded armaments, and I would hope that the decision to retain the Starfighter or not to retain the Starfighter and to retain the Honest John or not to retain the Honest John is made on a better and sounder basis than the fact that the previous government in 1959 or 1960 made a commitment. I trust that there is more logic and reason to the basis of the government's policy than is contained in the intimation we got from the associate minister. He looks a little concerned. I may have read something into his remarks that he did not think was there, but that is the impression I got from his final words.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention in taking part in the debate this afternoon to try to cover the waterfront with regard to the Department of National Defence. I thought I might confine my remarks to a subject with which I have had the occasion to become fairly familiar in the last year and that is the Canadian role in NATO and, more particularly, the Canadian role in the NATO parliamentary association.
I had the honour of being the only member of the house who attended the NATO meeting last year, visited the NATO countries from Turkey through to Norway and again attended the NATO conference in Paris this fall. I

should like to give some of the observations I made and the opinions I gathered during these trips.
First of all, may I say it appeared to me that the Canadian NATO parliamentary delegation this year was able to make a much better impression at the conference than the delegation last year. This is not for the reason that was noised about so much in the newspapers approximately a year ago, but in my view came about because of the cooperation shown by the delegates who attended the conference this year. As I say, this is contrary to what happened last year. Unfortunately, some of the delegates last year seemed to be more intent on making political capital than they were in representing Canada at an international conference. I might add that some of those delegates now hold cabinet positions in the government.
I am very pleased to say that this year this was not apparent. The members of the delegation co-operated very well and I think the results at the conference showed that this is the proper way for a Canadian delegation to act when attending an international conference. In fact, the co-operation that was shown by the delegates who attended the conference in Paris this year could very well be followed in this house sometimes, and if it was I think we could accomplish much more than we seem to have over the last three or four months.
With regard to the visit in September to the various NATO countries, I cannot emphasize too much the importance of a trip of this kind from the point of view of its educational value to people who are interested in NATO. The trip, while a very hurried one, enabled the delegates to visit all these countries and to see at first hand things that before they had only heard about in speeches or read about in books. It also enabled us to see just what NATO means to these various countries. It is all very well for us to sit back some 3,000 miles away and debate the obvious shortcomings of NATO, but when you visit these countries and places and talk to both elected representatives and people from every walk of life you get a much better picture of just what NATO means to the various NATO countries.
There is something else that in my opinion we can and should learn, if we really want to take our proper role in NATO. We can learn about some of the things that are going on in some of these countries. We know that only 20 years ago many of these European countries were desolated and completely smashed. They had been overrun and completely subjugated. I should like hon. members to stop and think for a moment just what that does
Supply-National Defence to the morale and pride of a country. Yet we find that in the short span of 20 years these countries have picked themselves up and have raised themselves to the point where today they have a higher standard of living than we have in Canada, which has had none of the problems to overcome that many of these countries have had.
We find, for example, that in a period of three years West Germany had to import over 800,000 Italian workers to fill jobs. We find that West Germany has a government agency whose task is to recruit workers in various countries to try to fill the jobs that industry is providing in that country today. Now that Italy is booming and the source of supply is dried up there, this agency has had to go to such countries as Turkey, Greece, Spain and Portugal, and according to the last information I have the agency was still running some 50,000 workers behind the demands of industry in West Germany. These are some of the things we can learn, bring back to this country and discuss in order to find out where we are falling short.
For example, let me take Norway, a country which had a political crisis while we were there. Some hon. members may recall reading in the newspapers that the government of Norway was defeated about the end of August or the first of September, but contrary to what happens in this country this did not force a general election. The leader of the opposition there was called upon to form a government but his government only lasted for three weeks. The leader of the previous government was then called upon again to form a government. The point I am trying to make is that if we would take a leaf out of their book we would not find ourselves, as we have far too often since I have been a member of the house, fighting the next election on the floor of the house instead of getting on with the business of the country. In Norway elections take place about every four years and in the meantime government continues in the manner I have outlined. In my opinion there are things we can learn from some of these countries.
We can learn from Sweden, Denmark, Italy and Norway how countries can get along very well with coalition governments. We should get away from the idea we have always had in this country that minority governments are a tragic thing, and that no country can operate properly with them.
As I say, when you look at these countries, when you see the standards of living they have and you see the manner in which they have recovered in the last 20 years, you realize that not one of these countries has had a government with a big majority such as we have had during this same length of

Supply-National Defence time. The problem is not whether we have a majority or minority government. The problem is what the government does with regard to the needs of the country. For example, we could see evidence all the way through the NATO conference this year of the almost overwhelming opinion that in the near future Harold Wilson would be forming the next government in Britain and Willy Brandt would head the democratic socialist government of Germany. In so far as Harold Wilson was concerned, this view was expressed by some of the Conservative delegates as well.
If these events occur, then it will mean there will be almost a solid front of democratic socialist governments from Sweden and Norway in the north clear through to the southern part of the NATO alliance, with one or two rare exceptions. Perhaps we will be able to learn whether or not there is any connection between the high standard of living and the obvious prosperity in these various countries, and the form of government that they have. We might then turn to democratic socialism in this country, instead of making it the bugaboo that the old parties and the newspapers of this country try to make it.
It is not enough, Mr. Chairman, merely to learn what we can do. If we are going to participate in NATO, to play our proper role, we must make our own contribution to this alliance. I must say that so far our contributions, other than a very minor military contribution, have not been great. Judging from what has happened in the past, if the Canadian delegates to NATO are wise, they will keep their mouths shut and their ears open in order that they may learn something. If they are not wise, they will open their mouths and display to all and sundry how little they know about this whole situation.
Why is this so, Mr. Chairman? I maintain that the reason for this situation is that we have a wrong attitude towards our participation in this alliance. We have sent new men every year to this conference. We have taken a stand that this is not a serious conference to be dealt with seriously. It is more of a junket by means of which we reward the faithful of the various parties. When it comes time to choose our delegates we look around to ascertain who has not yet had a trip.
I should like to give you two brief examples to illustrate my point. I refer to the hon member for Victoria (B.C.), a man who has a very distinguished background in the naval service of Canada, a man of unquestioned ability. In September he attended one of these conferences and visited the NATO countries from Turkey through to Norway. This year he was chairman of the Canadian military committee


to the NATO conference. This hon. member was a member of the parliamentary defence committee, but was told when we were leaving Paris that he was being removed temporarily from the defence committee to make room for somebody else who wanted to go to Europe for a trip. I might add, too, that the hon. member has one other qualification in that he is a supporter of the present government of this country. My point is that if there was one man in this whole delegation who should have stayed with this tour by the Canadian military committee, it was the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.). However, that is not the way we run our business.
I will give you another illustration. Last year the hon. member for Edmonton East was chairman of the Canadian parliamentary delegation to NATO, and again was a member of the tour in September from Turkey through to Norway. This year he was not sent to participate, so no use was made of the knowledge he may have gained last year.
Now, Mr. Chairman, what can we, as Canadians, contribute to this conference? I say that we are truly well suited to make a contribution. All we need is men of high calibre who have gained the necessary experience to enable them to make that contribution. We have, traditionally, had a role which we have carried out for the last 100 years of interpreting the United States to the United Kingdom and, in turn, interpreting the United Kingdom to the United States. This should be a land of born diplomats. We have the experience of trying to carry on the government of a vast country made up of two distinct national groups. Possibly this is a poor time to mention this fact, because we do not seem to be doing too good a job of it at the moment. However, I would suggest that if the newspapers of the country would pay a little more attention to the cool heads on both sides and a little less attention to the crackpots, we might not be approaching the crisis we appear to be at the moment.
We have something else, Mr. Chairman, Canada has an excellent reputation abroad. This was brought about, in the main, by the conduct of Canadian troops during two world wars. It has been brought about also, as has been mentioned by several hon. members, by the deportment of the Canadian troops who are abroad at the moment as Canadian representatives in the NATO forces, and other places. We met many people, both in military circles and civilian life, who had only the highest praise for the Canadian personnel who are carrying out Canada's commitment to NATO at the present time. These other countries are looking for something more from Canadian representatives than they have had so far. I should like to

give another illustration, Mr. Chairman. We have, in the person of Senator Connolly, a man who has had great experience and who has shown tremendous interest in the NATO alliance. He is well qualified to be chairman of the whole NATO conference, but this will never be brought about until we have delegates behind him who can carry their proper role in the NATO conference. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that these are some of the things we should think about the next time we send delegates.
First, we should choose people who are really interested in the NATO alliance. We should choose people who have recognized stability. We should appoint them for the duration of this parliament, and not just for one trip, be it to Paris, Berlin or any other place. They should continue their interest in this alliance the year around, and not just in the fall when the annual NATO conference is held. In fact, I would like them to hold monthly meetings in order to keep themselves posted on the latest developments in NATO. We should insist upon reports, both to the various caucuses and, by the chairman, to parliament itself, concerning what has been done by our representatives there. We should not hesitate to change any representative if we find he is not carrying out his duties properly. If we want to carry on as we have in the past, just rewarding the faithful with trips to Europe, then let us not make those trips to the NATO conference. Once we recognize the importance of this alliance, once we recognize what we could contribute to NATO and what we can contribute to this country by knowledge gained by NATO, then, and only then, can we play our proper role in NATO, make our proper contribution and make a greater contribution to the service of Canada itself.

Mr. Chairman, members of parliament are frequently asked why we should place the emphasis we do on this matter of defence. Many members today have had phone calls from militiamen in their areas who have very strong views with respect to the service they have given to Canada and they, of course, regret it has been found necessary to cut back the amount that will be allotted for their own service.
We have other people, good people, who wonder why Canada is spending as much money as it is on defence. I think at the outset I should say the answer I see is that there is in existence a red army of 2.5 million men, highly mobile, well trained, fully equipped with nuclear as well as conventional weapons; an air force which is judged to be considerably over 12,000 aircraft; and a greatly strengthened navy of formidable submarine strength the like
Supply-National Defence of which the world has never seen before. Those are the reasons that we have to look most earnestly at what we are doing in the area of national defence.
I remember back 40 years and have impressions of the military of that day. I was a little boy at that time, but I remember going down regularly to listen to the spritely music of the Royal 22nd band on the esplanade in Quebec, and visiting Repulse, Renown and maybe old Hood whenever they came into port. There was also the summer training at Petawawa and Valcartier, and all this represented the military effort of those days. It was pretty symbolic; but today we have an armoured brigade in Europe which is characterized as the best in the world. I do not think there is any dispute about that. I spent some time with the R.C.H.A. in Soest and I knew this regiment and its state of training in 1941, 1942 and 1943 when its quality and spirit was comparable in many respects to what is demonstrated today at Soest.
We find components of our army, navy and air force in Laos, Cambodia and Viet Nam. We find components of our army and air force in the Congo, and components of the navy and army operating in the Yemen. I mention these only as illustrations of the kind of extensive operation undertaken by our armed services today.
In my view, Mr. Chairman, defence is just one aspect of Canada's external policy, Canada looking out at the world, and here there is something of a contrast that we must face. I think we have three external departments, defence, external affairs, and trade and commerce, and ideally we would be very happy if these three branches of our government, our extrovert reaction to the world, would move in generally parallel directions. But we find they do not, and we deplore this.
The external affairs department takes the somewhat urbane and sophisticated view that we have got to live with everybody, that everybody is reasonably decent, that we want to extend our relations with them and communicate with them, that we want to understand people everywhere, and that the world is not made up of good guys and bad guys, cops and robbers. It is not like that at all. Today it is a case of where we must adjust, influence, make compromises, with the hope of extending the ring of friendship wherever we can.
Trade and commerce has quite a different point of view. There has been an aggressiveness displayed, particularly during post-war history, by both administrations, which shows that it is quite proper in the field of trade and commerce to trade zealously with our ideological enemies and be as good customers

Supply-National Defence as we can with them. We want to give them our wheat in good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over, and we deplore anything like bottles or glass in shipments to them. We are proud of the fact that we are able to move forward with the China Resources Company to important new contracts, and we have new extensive contracts with the U.S.S.R. providing for the sale of some 247 million bushels of wheat and flour. On October 8 Bulgaria signed a contract to buy 3.7 million bushels; on October 29 Czechoslovakia signed a contract to purchase 44 million bushels, and on November 5 Poland signed a contract to buy another 44 million bushels.
I am just mentioning these details because they demonstrate on this side of our external policy, that of trade and commerce, that we have come to regard these people as our very good customers and business friends. There is something paradoxical about the fact that we now regard these people as our good customers, and not as our enemies. I am sure that Canada is in the position of wishing that her external policies, involving trade and commerce and defence, could move along more generally parallel lines. Maybe one day they will.
Why is it we find ourselves in the particular defence posture that we do today? I submit, sir, that if we look at the pattern of the defence structure in Canada we find the only thing we are doing in defence is living up to alliances with our allies, and these alliances have been formed because we consider they are in the best interests of Canada, the free world, and the world at large. Perhaps it would be proper to list them chronologically, in a somewhat different way.
On June 26, 1945, the United Nations was formed, and there are a number of distinguished senior members in this house who actually were there and who can attest to the fact that the purpose of the United Nations was to maintain international peace and security, and to be a centre for harmonizing the actions of nations in the attainment of these common ends. That was the purpose why so many countries gathered together and entered into the United Nations organization. We remember that this did not work out, and because of the failure of the United Nations to do the things that were its declared objectives, there was formed the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. It was established on April 4, 1949. What are the objectives of the NATO allies?
They seek to promote stability and well-being in the North Atlantic area.
They are resolved to unite their efforts for collective defence and for the preservation of peace and security.


The parties to the agreement undertake to maintain and develop their individual and collective capacity to resist armed attack, and there was this most important undertaking that an armed attack against any one of them in Europe or North America was to be considered as an attack on them all.
Then on May 12, 1958, we entered into the NORAD contract, and there we find essentially the same philosophy but of course on a more local basis. In the documents covering NORAD we find this:
It was essential, therefore, to have in existence in peacetime an organization, including the weapons, facilities and command structure which could operate at the outset of hostilities in accordance with a single air defence plan approved in advance by national authorities.
I think this was expressed most felicitously by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, on February 20, 1959, when he was prime minister, as recorded at page 1223 of Hansard for that day. He said:
Under the irresistible dictates of geography the defence of North America has become a joint enterprise of both Canada and the United States.
Mr. Chairman, it has been my privilege to be a member of the special committee on defence, and I have tried to be critical, to discover why it was that we are involved in the relationships and commitments in which we now find ourselves. Looking over the whole pattern of NORAD and its defence structure I cannot see a place where I feel there was a decision taken that was not very well considered, very thoughtfully considered from the standpoint of the best advice available at the time, and taken in the interests of Canada and the alliance. The particular alliance I am referring to here is our special military alliance with the United States. It seems to me it is proper I say this because many of us have asked whether these alliances we entered into were in the best interests of Canada.
In terms of actual material and personnel, Canada's contribution to NORAD may not be very outstanding, but what an amazing thing it is to be part of this tremendous defence complex of scientific and mechanical devices, defensive weapon systems, and dedicated personnel. The fact that our Air Marshal Slemon has been able to serve as deputy to three NORAD commanders shows the respect in which this country has been held.
Looking at NATO now, Mr. Chairman: NATO has been under fire at different times and by different people. I have not seen all the NATO countries but I have been in several of them this summer. In particular as a member of the defence committee, I have asked one question in every NATO country that we visited on this recent trip to Europe.

The question was this: In the event that Canada should feel, perhaps politically, that it was in her interests not to be involved in this particular role, the strike reconnaissance role, the CF-104 Starfighter role, delivering nuclear bombs, if we wished to get out of this role would we be doing a disservice to the alliance? I want to tell the committee, Mr. Chairman, that in every country in which I asked that question I received a very categorical and frank answer-and the answer was yes. This may not be an answer for all time, perhaps, but it seems perfectly clear that this role is an important one, probably dictated by military considerations at a very high level in the alliance.
We wondered, of course-particularly the members belonging to my party-why we got into the business of the delivery of these very offensive bombs. The answer appears clear. First of all, for five out of six years we have won both the team and individual competitions in Europe as flyers of interceptor aircraft. Our boys are just the best flyers there are in Europe. This is recognized. Also this country has had a tradition of political stability and it is appreciated even among our enemies, that we do not want to perform a disservice to anyone or take offensive action against anybody anywhere. I asked this question in the neutralist part of NATO, in Denmark. I asked it in France, with its considerations of force de frappe. What answer did I get-"Yes, this role is significant; it is important". The members of this committee asked this question in Germany and the answer by a responsible German was, "If you withdraw from that particular role, someone has to take it over"-probably Germany. Do you want Germany to take on this role?
If you ask this question in the Nordic countries, what is the answer? It is, "We have recognized it is an unattractive role. We do not have that role ourselves. We do not want it. But if you relinquish this role the fact is that someone else has to take it on; and it is a necessary role". And so say they about the role of our forward brigade. Why is it that one little Canadian brigade, that Alastair Buchan says costs the equivalent of two European divisions, and not even very magnificently equipped, I might say, is so important in that forward position? It is because it is a symbol of the integrity of the alliance, of the strength of the alliance. It is a symbol that North America cares.
Particularly after the ramifications, pub-licitywise, of operation Big Lift, this is highly important. At this time, it seems to me, we cannot countenance for a moment the withdrawal of this forward brigade from its present role. We know that a brigade cannot stop anything very much; we know that our 28902-5-353
Supply-National Defence brigade is right on the front line facing all this Russian strength; but the Russians know there is no offensive intent in a Canadian brigade. I am leaving aside questions of military hardware, questions of tactics, and so on. To me they are secondary to the continued location at the front of our brigade. We cannot fail to recognize the importance of our NATO relationship and particularly at a time of strains and stresses. We may be the factor to change, to alter, to shift NATO's strategy or even to reverse NATO's strategy with regard to the importance of tactical nuclear arms. I believe there will be this kind of shift; at least, I hope there will be.
The heavy reliance on tactical nuclear weapons in Europe I believe has been a mistake. There will have to be shifts to the conventional but they will have to come cautiously at the proper time. The way for these shifts to take place is collectively with leadership from a good ally that does its job superlatively, and Canada is the country that in my judgment can provide precisely that leadership within the NATO family.
I have touched on two of these alliances, Mr. Chairman. I do not want to weary the committee, but I think I must refer briefly, because this is so important, it seems to me, to the direction in which we are moving in the universal alliance known as the United Nations. This trend is highly significant. The U.N. was our first hope in defence. If that alliance could have been successful after 1945, as we all hoped it might, these two and a half million Russian troops would never have been maintained with expensive armour, guns and ultimately nuclear weapons. Had we been able to dispense with the costly defence of Europe, how much richer a world we would have been; how much richer a world in every important sphere. But unfortunately this hope has not materialized. We are still struggling with the hope that the United Nations will one day take over and move into this area which NATO has been compelled to fill, and which in its own sphere NORAD has been compelled to fill.
Our Prime Minister, in his speech to the general assembly on September 19, 1963, gave positive leadership to this principle of universal security with a proposal that could lead to a pooling of available resources and the development in a co-ordinated way of trained and equipped collective forces for United Nations' service to meet possible future demands for action under the blue flag of the United Nations. This was not just a casual speech. We find the then secretary of state for foreign affairs of the United Kingdom, Lord Home, on October 1, 1963, after discussions on this proposal saying:
