I want to see the element of Improvisation removed from such policing operations, and in particular a start made to strengthen on a permanent basis the chain of command at the disposal of the Secretary General;
The matter was pursued further by our Secretary of State for External Affairs, who on October 18, 1963, said before the first committee of the United Nations general assembly:
The Prime Minister of Canada urged others to adopt similar arrangements and he proposed that there should be an examination by interested governments of the problems and techniques of peacekeeping operations with a view to the development in a co-ordinated way of trained and equipped collective forces for United Nations service.
The Canadian Prime Minister was not advocating a standing United Nations army but rather the more modest objective of co-ordinated national preparations to meet the sort of United Nations requests a number of us have already repeatedly been called upon to fulfil.
We know this is technically and constitutionally difficult, but we know also that there are strong movements in this direction. The Nordic countries which have been happily able to stay out of this nuclear involvement altogether are able to present a nucleus for such a military force. We had the assurance of the Secretary of State for External Affairs at the external affairs committee last night that there was a collective interest in this recommendation. We should move along the lines suggested by Lieutenant General Guy Simonds when he said before the defence committee:
I believe that a role which Is suited to a country of our size and having regard to the financial burdens possible to be borne over a lengthy term, would be a tri-service force whose main objective was peacekeeping. I believe its organization should be very much like that of the United States marine corps which is a mobile force complete with all its ancillaries and able to meet what are commonly called brushfire situations.
I think that is what the associate minister of defence means when he speaks of the objective of more balanced, more effective and more versatile armed forces. John Strachey puts forward this view:
The introduction of tactical nuclear weapons to redress the balance between the ground forces in Europe was a wholly unsuccessful move. But this is not to say that they could now be abandoned.
If Canada could play a part in the role of practical nuclear disarmament when such proves possible we would be bringing our defence policy more nearly into line with our other external policy of trade and commerce.
I listened with interest to my hon. friend representing the island of Cape Breton when he went after my colleague, the member from the bigger island of Newfoundland last night. As he was talking I was reminded of the minister in Little Cumbrae on the Clyde, who

always prayed for the people of Little Cumbrae, then for the people of Great Cumbrae, and finally for the people of the adjoining islands of Great Britain and Ireland. Thus in our defence policy in Canada we must have regard for the defence of the North American continent under NORAD, and our common defence under NATO, these being our closest and most trusted allies. The democratic alliance of these NATO nations must be kept strong if it is to survive. But we must always bear in mind the ultimate purposes of the United Nations.
I will conclude, Mr. Chairman, with only one comment. Throughout the period of the sittings of our defence committee I personally have been disturbed and concerned with the fact that the proportion of our navy dollar, our army dollar and our air dollar devoted to equipment has declined each year since the Korean war. This decline has been rapid. This has happened under both administrations and it seems inevitable that as we proceed costs tend to increase. The cost of living is going up and we have been on a fixed budget with the result that we have been living on equipment capital in the army, navy and air force to a progressive degree for the last five to ten years.
I do not know what the proper proportion or balance should be. I have asked this question in a number of other countries. In some I have been told that the proportion of each dollar spent on the army, navy or air force should be 50 cents as to equipment and 50 cents as to the rest. In other countries I have been told that it should be something in the order of 30 cents on the dollar for equipment and 70 cents for the rest. But obviously we are compelled to make adjustments, there cannot be a progressive paring of equipment costs without specific displacement of our forces. Our brigade in Europe speaks of two great needs, that of armour and carriers on the one hand and adequate artillery on the other. Our guns at the present time are outgunned by equivalent German or Russian guns by 3,000 metres, and that is too serious a matter to leave unremedied. I know we must look at the whole matter of the militia again. One thing I deplore is that in all these statements which have come down from our service chiefs very little emphasis has been placed on the useful part the militia has played in any of its activities. Perhaps we in the committee have been negligent in not asking specifically for greater information on this question. A number of us have asked questions on the point, but perhaps not with the concentration which was necessary.
I know there are many who wish to contribute to this debate so I will conclude my remarks.

I regard the hon. gentleman as one of the important leaders in our committee. I think it is fair to say that as a result of the committee sitting so regularly and having gone to so many places and interviewed so many people it may be that this matter of militia has been overlooked. I am sure we have not yet covered all the ground necessary to give a complete report, and I feel personally neglectful on the matter. I asked questions relating to militia of a number of witnesses, and I know that the hon. gentleman who asked me this question has as well. He has demonstrated the same concern. All I am saying, and I am sure he will agree with me, is that the evidence on the record to date does not give a very compelling argument in favour of the role of the militia. That is certainly the case with respect to the briefs presented by the service chiefs. I think the matter should be re-examined.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a question?
He is not a minister.

In view of the threats caused by nuclear weapons, is the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson)) not of the opinion that it would be better for us to engage in peaceful pursuits instead of preparations for war, and that our efforts should be directed towards the setting up of peaceful undertakings?

In answer to this question, Mr. Chairman, no person more than the members of the defence committee is concerned about peace. Everything Canada has done in defence is designed only to prevent war breaking out. If I may take an extreme view of this defence thinking, it is that 28902-5-353J
Supply-National Defence expressed by the French people we interviewed, with their idea of force de frappe. When we questioned them about their independent nuclear force as to whether or not it was adding to the dangers, they said no, because it was their insurance that if there is any trouble anywhere in Europe nuclear war would be involved at once and it accordingly followed that this made war absurd. I am not saying that their logic is my logic. It is not. It seems to me that there has been leadership given by the late President Kennedy and Mr. McNamara with respect to the need for balanced response, which perhaps was not quite as clear under the former United States administration. But it was precisely because some Europeans were concerned that the Kennedy administration was soft on making real nuclear war on Russia if necessary-this was the argument made both in France and in Germany- that there has been this proliferation of nuclear arms. I hope ultimately we can get out of this impasse.

With the hon. member's permission, I should like to ask him a supplementary question. Is he not of the opinion that the first people to benefit from the huge amounts spent on national defence are not the Canadian people, nor those who work for defence production, but rather the moneylenders who, with millions, finance military expenditures.

I agree with something said by my hon. friend for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, that if we could put the same brains, capital and energy into other activities than the manufacture of war implements we would be immensely further ahead. I think ultimately that is what we are all working for.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to assure you that originally it was not my intention to take part in this debate. However, in view of some of the points raised in the minister's speech yesterday I think it might be appropriate for me to mention one or two items in this report. My association with the army and the militia for many years has taught me the importance of these departments, but I want to assure you that it does not qualify me as an expert. I appreciate the importance of his department and recognize that world conditions demand that our defence must be maintained at a very high standard. I recognize that world conditions demand that we be also prepared to assist our allies, particularly in the maintenance of

In recent weeks, as a member of the defence committee, I have been exposed to a variety of terms which have been strange to me. I do not intend to employ them in this debate on defence estimates today. It might be wise to avoid the use of the term "posture" on this occasion. I shall not detain the committee by employing the various adjectives used to qualify the word "deterrent"-active, minimum, negative and passive. We have heard much about a force de frappe nationale, forestalling blows, cost effectiveness, and similar mysteries. I have also become familiar with Corporals, Honest Johns, Hound Dogs and Davy Crocketts, in addition to such specialized expressions as I.C.B.M., logistics, interdiction and hard bases.
I apologize, if after all this work in the defence committee, I refrain from using these most informative words which have been added to my vocabulary and try to examine, perhaps in a simpler form, the position in which we find ourselves today.
Only three months remain of the current 1963-64 fiscal period. A review of the defence estimates in December precludes any meaningful revisions of the projected expenditures. Our normal calendar of events has been upset by an April election and a change of government. The current year's estimates reflecting the policies of the previous government will not, therefore, produce the usual sharp criticism of the official opposition.
Supply-National Defence
On the other hand, the minister of defence is now engaged with defence policy considerations preliminary to his submission of the 1964-65 estimates. It is a commitment of the present government to revise Canada's defence policy. It has already taken steps in that direction. We are aware of the urgent need to review and revise our defence policy. It arises from serious problems with our balance of payments-current deficit financing, increasing the already heavy burden of interest charges; the needs of the provinces and municipalities for resources with which effectively to perform their responsibilities; the pressing need to remove the tragedy of unemployment, particularly in areas such as Bell Island in Newfoundland and Cape Breton in Nova Scotia. Steps have been taken in this direction in recent months.
We are grateful to the previous government for having established an oceanographic station in my constituency. Likewise, we appreciate what the present government has done in this direction. Some mention has been made during this debate of developments in Cape Breton in connection with the supply of heavy water. Here again, we must recognize an example of the kind of thing that happens to the economy when you start adjusting defence expenditures within provinces, and other provinces engage actively in promoting economic development within those provinces. As an example, I might cite steel in Quebec and steel in Cape Breton. The problem, therefore, stands as one of varied complexity for the government at federal-provincial and municipal levels.
Apart from these considerations, the fantastic cost of defence hardware in this nuclear age compels drastic steps to remove every item of waste, inefficiency and obsolescence within our military forces. It is vital to our national existence, Mr. Chairman, that we contribute to the deterrents within NATO and NORAD to prevent an all-out nuclear war. Under the umbrella of such deterrents we must make our contribution to the police force services of the United Nations. Economic problems in our domestic affairs cannot be neglected. An effective military contribution in alliances with the western world democracies, our trading friends and neighbours, cannot under any circumstances be avoided. Government measures to combat our economic and social problems cannot be undertaken in isolation from defence policy. Changes in defence measures cannot be accomplished without consideration of the far reaching effects on the economic and social affairs of our nation.

Supply-National Defence
Major changes in the character of defence expenditures will, without doubt, shift economic benefits to some areas and subtract from others. Subtraction of the import dollars to cities, towns and regions by this process will vary from minor adjustments to major hazards to their economic base. Despite this, no government can avoid responsibility for combatting the conditions I have described. No government is worthy of the compliments of Canadians that fails to comprehend the realities of our position, and thus shirk its responsibilities.
To clear the decks for action, we require new tools with which to perform our tasks. We need them to meet the social-economic conditions at home. We need them to perform our contributions to the alliances we make with other nations. We have already undertaken measures to that end. There is the economic council, to provide government with advice on economic matters independent of narrow partisan consideration. In the light of that advice and information, we need the Department of Industry with its areas development agencies organized to encourage or establish a stable economic base either in the servicing or manufacturing fields in cities, towns or regions suffering from chronic unemployment and, in particular, those areas that must withstand, now that we have come to grips with this problem of a new defence policy, the shock of changes in defence expenditures.
We need, and are gratified to have, the all-party defence committee to spread among all members and all parties in this house the harsh realities of our necessary contribution to the common defence of the western democracies against the threat of communism. Without doubt, that committee report should be filed with the minister before the issuance of a white paper on defence policy. This procedure is essential if we expect to achieve an acceptable policy without delay and with a maximum of co-operative effort on the part of all members of this house. We need it, to have less than a minimum of goading and gloating over past policies that disrupt and confuse our national sense of direction.
Without the tools of government I have described, without an all-party defence committee in this house of minority government, lacking that prior organization of this house for the important task, any major change in defence expenditures would be disastrous and only compound our present difficulties. Parliament has seen fit to approve of this direction of preparations and of the necessary measures to provide us with the means of a proper approach to our defence policies. Full use of these measures will certainly be

the constant concern of every member of this house. We on this side, who are not members of the cabinet, will be aware of the existence of these measures and will apply them ceaselessly through the party caucus and through other means of consultation, to maintain that awareness of the great urgency which exists when you undertake a major change of defence policy. We will do so with good will, because we know that our government's policy is oriented to do just that, but they also need constant awareness from the constituency level. We will welcome the constructive efforts and criticisms of any member of the opposition, like-minded and concerned with the defence of Canada and the objectives we seek.
It is not my purpose at this time to present final conclusions reached from my work as a member of the defence committee. They include an awareness for Canada to stay out of membership in the nuclear club for the production of thermonuclear strategic weapons; the need to participate in the military control of the air space and the ocean waters of the North American continent. The conclusions I have reached on those and other matters of defence policy should be objectively presented first to the all-party defence committee. I can, however, declare that the studies shared with all my colleagues on the defence committee deepen my awareness of one inescapable fact, namely that our nation must share with its friends and allies the heavy responsibility of deterring the ambitions of the U.S.S.R. to force its ideology throughout the world. In that role we are not fighting only for the technological or economic perfection of our free enterprise economic system, we are fighting for the right to continue our efforts to establish the maximum of social justice for our people, in our nation, in our time. We are fighting to preserve the right of self-determination of individuals and people.
It is our duty, Mr. Chairman, to fully grasp the over-all prospect for the decade ahead of us. If we do, we will agree with that distinguished late president of the United States, John F. Kennedy, who stated:
We are confronted by the challenge of the century. We have no alternative but to take up the challenge.

Mr. Chairman, I shared with the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Lloyd) who has just spoken, and other members, the experience of being on the special defence committee and going to Europe. As all members know, that committee has not yet made its report and I will reserve, with the degree of self-restraint that other members of the committee have, my detailed comments on defence policy until that committee has had

a chance to discuss its conclusions and tries to justify its existence by making a worthwhile report to the house.
I hope it is going to be able to achieve that. If good will, hard work and a nonpartisan approach to our task can achieve that, then I think it will in fact be achieved, but of course I do not want to underestimate the difficulty of the task we have to face, and no doubt we shall have disagreements and draw different conclusions from the same facts.
I would, however, like to make a few observations in this debate. First of all, having had the advantage of this trip I would like to join with the minister and the associate minister, and others who have spoken, and tell the committee of the very excellent impression that our forces in Europe-and I think I should include as well those at Colorado Springs-are making upon those with whom they have to work. In my judgment and from what I saw, we have every reason in Canada to be proud of the high morale and efficiency with which our services are doing the tasks assigned to them.
But, Mr. Chairman, having said that I would like to go on to express my very grave sense of disquiet at the tasks which are in fact being assigned to our forces. I want to address, not only to the members of the special committee, but to this committee and the minister, a plea for a radical review of our basic military policy and military doctrine, on which all we do in defence must be based.
In introducing his estimates the minister has announced, as he calls them, a number of housekeeping items. I do not propose to comment on those. We have also been told, and no doubt quite accurately, that a general review of policy is under way. I hope this review will be pursued and the conclusions which emerge from it will be firmly and courageously put into execution. I think we have already seen from the changes already made-and I do not want to call them minor changes because they are important to a lot of people-some of the difficulties that pursue any government in doing its duty, which is to use as efficiently as it can the limited resources it has for the purpose of acquiring the best possible defence and security measures that can be taken, without regard too much to local or political pressures, however necessary or important those pressures may be. I hope the minister will not be in any way deterred from carrying through whatever conclusions this review leads him to.
In my view the military role of Canada has been based on certain fundamental misconceptions, and I do not mean just in the past. I mean those misconceptions are still to some
Supply-National Defence extent with us. On June 18 last the minister appeared before the special defence committee at its initial meeting and gave us a public statement on the basis of Canadian policy. He said:
At the same time that the free world has an adequate or better capacity in strategic forces, there remains demonstrable deficiencies in its conventional and tactical capacity in Europe.
Again, as recorded at page 15 of the committee proceedings he said:
The dependence upon nuclear weapons against both strategic and tactical targets has been brought about for two basic reasons:-the marked superiority in Soviet manpower vis-a-vis NATO forces in being, and the knowledge that the Soviets have similar weapons in operation.
I may say that this observation of the minister was repeated by him at other times and by other witnesses as a basis for Canada's continued acceptance of the so-called tactical nuclear role, both for our strike reconnaissance force and for our army division in Europe.
We are told of the supposed deficiency in tactical nuclear weapons available to allied forces. I asked the minister what these deficiencies were and he quite properly, I presume pleaded that the security consideration made it impossible for him to enlarge on what these deficiencies were.
He also referred, and we were referred to it again and again, to the supposedly vastly superior Soviet conventional force as related to the particular role and effort we should make.
Both of these points turn out to be myths, and policies based on myths are apt to be useless, expensive, and indeed dangerous. Why do I say they are myths? Again I want to refer to the speech that was made in New York on November 18 by defence secretary McNamara. What he said then was not new, but he collected together an account of the development of strategic doctrine and a re-assessment of some of the military facts upon which that strategy had been based. I do not wish to go into all he said in detail. I want to confine myself to those references which are essential to the point I am making, and which I think destroy the very basis upon which the minister told the defence committee that our defence policy rests.
Secretary McNamara, after referring to the tremendous superiority of the strategic nuclear power of the United States, proceeded to say:
In the field of tactical nuclear weapons, the picture is in important respects similar. The U.S. at present has in stockpile or planned for stockpile tens of thousands of nuclear explosives for tactical use on the battlefield, in antisubmarine warfare and against aircraft. They include warheads for artillery, battlefield missiles, demolition munitions, bombs, depth charges, air-to-air missies
5540	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence and surface-to-air missiles. The consensus is that the U.S. is presently substantially superior in design, diversity and numbers in this class of weapons.
I ask the minister, what becomes of his statement on which he based our policy in Canada-that there was alleged deficiency on our side in tactical nuclear weapons?
Mr. McNamara went on to deal with the other myth, the myth of the so-called massive hordes of Soviet forces in Europe, which requires our dependence on the strategy of the almost immediate capability of tactical nuclear weapons. He pointed out that in fact the some 160 divisions were in fact half that number, that the divisions available were half as large as divisions measured in American terms. He went on to point out that the contingencies which would most likely have to be met were not contingencies of the-and although the hon. member for Halifax has warned us of the danger of using these expressions-dangers of warfare at what are called the lower end of the spectrum, and not in a massive attack to be repelled by the tactical nuclear response, which in itself will assure a holocaust and world destruction.
He added that what we have to deal with, what we have to have a force with mobility and the capability of dealing with, are the troubles at the so-called lower end of the spectrum, the end where relatively minor troubles occur. I suggest that we, in rethinking our policy, have to rid our minds of the myths that have prevailed in the strategic doctrine, and which are no longer the basis of the real facts of the situation.
I want to refer to one other passage in the speech of defence secretary McNamara. He says this:
The fact is that at every level of force, the alliance in general, and the U.S. armed forces in particular, have greater and more effective strength than we are in the habit of thinking we have-and with reasonable continued effort we can have whatever strength we need. I have spoken already of strategic weapons, where the great superiority of the United States is the superiority also of the alliance. In tactical nuclear weapons a parallel superiority exists-and while many of our allies share with us in manning the systems which would use these tactical warheads in the hour of need, it is not unfair to point out that, even more than in the strategic field, the tactical nuclear strength of the alliance is a contribution of the United States. That strength has been increased, on the ground in Europe, by more than 60 per cent in the last two years. Today the thousands of U.S. warheads deployed on the continent for the immediate defence of Europe have a combined explosive strength more than 10,000 times the force of the nuclear weapons used to end the second war.
So I think it is a myth that we have to worry about the need to meet deficiencies in the tactical nuclear field. We belong to an alliance. If we are to have any significance at all in the defence of the world today, it


must be as partners in a concerted and dependant effort; but it must be one that gives us a certain freedom to choose that role which makes sense, not to supplement what is already a vast and overwhelming superiority of force; to do those things that are needed, rather than those things that are not needed.
I suggest that nothing could be more foolish than a country like Canada, with relatively limited and small resources, trying to supplement this tremendous mass of power which is deployed in Europe to such an extent that its deterrent effect makes any attempt to use those forces insanity on either side. All the evidence seems to point to the need for conventional, highly mobile troops. One of the things we have learned in our defence committee is that a great many of our planned forces and our forces in being, efficient and able as they may be, cannot be transported to the scene of trouble in time to do any good in the sort of hostility that is likely to break out. We should be hearing about this area and what is needed in it. Our present strike reconnaissance force-and this is something the defence committee will have to consider -seems rapidly to be becoming obsolete. It is highly vulnerable. Unless it were used in a first strike it would probably be destroyed before it could be used at all.
Even in Europe within NATO our real danger is on the fringes, on the flanks, perhaps in Denmark, Norway, Turkey or Greece. There is an urgent need that if some force is to be contributed by Canada to NATO, it should be in the nature of a force that can be moved quickly to where there are trouble spots, to prevent these trouble stops expanding into a full scale war in Europe. I believe that is the sort of thing we should be considering and it is in that sort of field we would make the maximum contribution within the alliance. It surely makes sense to look over the whole field of possible contribution and pick out that which is needed, rather than contribute to that of which there is already a tremendous surplus. We should pick out that field in which Canadian capacity, experience and ability makes it likely that we can make a most important and indeed a very worth-while contribution.
We must learn to relate our defence policies to our international policies. I was at a committee meeting yesterday which was addressed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He told us about his desire to enter into discussions with-I think he had already started the process-Scandinavian countries, and with one other unnamed country, to provide standby forces for the United Nations for peacekeeping, for a fire extinguisher sort of role. If we were to concentrate on a highly

mobile, versatile, tri-service force that could be moved to any part of the world quickly, we would be fulfilling that major political objective, which is to help to build up not only the regional alliance of NATO but the forces of law and peace throughout the world as a whole.
How can we do this? We are told we have a force earmarked for this purpose. But what sort of a force is it? I think it would take a minimum of 30 days to get it quickly to where it is likely to be able to be used. By that time the trouble would be over or the fire would be long past extinguishment, and peacekeeping activities would be meaningless. We have to concentrate on doing those things which are required and which coincide with the policies we adopt in international affairs. I suggest it is possible for us to do that. We cannot do it overnight, but we must look very, very closely at it. At the present time it seems to me-I was going to say "we were prepared" but in the interest of accuracy I should say we are half prepared, and I adapt the words of a famous United States general, to fight the wrong war, at the wrong place and with the wrong weapons as far as Canada is concerned.
I think it was the hon. member for Vancouver East who complained earlier in this debate that we had never had a defence policy in Canada. Considerable objection was taken to that remark by a good many people, including the former minister of national defence. He said, "Of course we had a policy", and he said he had announced it. I think what was meant was that we had never had a made in Canada defence policy. We have been told this by witnesses who appeared before our committee. We were perfectly agreeable and content at one stage of our history to be part of the British commonwealth of nations, or the British empire, and to fit in with its defence plans. That is the role we were called upon to play. Of late we have been part of an alliance in which the United States of America has been the major and predominant force. I suggest that our policy has been to adopt, almost uncritically, the strategic doctrines and theories current within that alliance. It seems to me that Canada has made and is making a first-rate contribution to the actual execution of military policy within the alliance, and it is high time we started to make a contribution in the thinking-out of the military policy within the alliance.
I believe that if Canadians are able, and undoubtedly they are, to make a major contribution in the execution of policy-an important contribution-it is about time they started making a Canadian independent policy, thought out in Canada, dealing with
Supply-National Defence the whole strategy of the alliance and our part in the alliance. This is what I mean when I say we have not had a Canadian defence doctrine or policy, and we urgently need it. I do not blame the minister for not announcing it at this time. I am sure I would have criticized the minister, as would other hon. members, if he had attempted to give us at this stage a detailed outline of defence policy. But I do believe that growing interest in this country in defence-evidenced I would suggest, if not by the attendance in this debate, by the anxiety of hon. members who speak in this debate-and the fact that at long last we have a defence committee which has been studying these matters, and the review the minister is making, all lead to the position where we are going to develop a policy made in Canada which will involve a role for Canada, suited to Canada, within the alliance. I have no doubt whatever that this is necessary if we are to talk meaningfully at all about defence or security. I believe we are moving toward that end. I would like to finish as I began, Mr. Chairman, by saying to the minister that he should not be deterred from taking a radical and firm view about what is required to be done in this field, in Canada's interest.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks I have to make on the minister's estimates will not be at all lengthy, but I do want to express my views on defence policy since the minister, in introducing his estimates, saw fit not to do so. Perhaps my views, together with those of other hon. members, as far as defence policy is concerned might assist him when he is preparing his white paper for whenever that might be tabled in the house.
I think there is certainly a vagueness about the defence policy, or lack of policy, which exists in Canada. I believe we should be defining the issues before speaking about what specific forces are required for Canadian defence and how these forces are to be employed. I was very impressed, in the short time I was listening to the evidence given before the committee, and sitting on the committee itself-I refer to the special committee on defence-by the evidence of several witnesses, one of whom I recall saying that Canada had no real defence policy and that the tendency was to slavishly follow -I believe these were his words-the policies advocated and set down in the United States. He separated the defence objective by saying there should be a truly national defence policy and, of course, on the other hand we must also shape our policy to discharge our political commitments with regard to such

Supply-National Defence alliances as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Then, of course, there is the third field that our policies should be directed to, and that is the United Nations and the requirements of that organization with regard to international peacekeeping operations.
From the evidence I have studied in the special committee on defence it seems that what we should be striving to do with respect to the first aspect of our policy, namely our truly national policy, is to provide security for our national boundaries and the seas surrounding them, as well as the air space above our national territories. I think this objective must be established before we can determine what force is necessary to bring about that security of our national boundaries, our waters and air space. From there we can proceed to decide how that force is going to be used; but as politicians at the policy level it seems that our job is to establish the national objective in the first place. Once that has been established the requirements can then be determined in a logical fashion, and then the experts in the defence of our country can use that force in order to provide that security in the best military fashion possible.
I have referred to the second aspect of our national defence policy as our political commitments. I feel that our commitments to NATO are indeed political. What we are doing in supplying forces to NATO is making a contribution to maintain Canadian prestige and having a voice in international affairs. Because as the previous speaker pointed out, a nation of our limited means cannot make any substantial contribution which is going to have any great effect in any international conflict. I believe in that school of thought that concludes that there is no possibility of a limited nuclear war, and that any nuclear holocaust is going to be all out and unlimited. Therefore, the remarks of the hon. member who preceded me are very much in point when it comes to determining the precise extent of Canada's contribution to the international effort through organizations such as NATO.
With regard to the United Nations and our obligations to that organization, as far back as 1945 the right hon. Leader of the Opposition suggested that Canada could effectively contribute to a United Nations police force; and after the passage of almost 20 years it seems perhaps that we should be directing more attention toward promoting the establishment of a permanent United Nations police force to assist in the keeping of world peace.
With those remarks on the over-all defence policies of the government, which I take it will be established sooner or later,

I will leave that subject. Certainly we anticipate that the minister will bring down his white paper in short order. The usual procedure as I have been accustomed to it is that before or at the time the minister's estimates are brought before the house we have either studied or are given the opportunity to study the white paper before engaging in debate on it.
The remarks now following will be devoted to the specific announcement the minister made last night in committee with regard to certain housekeeping arrangements, as he styled them, in order to save the national treasury money so far as defence is concerned. The bulk of my remarks are directed toward the air force, because I am more familiar in that area, having spent ten years in that service. I know something of its wartime operations as well as its peacetime operations.
The first observation I have to make concerns the decision of the minister with regard to the auxiliary squadrons. I feel quite strongly that the defence of Canada is going to be primarily an air defence; that any attack Canada would experience will be an attack from the air; that any move by the minister to reduce or diminish the effectiveness of the Royal Canadian Air Force is a move in the opposite direction to that which we are taking. I feel that the transport role of the air force should be enlarged so that it can provide that mobility which so many members have spoken of in these estimates thus far; so that it can provide mobility for all our forces in meeting any threat to our security, whether it comes from the air or from the ground.
The transport arm of the air force has been enlarged in the last few years, but in my view it is far from reaching that stage which provides the degree of mobility which I think essential in order to ensure the standard of security to our national boundaries for which we should be striving. Therefore, I believe the minister's decision with respect to the auxiliary squadrons is wrong. The cut is quite a substantial one. The personnel is cut from 2,200 to 860. It is the intention to retain in the reserve only six auxiliary flying squadrons and their associated wing headquarters, the auxiliary wing squadrons at Vancouver, Calgary, Saskatoon and Hamilton being disbanded. I take the implication from the minister's remarks in Hansard that the reason for this is because these locations at Vancouver, Calgary, Saskatoon and Hamilton do not have other air force services on the units, that it is uneconomic to retain them.
However, I suggest that it is foolhardy to disband them. Not only must Canada's air

force be in a position to react immediately to any threat which may come to our national boundaries and the air spaces above them, but it seems to me it is vital for Canadian defence to maintain an effectively trained air force reserve. If we start slowly eroding the foundations of our auxiliary forces in Canada, particularly the air force, we are going to disband completely the effective trained force which would, I feel, make a substantial contribution to any defence effort that the air force might be called upon to make in an emergency.
I believe that the minister's decision to disregard the possibility of jet training at Penhold-although this decision may not have been the sole responsibility of the minister- is wrong. I think the minister will agree that the training facilities in the air force, particularly the quality of personnel performing those training functions, are top line. I do not think that anywhere in the world would be found instructors, officers and men more dedicated to their task. But I think the morale of these forces is deteriorating. One of the reasons, judging from my conversations with air force personnel, is that these people do not know what is happening. They do not know whether they are going to be called upon to continue performing a training role for staffing a nuclear strike force in Europe or for performing a transport role. They are rather vague as to the direction they will be taking in the future.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Chairman?

I would be glad if this were a provincial matter, but unless something has happened of which I am not aware there is still on the statute books of Canada an act known as the Indian Act. As long as it remains there, I believe the subject matter of my bill is very much of concern to members of this house.
This measure, as I need hardly point out, is one which proposes an amendment to the Indian Act. It deals with a minor matter, in a relative sense. Nevertheless, I think it is a subject which calls for action and I do not think much difference of opinion could really arise among members of this house, in this day and age, as to its merits. If hon. members will look at the explanatory notes set out with the bill they will see that this measure seeks to carry out a recommendation which was made to both houses of parliament by a joint committee on Indian affairs presented on July 8, 1961. I think it will be agreed that scarcely any of the recommendations of that committee have yet been implemented.
In relation to some of the other recommendations which have to do with health, welfare, education and the development of human resources, the measure before us today sets out to deal with a topic of minor importance, perhaps; but, in my view, progress along the lines I suggest would represent a further step in enabling our native Indians to enjoy the full rights of Canadian citizenship. The purpose, here, is to make provision for Indian people to enjoy, within a province, the same rights as any other Canadian citizens in respect to liquor laws which are

As I was saying, this would place the responsibility for the use made of alcoholic beverages by the Indian people where it properly belongs, namely in the hands of the provinces. It would make Indians entirely subject to the ordinary laws of the province in that respect, except that it would substantially preserve the rights of the Indian people to the use of the local option idea as far as the consumption or possession of alcoholic beverages within their reserves is concerned. The bill is completely in line with the recommendations of the committee. It is something which, so far as my knowledge of the situation goes as a result of discussions with the Indian people, meets with their approval and desires. I think perhaps that the actions that are being taken by the Indians in regard to holding plebescites on their own reserves, show that they are interested and concerned in this matter. I think the sooner we get on with the job of implementing the recommendations of this joint committee, not only in this connection but in a number of others, the better it will be.
I was not a member of the house at the time this report was introduced. I do know that the presentation of this report and its acceptance by the house was hailed with a great deal of delight by many Indian people, certainly in my area. They assumed that the approval of the recommendations in the report practically made them law. I felt constrained, as a matter of fact, on several occasions to point out to them that the mere adoption of the committee's recommendations in the house did not mean that

the committee's proposals had become the law of the land. I tried to give them some warning, and events certainly have proven me to be right, that it might be some time before the changes which they hailed would become law.
Certainly, I suppose one would have to admit that political events since 1961 might have had something to do with the delay. I suggest, however, that the passage of this bill at this time would constitute a small crumb of acceptance of the committee's report and would, in some respects, be a vindication of the Indian people in this parliament of Canada. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) has proposed in Bill No. C-34 that sections 93 through to 96A of the Indian Act be amended, and he has proposed that sections 93 and 94 of the present Indian Act be amended to make them applicable only to persons on reserves. The present Indian Act makes it illegal for any Indian in Canada, even off a reserve, to have liquor in his possession or to be intoxicated. The act makes it illegal for a person to give or sell liquor to an Indian off a reserve. I think everyone in this house is in accord that this is a pure anachronism. I think it is one of the many statutes we have on our law books that are neither enforced nor enforceable.
In addition, in Bill No. C-34, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni seeks to repeal sections 95, 96 and 96A of the original Indian Act and replace them with a new section 94 which removes the necessity for the lieutenant governor in council of a province, through the governor in council, proclaiming that subparagraph (a) of section 93, which relates to selling liquor to Indians off a reserve and paragraph (a) of section 94, which relates to an Indian having liquor in his possession off a reserve, so that they are no longer in force. I think all members will agree, that this is a welcome change. Moreover, this amended section 94 proposed in Bill No. C-34, retains the right of the governor in council to make regulations respecting votes and referendums

and defining a reserve, as outlined in paragraph 4 of the present section 96A, and also maintains the requirements outlined in section 96A, paragraphs 3 and 5, conditioning the proclamation of the governor in council on a resolution of a band council and upon a referendum of the band in question.
Bill C-34 also eliminates the necessity for a request by the council to the attorney general of the province in which the reserve is situated. This, too, is a needed change and I have no quarrel with the amendments offered by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni so far as they go. I believe the bill is a step forward. I submit, however, Mr. Speaker, that the bill does not go far enough. It is a step forward but it retains, and I do not think this was the intention of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, discrimination, in that members of Indian bands who live on a reserve will continue to be in a position where it is illegal for them to have liquor in their possession on the reserve.

In order for me to illustrate what I mean by saying that the discriminatory effect would remain in our laws governing the use of liquor by Indians, even if Bill No. C-34 were adopted, I think I should run through the present circumstances of the Canadian Indian. I am going to start with the Indians in my own riding. I have more Indians in my riding than there are in the whole of the Northwest Territories. The Caughnawaga Indians and the St. Regis Indians have been located on reserves since 1680. I think I am correct in saying that the Indian affairs department was originally set up in 1774 for the Indians who were living on those two reserves. Initially, it was under civil control and in 1816 it came under military control, and then in 1830 it went back under civilian control.
Eventually the present Indian affairs department evolved out of this original Indian department that was created for the Indians in my constituency. Now, the Indians living
Indian Act
on the two reserves of my constituency are not faced with the problems that confront many of the bands who live on reserves in the northern areas of our provinces. I think the average wage of Indians living on the Caughnawaga and St. Regis reserves is probably higher than that of any other group of workers in the province of Quebec. The reason for this, of course, is that these men are experts in high steel work and earn a rate of pay that corresponds to the very dangerous work at which they are so expert.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, these Indians who are living in Caughnawaga and St. Regis have a number of problems. These problems exist, I think, perhaps only because of the lack of good will between the Indian affairs department and the Indians living on these reserves. There are no economic reasons for serious problems on the two reserves I have mentioned, yet problems exist, misunderstandings exist and mistrust exists to the extent that during the last federal election only eight people out of over 3,000 electors voted. This, I submit, is a clear indication of the mistrust that has built up on perhaps the two most prosperous reserves in Canada.
Now, if this problem exists in the two most prosperous reserves in the country, surely the situation in those areas that are just emerging from a hunting and fishing economy must be worse. As a matter of fact, indications are that the problems are far more serious for the people in the northern tier of our provinces from Quebec to British Columbia where most of our Indian population resides.
The Caughnawaga situation holds out hope for the rest of the Indians in the country. The Caughnawaga people and the St. Regis people have adapted themselves to our economic system. They have found areas of work in which they can become experts second to none. As a result, and because of a long history of extremely well known representatives from their own bands, and because of their proximity to Montreal and Cornwall, these Indians have developed a very real pride of race, a pride in their achievements and a pride in their Indian way of life. These are some of the reasons that they have been so successful in finding a part to play in our mid-twentieth century economy.
The Indian living on the reserves further east in Quebec and in New Brunswick tend to be in somewhat similar positions to those Indians who are presently emerging from the hunting-fishing type of life along the northern tier of all the provinces. This emergence has become very rapid since the war, and in their new life they are confronted

Indian Act
daily with problems of integrating into mining communities and acquiring skills in order to take part in the many industries opening in our northland.
This evolution that has taken place in the last few years has brought our Indian population to a point where, unless we rid ourselves of the archaic Indian Act and-though I do not like to use the word but it is justified in this instance-the archaic administration of Indian affairs, unless we rid ourselves of this antique apparatus then very quickly we will find that Canada will be in a most embarrassing position, although I do not consider this the reason that we should do something about the present circumstances of the Canadian Indian.
As conscientious Canadians we must recognize that our Indian brothers have rights to the same type of livelihood, standard of living, jobs and educational opportunities that all other Canadians have. The Indian affairs department has made giant strides in the last few years towards making educational facilities available to our younger Indian population, but this has resulted in accentuating the problem which exists in the northern part of our provinces of adapting our Indian people to the social standards of the areas in our northland where their future lies.
I can give an example of this. In Chibou-gamou the local Cree population is emerging very rapidly from the hunting and fishing economy, and yet with few exceptions the local corporations have failed to take on Indian personnel. This is not the fault of the local corporations in Chibougamou, because four years ago an association was set up there called the northern citizens guidance association, composed of members and heads of practically all the mining companies in the area. For four years these people have worked towards meshing the local Cree population with the local mining population. They have achieved some degree of success, but that success has not been the result of any help from the Indian affairs department.
As a matter of fact, they have been unable to make progress in the last two years with efforts to acquire housing for these Crees who are moving in from the Mistassini reserve into the Chibougamou and Chapleau areas. They have been unable to move the Indian affairs department in the direction of supporting the Indians in obtaining national housing loans for the erection of individual homes. The national housing people have indicated they are quite willing to listen to any proposals that may be brought forward. It has been two years now since this proposition was brought to the attention of the Indian affairs department and the national housing 
people, but so far not a house has been started. This is just an example of the thinking that has been behind the actions of the department over the past few years.
Mr. Speaker, I am confident that a fresh wind is now blowing through the department. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has an extremely broad and open mind on the subject, and there have been some changes made in the department which augur extremely well for the future. In fact I am confident the necessary changes will be made in the administration of the department as well as in the act itself. But at the moment, although changes are absolutely necessary in the act and in these archaic regulations, which we are discussing-

speechtext:
Bill C-34, although considerably more flexible than sections 93 to 96 of the Indian Act, is considerably less flexible than what is needed in 1963. I think we are all prepared to admit that the abuse of liquor increases at a rate proportional to the number of restrictions placed upon its use. This was amply demonstrated during the days of American prohibition, and this truism is no less applicable to our Canadian Indians. There is no question that the Indian Act regulations governing liquor must be amended, as must many other sections of the Indian Act to keep abreast of the rapidly changing circumstances of the Canadian Indian.

I am hopeful, as I said earlier, that the present government will decide in the near future to alter the existing liquor regulations applicable to Indians in a manner that will allow Indians throughout Canada to be subject only to the liquor regulations of the province within which their reserve is situated. In order that the transition from stringent liquor regulations to the normal existing provincial regulations should not result in excesses in northern areas of our provinces where liquor regulations have to date been rigorously enforced, I think the minister should be given discretion to maintain certain of the existing regulations in specified reserves, only with the approval of the local band council or in reserves where he was requested to do so by the local band council.
I would submit this is the type of flexibility that is necessary and which is not afforded by Bill No. C-34. Bill No. C-34 would retain the anachronisms that I mentioned earlier. In Caughnawaga, which is a suburb of Montreal, an Indian would still be breaking the law if he invited me into his house and served me a drink.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question. Has the Caughnawaga band not conducted a plebiscite?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POSSESSION AND CONSUMPTION OF INTOXICANTS
speechtext:
They have not. This is the result of the fund of mistrust that has been built up in Caughnawaga over many years through the lack of a proper approach to Indian affairs. The paternalism that has characterised our Indian affairs department ever since it was initiated has sown the seeds of the very situation that exists. The Indians in Caughnawaga are against voting on any question; it has reached that point. I think it will improve but this is really the reason they have not voted in a plebiscite in favour of liquor, because at the moment they are against voting in general.
I would submit that any regulation which reaffirms the theory behind the Indian Act liquor regulations, which theory really says that the Canadian Indian is not equal to his fellow Canadian, that he does not possess the qualities of self-control and self-regulation which the remainder of the population possesses, is, I am sure everyone in this house will agree, a regulation based on a theory which is without foundation and has encouraged, as it would in any group of people, the very excesses it was designed to curb.
The third major objection to Bill No. C-34 is that it is a piecemeal approach to remedying the anachronisms of the Indian Act and is not what is needed today. We need a general overhaul of both the Indian Act and,
Indian Act
as I said earlier, its administration, and I am confident that this general overhaul will be made soon.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this bill I wish to say that I think its intent is very good. In the explanatory notes it says the intention is that the same rights extended to non-Indian citizens of the various provinces shall be applicable to Indians. I think it is quite fit and proper that Indians should be allowed to have liquor on the reserve, and by "liquor" I mean any form of intoxicant. But if under this bill, as I read it, we allow them these rights, then of course they come within sections of the various acts of the provinces. I seriously question whether we are doing any great service to the Indians of, let us say, the province of Ontario, from which I come, by putting them under the liquor control act. This act is a pretty tough piece of legislation. In the liquor control act practically all the presumptions are against the individual. Nowhere else in our Criminal Code, with the exception of certain offences such as the possession of stolen goods, do we find this presumption of guilt if a prima facie case is shown against the individual.

speechtext:
To this extent it will, and I was coming to this point. I think I can show that the bill would alter this situation to some extent. I should like to deal further with the presumptions under the liquor control act which apply to the Indian on the reserve as well as to the Indian off the reserve. If you have a bottle and it bears a label saying "Dow ale", as long as a police officer finds you with such a bottle, even an empty bottle or one with very little in it, because of the label on the outside the presumption is that you have a bottle of beer. Then the accused person must rebut this and prove that it was not a bottle of beer.
What is even more serious, I submit, with regard to the liquor control act-and this is

Indian Act
something to which Indians on the reserve would be subject and I think it is a disgraceful thing-is the practice in Ontario of having a blanket search warrant. If someone is suspected of being a criminal, under the Criminal Code a police officer or officers must go to the appropriate justice of the peace and obtain a search warrant. But this is not the case under the liquor control act. If any police officer has what he thinks is a reasonable suspicion that liquor of any kind is being held or kept illegally in any residence, officers of the provincial police force of Ontario can go to that home, without having to go to a justice, and can demand entry under this blanket search warrant.
We pride ourselves, and rightly so, on our criminal law and the fact that the individual is innocent until he is proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. Under our criminal law there is no question about this, and it is fit, right and proper that it should be so. But we do not do this under the liquor control act. All the presumptions are there; this blanket search warrant is there. The idea of this bill is excellent, but by its implementation we would be further extending what I consider to be a grave abuse. Another question I have in connection with this bill concerns the provisions for voting. It is good that a vote should be taken on any reserve. But what is it to be? Will one vote of more than 50 per cent carry it; or does it require 60 per cent, as is the case in the province of Ontario? As I have already stated, the presumptions under the liquor control act makes it very, very difficult for the individual. The previous speaker stated, and I think correctly, that intoxication increases in proportion to the number of restrictions. It flashed through my mind, of course, that it also increases in proportion to the amount of liquor consumed.
In the constituency of Hastings South, which I have the honour to represent, there is a very ancient and proud band of Mohawks on the Tyendinaga Indian reserve. They settled there many years ago and they have produced some outstanding citizens of Canada. They have produced doctors and engineers, and as a matter of fact one of the medical doctors from that reserve founded the Indian order of foresters and was exceptionally well known in North America.
This concludes my few remarks. The reason I rose to my feet stems from the dislike I have for the provisions of the liquor control act. I think it is absolutely ridiculous that we go along with provisions of an act such as this, which we would not go along with so far as criminal offences are concerned.

It seems to me peculiar that if we can accept the fact that Indians as individuals are no different from any individual in other groups, why is it that we cannot accept the idea that Indians as a group are no different from other groups on the matter of liquor? If there is a difference then I think we have only ourselves to blame in that we have in the past taken patronizing attitudes towards them.
Although one point which I like about the bill is that it is a step in the direction of sweeping away these anachronisms, I agree with the opinions expressed by a couple of previous speakers that it does not go far enough. It seems odd to me that we lay so much emphasis on this aspect of liquor. I think more attention should be paid to the other problems Indians have, such as problems of education, employment and housing, which I think are every bit as important, if not more so, as this matter of liquor.
There are some features of the bill which I do not quite understand. I see in the explanatory notes there is a note which says, if I may be forgiven for reading it at length:
The joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on Indian affairs, in its second and final report presented on the 8th July, 1961, under paragraph (b) of heading VII, recommended as follows:
"Liquor
(b) In view of the fact that the possession and consumption of intoxicants off reserves by Indians is dependant on a request by the province, your committee recommends that all existing liquor restrictions in the Indian Act be deleted; and that the same rights extended to non-Indian citizens of the various provinces be applicable to Indians"-
-and this is the important part-
"-except that the right of possession and consumption on the reserve be granted only after the approval by a majority vote of the band".
This matter of the majority vote brings to my mind the question whether this is to be a simple majority, in which case I do not think it would solve the problem, or-

I should like to repeat the point made by one of the previous speakers that the members of this parliament will be able to assist the government and that in the near future the government will decide to bring in a more comprehensive bill covering the liquor regulations as far as they apply to Indians; and that at that time they will sweep away all restrictions completely as far as liquor and Indians are concerned.

At five o'clock, when we proceeded to the consideration of public bills, I was speaking about the cut-backs proposed by the minister in air force training and I

Supply-National Defence was making particular reference to the decision of the government in reference to the jet training program at Penhold.
There must be confusion in the government's policy here, particularly with regard to the course being followed by the Department of Transport and by the Department of National Defence in connection with Penhold. As I was saying before the committee rose,
I feel it is essential to the defence of this country that we should maintain a healthy and viable training program and a high standard of training for the R.C.A.F. I do not think we can do this if we close down our training establishment and training programs. I have suggested to the Minister of Transport that there is no good technical reason why Penhold could not continue to be used as a jet training base. I suggested to him, and I am sure he has discussed this with the Minister of National Defence, that it would be possible to re-route the three converging radio ranges so as to allow an area of 20 miles around this base in order to permit the training program to continue in this area. I am convinced it is technically possible, if the government is prepared to go ahead with this scheme.
There is no trick about the installation of radio ranges and other such facilities to aid navigation in the interests of commercial flying in this country so as to enable Penhold to continue to operate as a jet training base. Re-routing of this type has been carried out in many areas in Canada where there have been obstructions, whether by mountainous country, by the training of air force personnel or by other conditions. There are three converging radio ranges in the Penhold area and each of these could be re-directed so as to re-route commercial traffic. This would ensure the safety of the commercial traffic and, at the same time, allow the air force to carry out the role which I think it should play in the defence of Canada.
I believe the Minister of Transport said a comparison could not properly be made between the situation at Penhold and the situation at Portage la Prairie. I fail to agree. Though the same circumstances do not exist today, there was a time when Portage did lie within a ten-mile wide radio range of a frequently used air corridor, but the radio ranges were directed so as to allow jet training to continue at Portage. While I am on the subject of Portage I think, with due respect to that particular training base, that the minister might find it in his heart, having achieved all these monetary savings as a result of the cuts he has made in defence expenditures, to spare enough money to supply a little paint for the buildings there,


and perhaps to supply accommodation for the painting of aircraft at the base.
I wonder, sometimes, to what extent we realize the complexity of the machinery required to establish and operate a single air force air training base. To me, it is remarkable that the officers and men concerned with the operation of an air training establishment can accomplish their objective with the limited means which, in the recent past, have been made available to them. I should like to make some comments, now, with regard to morale in connection with air training. The air force personnel to whom I have spoken-and it might interest the minister to know I have spoken to air force personnel from one end of the country to the other in recent months- are very unsettled, indeed. I would not say their morale is at a new low but, certainly, it has been affected by the lack of ability on the part of the government to come out with a clearcut policy with regard to training. For instance, short service commission officers do not know whether their commissions are going to be renewed. They do not know because there has been no declaration of policy by the government to indicate where the government is heading with its air force program.
I have heard airmen and n.c.o.'s in the air force discuss this matter. They have done so without knowing who I was, and I have heard them say among themselves: Where are we going to go in civvy street now, in view of all these rumours about cuts? Some have been discussing the possibility of going into the commercial air transport field.
I can assure the minister, as I am sure he is aware, of the extremely high calibre generally of the individuals in the air force training program. The engineers, airmen and n.c.o.'s who maintain the serviceability of airplanes used in the over-all air force training program are of the highest calibre that can be found anywhere, and it is a shame to see this deterioration in morale. I think that the minister, through his officials and those responsible in the air force commands, can reassure the officers, n.c.o.'s and men in the air force that there is no need for them to think about seeking alternative employment. This is what they are thinking at the present moment. There is a very distinct deterioration in morale. I have spoken to air force officers, n.c.o.'s and men from Ottawa all the way west and what I am saying arises from recent conversations, not conversations of months ago.
Morale is being very seriously affected, first of all by a lack of announced policy. I am sure it is also going to be affected now because the men do not know where the axe is going to fall next. If reassurance could be given to these very capable individuals who

serve in our air force I think there would be an immediate raising of the level of their morale.
I have a word to say about the minister's announcement concerning Rockcliffe. I would hope that his announcement that fixed wing operations out of Rockcliffe airport are going to be discontinued will not affect the continued operation of that airport. I would hope that the minister and the Minister of Transport have had some sort of conversations which will result in the continued operation of this airport for fixed wing aircraft under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport. When the minister replies to the comments that have been made perhaps he might cover this point. I am sure he is aware there is a flying club at Rockcliffe and there are other smaller fixed wing aircraft which could use this airport efficiently, provided it is not closed down entirely. I think the Department of Transport should take it over if the R.C.A.F. operation is going to be discontinued.
I am very sorry to see the photographic establishment being done away with. Here is an establishment that led the way in technical skill and ability in photography in Canada, particularly in the role for which it was best suited, that of air photography. It has accomplished more in air photography than any other organization in Canada that I know of. It has led the way not only in Canada but in the world in its operations. It is a sad thing to see this operation being transferred to the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. However, unlike other members I have to agree that there should be some homogeneity in photographic operations in Canada and it would seem that this operation could be merged very efficiently with that now carried on under the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys program for the air mapping of Canada.
May I say a word about the army militia. I think it is a very sad thing that the minister has announced these great cut-backs in militia establishments in Canada. It seems what his announcement really means is that the emergency measures organization is being virtually forgotten. It means that all the plans which have been developed over recent years to use the militia as a civil defence organization are being abandoned, along with their training in survival operations. So far as unlimited nuclear war is concerned, which I believe is the only result if nuclear weapons are used, the militia has been trained in recent years to meet this specific emergency and by cutting back on the militia units across the country it seems to me that we are very
Supply-National Defence seriously endangering our civil defence organization. I believe this particular cut-back is going to have very serious repercussions indeed.
I would be interested in learning the real reasons for the disbanding of the 107 search and rescue operation at Torbay. It seems to me that this particular unit was performing a very necessary function. Search and rescue operations are essential to the safety of air travel in Canada and, as hon. members know, the search and rescue operation of the R.C.A.F. is the only organized search and rescue operation for all flying in Canada. Therefore I very much doubt the advisability of cutting back one of the key operations in the maritime provinces.
I cannot conclude my remarks without making particular reference to the plans of the defence department as they affect my own constituency. The minister mentioned, as found on page 5456 of Hansard, that an announcement had already been made regarding the northwest highway system being handed over to the Department of Public Works. In making this reference he said that it was not expected that the majority of the present civilian employees would be affected. He hoped that they would all be retained in the transfer.
I have made representations personally to the minister, which I am sure he will recall, urging him to approach this change-over with the idea that there should be a phased withdrawal of army personnel in the Yukon, because what the announcement means is that virtually every soldier and every family of a soldier will be leaving the Yukon. There will not be a single soldier left there. I am sure the minister realizes that this will affect the economy of the Yukon very seriously. What 390 soldiers did, a substantially lesser number of public works employees will be able to do. I do not say that by way of derogation in any way of the ability of the army personnel.
I notice that one of the former commanders of the northwest highway system is sitting in the gallery. He like all his predecessors did an extremely admirable job in the maintenance of the Alaska highway which does not only concern my constituency but some in British Columbia and Alberta as well. At this point I think I should pay a tribute not only to the commanders of the northwest highway system who have been maintaining the highway since 1945, but also to all of the personnel who have not only done such an excellent job in the maintenance of the highway but have contributed very substantially to the growth of the economy and the social life and every other aspect of the development of the Yukon. It is a very sorry

Supply-National Defence occasion to have to see all of these soldiers leave the Yukon after such very close relationships had been established with these men not only on a personal basis but on every other basis over so many years. I suggest to the minister that a phased withdrawal is essential in order to assure the least possible disruption of the economy of the Yukon generally, and particularly Whitehorse where a payroll of over $1 million annually is involved. Certainly, the payroll of the public works personnel will not even approach the payroll of the army. Then, of course, there is the consideration of some 500 school children. I believe the date the minister mentioned in his remarks yesterday was April 1. Well, school does not get out until June, as I am sure the minister knows. It would be my hope that his plans would involve consideration of this aspect so that the bulk of the army personnel would not be leaving until after the school term had been concluded.
Until recently the army has been responsible for the maintenance of the Haines cut-off. The minister of northern affairs, has replied to my numerous inquiries concerning negotiations between the governments of Canada and the United States in a rather belligerent fashion, while the Minister of National Defence has been most co-operative. I certainly do not claim exclusive credit for accomplishing the all-weather maintenance of the Haines road, but I am sure if the minister of northern affairs would admit the truth of the matter, he would see from his files or would be advised by his officials that I have been advocating this course since 1958. I feel a real economy can be accomplished.
I was disappointed to learn yesterday from the statement by the minister of northern affairs that United States equipment will be used and United States labour will be used on a section of the Haines road that is purely Canadian. It seems to me we have unemployed people in the Yukon who could be capably employed in the maintenance of this road. We have the equipment which could have been used, rather than calling upon United States equipment. Perhaps this question might be reconsidered by the minister and his colleagues in the hope that it might assist in eliminating the constant spectre of unemployment which exists not only in the Yukon but elsewhere in Canada, and which has not
