Mr. Chairman, on the evening of November 11 last I went with some of the members of the defence committee to the Arc de Triomphe. As you know, sir, France's unknown soldier is buried underneath that arch and an eternal flame burns there. De Gaulle had gone there in the afternoon to place a wreath on the grave. When we arrived we could see in the glare of the floodlights the flag of France, the tricolour, filling the whole of the arch. One almost felt that de Gaulle himself had called on the wind to fill out this symbol of the glory of France.
In the next three days we were never permitted to forget the presence of de Gaulle or the glory of France. De Gaulle is by nature an intellectual, rather like the late John Kennedy, and he tends to surround himself with men of keen intellect and tough fibre. The men who briefed us were incisive, tough and confident. All were men of considerable

achievement. All felt the same intense loyalty to de Gaulle and to France. They understood their national policy; they believed in it. They knew where they were going and they felt sure that they knew how to get there.
This is what they told us. With the end of the t.n.t. age and the advent of the nuclear age, the principles that govern warfare have changed. Few have bothered to recognize that a new and clearly defined body of logic ap-lies to the subject of war and peace in the nuclear age.
First, whereas it was possible for a nation to engage in a war of limited risk in the t.n.t. age, it is no longer possible today among nuclear nations. War is no longer, as Clause-witz said, an extension of diplomacy by other means, for in conducting nuclear war it is not possible to limit or control the extent of the destruction of national wealth which either or both sides may suffer. In Clausewitz' day in eighteenth century Europe, it was possible to send a small mercenary army against a neighbouring principality and to capture it. Thus, by risking the loss of the mercenaries, a valuable and comparatively undamaged territory might be won. In world wars I and II, the United States risked its expeditionary forces in Europe. These were calculable and limited risks on behalf of their allies and in the interest of restoring peace with all its benefits.
Nuclear arms now nullify the validity of all such military alliances. They are, according to the French, no longer valid or tenable, for the law of limited risk now no longer applies. The nation which goes to the support of its neighbour today may be exposing itself to complete or virtually complete destruction. If a beggar asks you for a franc, say the French, you may give it; if he asks you to risk your life for him you will quickly pass him by.
What country could persuade its people to wage war on behalf of an ally knowing that in doing so it might be inviting 10 or 20 or 100 Hiroshimas on its own soil? Would any president urge such a course upon his people? Would any people follow such a leader who promised, not a limited war of blood, sweat and tears, but total war and eternal oblivion? France does not believe that it should ask an ally to undertake such a suicidal mission on its behalf.
Hence, the first principle to be observed in the new logic of the nuclear age is that military alliances are no longer valid. Collective security has little meaning for nations facing each other with nuclear weapons in their hands. If a nation wishes to survive in the nuclear age it must have its own nuclear
Supply-National Defence deterrent and a delivery system capable of surviving and retaliating, say the French.
That is why, we were told, France has established its own force de frappe and why it will have within a few years a delivery system of supersonic bombers, missiles and nuclear submarines of its own. Moreover, they assure us, no committee of allies will weaken the credibility of their deterrent. France's enemies will know that there is only one will behind the force de frappe, one finger on the trigger.
The second principle of war in the nuclear age is that armies are virtually obsolete in the face of nuclear weapons. An army has strength only when it masses the fire power of its individual members. But, when an army is massed or concentrated upon a narrow front in order to obtain maximum firepower, it also becomes an excellent target for nuclear bombs. Thus, the more it concentrates its power the more it invites nuclear attack and total destruction. An army is a cumbersome and inefficient way of concentrating firepower compared with nuclear bombs or missiles. Armies, therefore, will not hold the same importance as they once did.
In support of their theories the French told us that they were applying 50 per cent of their military budget on new equipment while cutting back on the total numbers in their armed forces. France's army of the future will be a strong army of only five divisions but dependant on the force de frappe if an enemy should attack the flesh of France.
The third principle to observe is that a comparatively small nuclear power like France can deter the attack of a much larger nuclear power like Russia. To illustrate this point the French tell a story, that France was anxious to own Monaco so it threatened to drop a nuclear bomb on Monaco if it did not capitulate. Monaco replied that it too was a nuclear power for it owned a fast plane loaded with two nuclear bombs. France laughed at the temerity of Monaco and dropped a bomb on it, destroying it utterly, but not before the one-plane deterrent force of Monaco took off and dropped its two bombs on Paris and Lyon. Thus France had completely destroyed the valuable prize it had hoped to seize and for its troubles two of its greatest cities were reduced to rubble. Did the great nuclear power win the war against the little nuclear power?
The story illustrates the point that, unless it has a completely impenetrable defence against nuclear attack, it is not rational for a big power to attack a smaller nuclear power, for in doing so the big power is unable to limit the risk involved.

These arguments lead step by logical step to the conclusion that there will be no nuclear war. The world of the future will consist of nuclear powers in balance and non-nuclear powers in ferment.
If these ideas seem strange to members of this house-remember, it is not the first time that de Gaulle has put forward new military ideas. He is one of the most brilliant of modern military theoreticians. In the 'thirties he outlined the principles involved in blitzkrieg warfare and urged their adoption. The French ignored him but the Germans read the book and applied it to France. He warned against dependence on the Maginot line and upon the theory of a static front. Again he was ignored. And when the time came the Germans went around the Maginot line, and France was overrun by fast-paced panzer divisions who had learned what France refused to learn from de Gaulle.
Now let us cross the Rhine into Germany. I do not propose at this time to dwell in detail on Canada's role in Germany where we have our air division and army brigade. What I want to discuss in more detail today is Europe itself in which we Canadians are so heavily committed, and upon which we depend for the security of the free world. For if we understand Europe and the forces at work there we will better understand how to approach the problem of defence.
While we felt in France that we had arrived in a country where the cold war is regarded with life-and-death seriousness, we felt when we crossed into Germany that we had arrived at the front. Twenty of Russia's best divisions are stationed in East Germany and Czechoslovakia. They can attack in force immediately without build-up and without warning-like Pearl Harbour. Forty more divisions are in the satellites and 100 are held in Russia. Yet in Europe we have within NATO only 22 divisions to meet the Russian threat. A Russian thrust into West Germany would immediately involve major cities. From the border of East Germany the city of Hamburg is only 30 miles away; the Kiel canal, 40 miles; Frankfurt 70 miles and Munich 100 miles from the border of Czechoslovakia. Cologne and Bonn are only 125 miles from East Germany and the port cities of Antwerp, Rotterdam and Amsterdam no more than 250 miles away. By striking 200 miles across southern Germany from Czechoslovakia, Russia could bring its armoured divisions face to face with France across the Rhine. From take-off time to bomb release time no city in this area is more than six minutes away from Russian strike planes.
Let us lay these distances out on more familiar ground. To capture Hamburg a Russian division would have to travel no further 

than the distance from Ottawa to Carleton Place. Frankfurt would be no further away than Brockville; Cologne or Bonn no further away than Belleville; and the coast of Belgium and Holland would be less than the distance from Ottawa to Toronto. Thus, we hold today in Europe no more than a narrow bridgehead upon the great land mass of Europe and Asia.
Some people of good intention, striving for ways to lessen the tensions of the cold war, or seeking means to reduce its costs, have asked why do we not pull our forces back and disengage from the cold war front. On the narrow strip of Europe on which NATO now stands we would have to move back to North America to disengage.
Why not then, hold our troops in Canada and fly them in when they are needed? The American operation, Big Lift, showed the delicacy of matching planes and men from North America with their equipment in Europe. But what would happen in wartime? There is greater likelihood that Russian soldiers would reach our equipment before we could and greet us with a well planned reception.
Why not establish a buffer zone between our NATO forces and the communists? We have such a zone now, clearly marked on all NATO military maps. It is there for the purpose of preventing our boys from inadvertently wandering across the iron curtain, and it is backed by electronic warning devices. This is a voluntarily imposed buffer zone. Why not negotiate a deeper one-say 25 miles on each side of the border, and remove all military personnel from the area? If the average east-west depth of Germany from the Baltic to the Rhine is 100 miles-and that is approximately correct-then a demilitarized zone of 25 miles on the west side of the border would reduce by 25 per cent the depth of the field in which NATO has to manoeuver. At the same time, Russia, making a similar concession would hardly be affected at all, as its depth of field extends to the wall of China.
Germany is scornful of France and its force de frappe. France still follows the myth of national grandeur and sovereignty, they told us. She is draining away the efforts of NATO to establish a strong conventional force and she is using the force de frappe to blackmail her allies. There should be co-operation in nuclear defence and not a drifting apart into separate nuclear blocs, they told us. Our conventional forces in Europe are not big enough to repel more than preliminary probes. Moreover, the loss of Berlin would destroy the whole credibility of NATO to defend the western world. Germans wrap themselves in Wagnerian gloom when they contemplate the

cold war. NATO will never get into action in time to save them, they say; and they have written to Mr. McNamara asking him to permit the firing of battlefield nuclear weapons in the very first stages of attack. NATO must strike early to prevent being overrun and to preserve what strength it has, they say.
Much of what I heard in Germany confirmed what I had already heard in Paris. There are not the conventional forces in Europe to do more than hold the Russians for a short time, and the west has no intention of providing them. The United States in fact, is more than anxious to reduce the burden of maintaining a quarter of a million men in Europe. Western Europe is so small that a superior force of fast moving armoured units would overrun it in a week or two. Knowing this, the people of Europe have no intention of delaying the use of battlefield nuclear weapons.
Europe is gearing itself for trip-wire war. The doctrine of measured response in which we North Americans were to be given time to reflect on the war while European cities were slowly reduced to ashes by conventional means has been put aside. Instead Europe is readying for instant nuclear war-not a war in which we wait to be hit first but, if the situation warrants, a pre-emptive war, a war of first strike.
NATO officials are more reluctant than the French or Germans to discuss these cold war facts. They give the outward appearance of being more cautious than some of the fast guns we talked to in France and Germany. But they go ahead with the preparations to carry them out-and so we must infer that they follow, as Mackenzie King might follow if he were here, a policy of trip-wire war if necessary but not necessarily trip-wire war. For example, our own brigade under NATO practices sand table schemes and exercises in which the members of the brigade act as game beaters and bushwhackers to drive the enemy into a position where they can hit him with the Honest John, on a first strike basis.
As for our CF-104, it is singularly constructed and armed to fulfil a first strike role. One cannot imagine its being held in reserve even for minutes, for it is a weapon of such overwhelming power that it must strike first or itself be wiped out by the first missiles from behind the iron curtain. No enemy would let a weapon of such ferocity go unchallenged for a second. By comparison our Voodoos, our Bomarcs, our brigade, are toys. In world war II the first 1,000-plane raid on Cologne went aloft with 3,000 aircraft engines, 6,000 men and 2,000 tons of bombs. It took an hour and a half to pass over the target and it wiped
Supply-National Defence out 935 acres. One CF-104 can carry out a somewhat comparable mission in a few minutes with its little torpedo shaped bomb. Their task, in military language, is to interdict the battlefield-to seal it off-by dropping nuclear bombs on all the eastern approaches to Europe in the first instant of war. In a nutshell, when the CF-104's come home eastern Europe will have been snuffed out.
In our journey through Europe the question was asked again and again: Is there a non-nuclear role for Canada? And each time it was asked we were met with the same enthusiasm a barman might have for a boy scout in a tavern calling for a lemonade. It was obvious from the first day of the tour that we are needed in Europe and that no one expects us to dilute our role there. The French, the Germans, NATO, the British, all made this clear. So in planning our long range defence role there are some conclusions about Europe which we should consider here, for we are involved in Europe.
First, NATO is no longer an alliance grouped around the single deterrent power of the United States. It has become a much looser alliance of nuclear powers including the United States, England, France, and perhaps within a decade some others, including Germany. As Woodrow Wilson might put it if he were here, the future of NATO offers open schism openly arrived at. In such a NATO Canada would not likely be required to carry out a nuclear role on the continent of Europe. But we are needed there now, and for some years to come, as much as we have ever been needed by our allies and by the people of the free world.
Second, because no country can defend itself completely against nuclear weapons, no country will invite nuclear war. The age of limited risk has passed. The age of unlimited and incalculable risk is here. As long as Europe is able to threaten instant nuclear retaliation, as it does now, there will be no war with Russia, for no Russian leader will deliberately risk the instant destruction of the great cities of his beloved homeland. There is real hope for mankind in this fact, for man is learning that nuclear war is suicidal.
Third, with Europe in nuclear balance we may expect to see the cold war fought all over the globe in revolutions, uprisings and petty wars of attrition everywhere. This is where our next and most vital role may be, and it is going to be a conventional and a dirty one.
Mr. Chairman, in Cologne on Sunday we went to the great cathedral which our bombers had spared during world war II, just as theirs spared Saint Paul's and Westminster Abbey, and we heard the choir sing Martin

Supply-National Defence Luther's great hymn Ein Feste Burg, which I suppose has been sung there for 400 years:
A mighty fortress is our God
A bulwark never failing,
Our helper He amid the flood,
Of mortal ills prevailing.
Hearing it, Mr. Chairman, I felt that we were learning to live in the nuclear age and that there is no reason why Luther's hymn should not be sung in that same cathedral for the next 400 years.

Mr. Chairman, while we are studying the estimates of the Department of National Defence, I wish to state that I deeply regret the decision of the Canadian government, which asked the United Kingdom to build three submarines at a cost of $33 million. Had this order been placed with our own shipyards, it would have provided jobs for 10,000 workers in Canada. The authorities of Davie Shipbuilding in Lauzon feel that the company might have built the three submarines with slight differences in measurements, as they would probably have been somewhat longer and broader, but their quality would have been better, and they would not have cost more than $58 million.
In my estimation, it would have been a clever move on the government's part, since it would have allowed the Canadian shipyards to give jobs to our workers.
What surprises me also is that Japan filed tenders and offered to build the three submarines at a lower cost than the United Kingdom, without any loss in quality.
I would have liked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), or his associate minister to give us some explanations on that point. I am sorry to see that the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin) is not here. I am told he is in Montreal at present. I would have liked him to submit to the house a report on the interviews he had with the various representatives of Quebec shipyards, these same representatives who came recently to Ottawa to protest against the decision taken by the Canadian government to build frigates outside Canada.
I have here a press dispatch published some days ago by he Devoir and which says:
Sorel workers protest
Workers of the Sorel shipyards are angry at the government's decision to have three submarines built in the United Kingdom. "The contract is for $33 million, and that money will come from the Canadian taxpayers," said this week end Mr. Leandre Provost, secretary of the national shipyard workers' union, affiliated to the confederation of national trade unions.
"By this decision, the government is taking away jobs from Canadian workers and increasing unemployment and job insecurity," he added.


The article continues:
Hecently, Ottawa cancelled the building of eight frigates in Canada which were to cost $452 million.
I feel, Mr. Chairman, that this decision will certainly not help the Canadian government to reduce unemployment.
May I also point out that we would have liked the Minister of National Defence to refer to the position of French speaking Canadians in our armed forces, as well as about what he intends to do to improve the situation at the College Militaire Royale de Saint-Jean.

Here are the statistics for the year 1958:

3.	That the Royal Military College of St. Johns be officially affiliated to the University of Montreal so that the curriculum be perfectly suited to the previous training of the cadets.
4.	That the full course be given at St. Johns, without the cadets having to go to Kingston to complete their studies.

6.	That the Department of National Defence make sure that all military and semi-military establishments be provided with school facilities for the benefit of the children of French speaking and Roman Catholic servicemen who are stationed there.
Mr. Chairman, I have learned that the children of our French speaking, Roman Catholic servicemen in Europe have to follow a school program practically identical to the one which exists in Ontario; in other words, the teaching is the same as in that province. In my opinion, this is a serious disadvantage. It is important that children of French Canadian families in Europe should enjoy an education system similar to the Quebec system, because when these students come back to Canada they are confused since they must

continue their studies in colleges in the province of Quebec after receiving in Europe an education patterned after the Ontario school system. So, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the Department of National Defence should take the necessary steps to correct the existing situation.
Mr. Chairman, allow me to say a few words about the countries which are producing nuclear weapons and the countries which are accepting them.
In my opinion, to ensure peace and prevent world destruction, it is essential that the noncommitted nations, that is those countries which do not produce or store nuclear warheads, reinforce by all possible means the United Nations efficiency in their efforts to maintain peace and security.
Drastic action should be undertaken as soon as possible by such nations. They must present a united front so as to grant extraordinary powers to the United Nations disarmament committee, which comprises at present 18 nations. That committee should, in my opinion, include a greater number of non-committed nations in order to force by all possible means both eastern and western powers to destroy and ban their nuclear weapons.
The nations having and producing nuclear weapons have already committed dreadful crimes against humanity. The after-effects of nuclear tests have shocking crimes to their credit, particularly the pollution of the earth waters and of the air, which will result for generations to come in food pollution.
The so-called nuclear powers which accept on their territory nuclear warheads produced by other great powers are criminal accomplices and jeopardize the future of mankind; they also become satellites of a foreign power.
Mr. Chairman, it is truly shameful that only a short while after the signing of the thermonuclear test ban treaty, which does not apply though to underground testing, certain countries including Canada have accepted the stockpiling of nuclear warheads.
Geographically speaking, Canada is squeezed between the two great nuclear powers. In case of a nuclear war, we would be the target of the enemy and our cities would be destroyed.
At present, radioactive fallout which is perhaps greater in Canada than anywhere else in the world, contaminates our foodstuff.
It seems a good thing for mankind to sign a nuclear test ban treaty since nuclear weap-one have already been tested and proven.
The only logical means of ensuring the security of mankind is to give the disarmament committee full powers to stop countries from producing nuclear weapons and to force them to get rid of the stockpiles located 28902-5-354
Supply-National Defence on their own territory or that of their satellites as Canada is about to become one. If it had extraordinary powers, the committee could not only make inspections but also find means of destroying those stockpiles by burying them under the polar ice-cap for instance. An agreement could be reached whereby that territory would become the property of the United Nations.
The world might well rejoice because certain nuclear powers have signed a partial test ban treaty. It still remains however, that those countries are going to keep up the production of nuclear weapons and continue doing research work in their atomic laboratories for military purposes.
An embargo on nuclear weapons would result in a sharp reduction of military expenditures which could be earmarked for peaceful undertakings.
As far as military expenditures are concerned, it is estimated at present that all countries of the world spend approximately $120 billion a year for military purposes. This amount represents at least two thirds of the national income of all underdeveloped countries, and about 85 per cent of this total is spent by seven countries: the U.S.S.R., the United States, Great Britain, France, western Germany, communist China and Canada.
As for the use for peaceful purposes of resources released by disarmament, no country should fear it will not be able to put those resources to a useful purpose. Actually, there are so many ways of using those resources, that the real problem would consist in establishing a priority scale. Among those needs, one might mention the increase of individual consumption, more particularly in underdeveloped countries, the expansion of productive capacity, and investments in the social field, like education, housing, health and purely scientific research.
I appeal to all non-committed powers to launch a crusade to that end in the United Nations, in order to rid humanity of nuclear arms and thus ensure an era of true peace in the world.

Justice, right, reason and humanity-demand- that nuclear weapons should be banned.
and further:
Peace is a right, peace is a duty, peace is a gift.

I have been listening to some of the speeches and exposes made here this afternoon, tonight and yesterday on the subject of national defence. I listened attentively to the speeches made by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra tonight and by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. To his last citation concerning Pope John I could also add maybe that peace is also a state of mind and that you have to make it; it does not just lie on a platter. This is probably the main line on which to conduct the expose I want to give.
I should like to divide it into two sections. First, the position of Canada toward the allied forces in NATO, and the others, and then, Canada and its internal defence. We have an obligation toward our NATO allies, not only because we say we are Canadians and belong to the western bloc but because we owe those countries the help they may need and which we can spare them. It is not only the help we may give them, but also the help we might receive from them. Our participation in NATO is not only important on the military side.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra tonight gave an explanation of his tour with the NATO parliamentarians this fall and I came to the conclusion that he had probably attended the military meetings more than the others. I may say there is a defence committee, an educational and technical committee, a political committee and an economic committee. He was on the defence committee. What I wish to stress tonight is the role of the economic committee, which also belongs in the NATO alliance, and Canada's participation in that field of activity. From the military point of view, as far as I can gather on these NATO conferences and trips such as we had last summer, Canada is well accepted and greeted by the European countries in this

NATO alliance. Militarily, yes, but also economically and, maybe further than that, morally. I think one of the greatest forces in the possession of our European allies and friends is the moral support and the hope we give to these people. They feel secure. They feel there is a friendship on the part of Canada, and also, necessarily, on the part of the United States. I am thinking particularly now of Norway and Turkey which are among the NATO allies. Turkey is a country which shares one of its boundaries with Russia. Norway has one part of its boundary on the Russian border. Its people watched what happened in Finland not long ago. They need Canada, morally and also as friends, so as to feel that they are not alone. Friendship is not necessarily extended by military force on the soil of others.
I have had an opportunity to speak with parliamentarians from some of these countries. I think their greatest hope is that Canada will stay friends with them and continue to give support to them. As far as military weapons are concerned, we have not brought in too much artillery to those countries, but we have brought them hope that we would help them in case of an attack by the eastern bloc. When I consider the military aspect, I ask the minister to study the situation of Turkey at this moment, a country which has been drained of its economic resources by a succession of wars for the past thousand years. Turkey has been fighting ever since that country existed. What has it brought? Go to that country and there is one thing that strikes you: If 10 per cent of the national defence budgets in the past had been devoted to developing the country it would not be in the economic state in which we find it today. You cannot drain a country of its resources through continual warfare. I have never known a war bring prosperity to any country; you always pay in the long run. Turkey is one country that has had its share of war and realizes it now. It does not depend on Canada for artillery, but like many other NATO countries it depends on Canada for the economic help we can supply. That has been stressed and I have noted this fact on different occasions. It came to the surface in the economic committee. I found this to be true also in the technical and educational field. These countries need the economic help of Canada and also of the United States because they are all at a low level in that field, in fact possibly more so than they are militarily.
Canada cannot do otherwise but help these people, but we need not necessarily do so with artillery. It would be too expensive for Canada to try to follow some of our allies into

the nuclear race. There is one thing that Canada has to be on guard against, that we do not find ourselves in the economic situation Turkey is in now by trying to compete, or by trying to follow along in the nuclear race which is going faster than we can follow it.
We can play a role more or less like Sweden, which is situated between Finland and Norway, is playing, by adopting a neutral attitude toward the military side of things. Mind you, the eastern bloc is possibly more concerned with Sweden being neutral than with Canada being on one side. They understand the position of Sweden and respect it just as we do. Sweden is gaining the confidence of other countries. It has the confidence of Norway, its neighbour, and it has not furnished Norway with any military equipment or nuclear arms of any kind. Sweden escaped the last two world wars and its economic situation is possibly one of the best in Europe. Canada should follow this example of not going too far, so far as military warfare is concerned, but rather emphasizing more the economic help we can give to other countries based on our natural resources and the richness of Canada's own soil.
There is another aspect I want to consider, the internal defence of Canada, with which we possibly feel more at home. The scope is not so wide. We have two kinds of internal defence to face, that of wartime and that of peacetime. I agree that we do need a defence for our country, but in saying that I must also say that we have to have a defence that we can afford. It is all very nice to say that we like the Bomarc, we like the Honest John, we like the CF-104 or the Voodoo, but by the time we get them paid for they may be obsolete. The CF-104 was a very effective weapon, but the United States has since developed other weapons which are causing the CF-104 to become more and more obsolete every day, and possibly by the time we get our CF-104's paid for they will be obsolete. They may be paid for on the one hand, but we still have the debt on the other hand.
So far as Canada's own defence on our own soil is concerned I suggest that what we need is small effective groups of well trained men with up to date, modern, highly flexible, conventional arms, something that we can afford. We think about nuclear war sometimes but I think some of the world leaders fear it more than we do because they realize the repercussions of such a war more than members of this house or ordinary Canadian citizens. Canada cannot afford a nuclear war. We cannot afford to get the military equipment necessary to fight one, so we have to get what we 28902-5-3541
Supply-National Defence can afford, mobile forces of men well equipped with conventional, up to date arms for rescue purposes and for defensive and offensive needs that may arise. If we have a nuclear war I do not know what we could do with what we have by way of nuclear arms now, so that it seems to me that rather than preparing ourselves to face a nuclear war we should prepare ourselves to face an ordinary conventional war and equip our forces accordingly.
But what about the potential of trained men we have in the country in peacetime? Are we going to have them continue to shine their buttons and march every day of the week? That is all very well in giving them their basic training, but can we not find something else for them to do that would help the country in peacetime? We could train the men in all three of our military forces to help in the case of national emergencies, regional emergencies, conflagrations, which we often have in Canada, and in the case of floods which we also have in Canada. It is true that the army already provides help. The army did so in the sorrowful event that took place when the DC-8F crashed near Montreal. The army was on the spot. But we could use more of the men in the army, navy and air force if they were also trained in that way. We could use them a great deal more. We could give our soldiers specialized training in the commercial field and in other fields. We could give them specialized trade training so that if they did come out of the armed forces they would have a specialty. If there was a war we could then recall these men with their specialties and bring them back into the forces, but in the meantime they would not be wasting their own time and the country's money.
I was looking at an article, which I am sorry I do not have with me, but which dealt with something the minister said and which I also heard about while at the NATO meetings. I refer to the suggestion of bringing all three military forces more or less under one command. The navy, the army and the air force would all be on one base working together and there would be no preferences as between one force or the other. I have heard the minister say that he would like to unify the forces and more or less assimilate them. This might be good in one sense and bad in another. I have heard both sides of the question from military men themselves. This is very suitable for basic training in peacetime. You can afford to have a little conflict, a little bit of friction, between officers in peacetime. However, when war is declared there is no time to have conflict or sparks flying between your own allies,
5560	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-National Defence between your own generals. They have to have a common goal. This is no time to have prejudice against one or the other. This is no time to say the navy is better than the army or the army is better than the air force.
It is bad in this sense, Mr. Chairman, that today the tendency is toward specialization. We have had several boat crashes on the St. Lawrence seaway, but these accidents have not been as prevalent as the ones which occur on our highways. I must say that I feel secure when I get on a boat and I know there is a naval captain in command. I feel just as secure when I get on an airplane-
A ship, please.
Hear, hear.

I know the hon. member was a naval captain who knew his job. I would feel secure if I were to get on a ship and he were the captain, but I would not feel so secure if he were the pilot of an airplane. There are technicians who develop skills in their own fields. If they do not develop these skills, they are not appointed to the air force, the army or the navy. We have to have specialization in machinery, in artillery in the type of warfare that is waged today. We need that specialization. I do not see how you can get specialists when you are going to combine all the forces.
Another point, Mr. Chairman, is the question of promotion. I might be an army officer and I might have a liking for my army colleagues. I see an air force officer who is eligible for promotion and who has the same rank as the army officer. You can be as honest as you want but you can also have a little bit of reconnaissance towards the one fellow. You may push the army fellow, and shortly this will be a cause of friction and the sparks are going to be flying. This is a question that has been discussed between military men themselves. Last summer we were talking to the allied forces in Europe and there was an observation made to this effect. I think the Minister of National Defence should take a little bit of time to inquire into that problem and he may revise some of his ideas on the subject. He did make these comments some time ago.
If you unify the forces, Mr. Chairman, you put everybody on the same footing. I do not see how you can apply this principle to normal human beings without having them feel that they are just a small cog in one big wheel. If we are going to have an effective defence program, we have to have every soldier, from the private to the general, feeling that he is a useful member of the army.

I know, Mr. Chairman, that the minister has listened to quite a few speeches. I hope that he will take the best out of them. If I have made any small offering, I am glad I did. However, until somebody tells me I am wrong, I will feel the same way, Mr. Chairman. Before I close, I should like to tell the minister something about national defence problems in my own region. Thetford Mines has been asking since the last war for "menage militaire". Since 1914, two regiments have gone overseas from this region. We were talking about specialization and having competent men available for our armed forces. The asbestos mine in Thetford Mines would be willing to insert a clause in the contract of their employees that all the engineers working for the mine would have to spend some time at a military base before they would be employed. In this way, you would have engineers with military training. If a mining company such as this is willing to co-operate with the government, then I think the government should give some consideration to co-operating on a request of this sort. There are young people in that region who are willing to join the armed forces of Canada but who cannot do so at the moment because the local regiment is training outside in the snow in the wintertime. If it gets too cold they clean out a garage and train there.
You cannot interest anybody in a military career by giving him a glimpse of such a situation. I would urge the minister to look into that situation and do what he can to rectify it. I urge the minister to give consideration to the establishment of a versatile military force with conventional arms. This force could be used for the protection of the country in the event of an emergency. I think we should be proud to be a member of NATO, yes, but we should help the underdeveloped countries economically. I think we would have a stronger alliance, Mr. Chairman, if we had a little understanding instead of having fear. I think the greatest deterrent force is understanding and comprehension and not necessarily military power.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to trouble the committee for a very few moments. Perhaps I might be excused having regard to the fact that the Hagersville army camp that is to be closed falls within the ambit of the riding which I have the honour to represent. In the circumstances, I feel it is my responsibility to state plainly and frankly my position in this matter. I cannot conceal from myself that I am torn between the competing demands of my constituency on the one hand and of the national economy and national defence policy on the other. I acknowledge frankly that public opinion in my constituency

is acutely alive to the implications of the minister's announcement. That announcement, I also acknowledge, will set in motion a trying train of consequences both for the riding and, if I may be permitted to say so, for myself.
I realize that in the displacement of these workers some of the older men will be forced to go into a labour market to seek job opportunities where the scale is tilted in favour of younger men. It is in that atmosphere and in the light of these competing demands that I have to weigh the government's decision.
I must state that as soon as I heard the decision I went to the minister and, in the hope that he might delay the necessity of closing the camp, I asked him frankly if there was not some purpose that the Hagersville camp in the present circumstances or in the foreseeable circumstances could usefully serve. The minister, with equal candour, advised me that this camp was no longer essential, and its closure would save the Canadian taxpayers $1.5 million annually, and those savings would not include the cost of maintenance of the physical assets of the camp.
I realize economy must be fundamental in government decisions. It would indeed be easy to shape government policy if we did not have to consider money. Mr. Chairman, it would be easy and attractive for me to be seduced by personal and parochial considerations and therefore abuse the minister with the hope of advancing personal political fortunes. But I would only be deluding myself and my constituents to the realities of the need for economy and to the shifting circumstances of our defence policy.
Every unnecessary expenditure of the tax dollar does a great injury to the country, and a very grave injury. My mind was moved and my opinion was influenced by the knowledge that the minister had sincerely, searchingly and thoroughly examined the situation with the assistance of competent staff. There are increasing demands on the government for more money for social legislation, demands that cannot go long unanswered. There are increasing demands for more money from the provinces, and for a larger share in the tax sharing revenues. In short, we must cut the coat to suit the cloth. Indeed there is a duty upon the minister to cut the coat to suit the cloth, provided of course that the coat covers the wearer.
I should also say I have personally inspected the Hagersville camp on a number of occasions, and this camp has lived in the shadow of this decision for the past two years. I trust my hon. friends across the floor will acquit me of incivility if I draw their attention to the fact that it was only last
Supply-National Defence September that the former government discharged 40 per cent of all civilian employees in the Hagersville camp. That announcement was met with silence from the supporters of that Conservative administration. I took no satisfaction from that announcement. I had occasion to discuss it then, with the associate minister of defence and I accepted his submission that he was moved by the same consideration that moves the present minister, the necessity for national economy.
In these circumstances, and with the greatest reluctance I accept the decision of the government, but I am bound to say that I hope those who are laid off will not become slaves of this policy of economy. I shall be watching with attention and critical interest to see that the government discharges its obligations to those displaced workers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened very attentively to the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand as he indicated how he was going to bear the burden that is now forced on his shoulders in his own constituency. I wish I could share his views that various alternatives suggested by the minister have had the very careful consideration which he attributes to the minister.
I agree with him that economy is essential in any operation of government. At the same time, when you are dealing with the subject of national defence you have to consider the safety of the Canadian people and the country. Money is required for a vast number of things, for welfare purposes and social security, and we know the provinces are eager for a greater share of tax revenues. All those things are well known to us, but there is an overriding necessity on the part of the government to assure first of all the safety of the country and the survival of the people of the country. Otherwise all these other things count for nought.
Consequently my examination of the proposals put forward by the minister are not restricted to the effect that may be felt in any one particular area, but rather the overall effect with regard to national defence. The fact that I remained fairly silent today is no indication that I am any more favourably disposed to the lack of policies of the present government on defence than I was yesterday, but I wanted to hear from the Associate Minister of National Defence and I wanted to see what the attitude of the Prime Minister would be today.
I asked him one or two questions on orders of the day and he rested upon the collective responsibility of the cabinet, which is normal, and consequently he accepts full responsibility for the policies, or lack of policies, now being pursued by the Minister of National

Supply-National Defence Defence. I wanted to come to the rescue of the Minister of National Defence. He is under the gun. I think the Minister of Finance has a pistol at his head and has said to him, "Now, unless I am going to be ruined again twice within 12 months, with the largest deficit in Canada's history, you must cut down."
Every minister of finance looks with a jaundiced eye at the expenditures of the Department of National Defence, but I am surprised that the Prime Minister has not supported the Minister of National Defence. Why did he not resist the pressure from the Minister of Finance, unless the Minister of National Defence is going to say that the ideas he has put before us are entirely his own? If they are, then of course he is open to even greater criticism.
Why did the Prime Minister not protect the minister and the associate minister from the ravening hand of the Minister of Finance? Of course cabinet ministers are expendable and there are other people in the Liberal party who are ready, willing and able to take over at any given moment. So, I appreciate some of the difficulties that face the Minister of National Defence, but I question again these half-baked solutions that have been put before us today.
Yesterday I heard the Minister of National Defence praise the Associate Minister of National Defence. I do not know why he would do it. We accept him in the position which he occupies, but the minister asked us to consider how hard worked the associate minister was and what a great piece of work he was doing. Then today the associate minister asked us to appreciate fully the hard work the Minister of National Defence is doing. So, they patted each other on the back, asked for our sympathy and hoped that we would understand their position. Certainly it was all completely unnecessary. Cabinet ministers have a job to perform; they do not have to be thanking each other for the assistance they receive, or patting each other on the back.
When the Associate Minister of National Defence was speaking I heard this phrase through the translation system. He said, "What we are attempting to do is a housecleaning operation". I wrote it down because it differed a bit from what the Minister of National Defence said yesterday; he said it was a housekeeping operation. If there is housecleaning to be done, I think it should start in the ministerial offices. Let us get things cleaned up there first, because they are certainly on the wrong track with the things they are doing. The Associate Minister of National Defence told us of the tremendous work that is going on: Studies in depth, he

said. There are these vast studies in depth going on. I have never been quite sure how you make a study in depth. I suppose the Minister of National Defence and the associate minister have just been skating over the surface all these years and now they have discovered that there is more to it than met their eye when they were sitting over here in opposition. At any rate, they have entered upon studies in depth and all sorts of these studies are going on. The next thing we know, they will be having week-end seminars to determine what is to be done with regard to national defence.
I think all this is a bit of nonsense, putting up a pretence that this is a tremendous problem that nobody had ever looked at before but now these bright people are really making a study in depth and are going to find out what has been happening in the Department of National Defence. Of course they had a lot to learn and I hope they are learning, but I am disappointed that the learning is not proceeding very rapidly. Then there was talk about these comprehensive surveys that are going on. The associate minister said he doubted whether there were three people in the House of Commons who understood the magnitude of the work that was being done by the Minister of National Defence in these comprehensive surveys. I thought there were more than that within the Liberal party who should be given credit for some sensibility with regard to these matters. He was not very favourably disposed to his own members.
Mr. Chairman, it is not good enough. The associate minister-I am sorry he is not here because I dislike speaking about him in his absence, but we may not be back on these estimates again-said that I was now exhorting the government to accept nuclear weapons. I have been doing no such thing at all. All I am saying to them is, get on with the job. This government said that the minute they were elected they were going to make all the necessary arrangements so that the nuclear weaponry would be available to our forces. My accusation is that eight months have gone by and they have not completed the task. I do not know what the answer is to this except a careless indifference to defence matters. If this was what should have been done-and this is what they said last year-why have they not got on with the job? There is not a thing for the Bomarcs; they are sitting there unarmed, gaping up to the sky. If an attack occurred tomorrow, nothing would happen. This is what they were saying last winter, and eight months have gone by and nothing has been done.

They said our Voodoo 'planes will not be fully effective unless they have nuclear weapons. What have they done about it? They say, "Oh, well, you have to sign a general agreement with the United States, and then a technical agreement", and apparently they have done those things; the dates were given to us, August and October. But they are postponing letting out tenders for the missile dumps because it is not the appropriate time to do it. I would be willing to wager that a year will go by before nuclear weapons are available to the Voodoos. This is the speed at which this government is moving.
Then the associate minister was talking about the air division over in Europe and there was an exchange of remarks with regard to the missile dumps. I interrupted the associate minister when he was talking about the missile dumps and asked him a question. He spoke to his mentor about it, and I jotted down what he said. The answer was: "My colleague informs me that the infrastructure that was being built was held up because of the fact that the government"-that is, the Conservative government-"had not agreed to sign any agreement with the United States". I said: "I regret that I cannot accept that statement". The Minister of National Defence said: "It is true, whether you accept it or not". Then I said: "It is not true", and he said: "Certainly it is". This was just one of those friendly exchanges across the floor of the house.
Let us examine the facts, Mr. Chairman. I think it is regrettable when any hon. member misleads the House of Commons. There is perhaps a heavier responsibility on a minister of the crown. The missile bases by the air base at Zweibrucken were under construction last winter. The contract was let by the NATO authorities. This work is being done under the infrastructure arrangement; the associate minister said so today. I saw the commencement of the construction of the missile dump at Zweibrucken in February of this year. I asked about the delay, and the answer was that the German contractor was unfamiliar with the pouring of cement in very severe winter weather-and it was a very severe winter-and there would be perhaps a six months delay in the construction of the missile dump. No agreement had been signed between Canada and the United States. Since that time the construction work has gone on. The associate minister so informed us today, and he said the work would not be completed until perhaps next spring or later. Then he disclosed the fact that the technical agreement with the United States has not yet been signed and may be signed soon.
Supply-National Defence
Where does this leave the Minister of National Defence? He said the delay in the construction of the missile dump at Zweibrucken and the other station in Germany was due to the fact that we have not signed an agreement with the United States. He has not yet signed an agreement with the United States, and the construction was under way last winter and is going on now. I say that the minister misled the house when he said this delay was due to the fact that we had not signed an agreement. Exactly as I said last winter, this was a NATO obligation. NATO headquarters had to make the arrangement. It has nothing to do with Canada at all. We do not own any territory there whatsoever. It is German territory and the agreement was with the Germans. I hope that settles this particular matter and I express the hope that the minister will not continue to mislead the house in this way.
Mr. Chairman, the importance of the subject of national defence is such that there are quite a number of things I would like to say and some answers I would like to receive with regard to this particular subject. I was disposed yesterday to move along very quickly with the estimates of this department, until I heard, examined and considered the statement made yesterday by the Minister of National Defence. I think the disturbing part of his statement, ignoring for the moment the fact that he enunciated no satisfactory over-all policy, was the announcement of the reduction in the reserve forces of Canada. That reduction will heavily hit the reserve forces of the navy, the army and the air force.
I am much more familiar with the reserve forces of the army than with the other two forces, because of 15 years experience with the militia of Canada. I know the minister does not think very much of the militia or he would not take this action. He has an impression, that is shared by other people in Canada, that the militia is an expensive operation and is ineffective. I spent 11 years between the two wars in the militia and I know the attitude. True, there was a depression at that time, but even when the depression was easing and the threat of war from Hitler was hanging over the world the government of Mackenzie King took no effective action on the militia-the non-permanent, active militia. For 11 years I was a member of that militia, but when the second world war broke out the same thing happened as had happened in the first world war: The first people to go to the colours and swear in were members of the militia. In Canada on August 31, 1939, when war was imminent,
10,000	militiamen were enrolled and were doing guard duty on the canals, railway

Supply-National Defence bridges and places which required security protection. In September, 1939 in the city of Winnipeg-and I speak of things of which I am familiar-the Fort Garry Horse, the Winnipeg Grenadiers and the Camerons were enrolling their officers and men. Nearly all the officers and all the senior N.C.O.'s in those three regiments were from the militia. That is the response the militia makes in time of trouble. When the Korean war broke out in 1950 I stood in the armouries at Winnipeg when a troop from the Fort Garry Horse volunteered to serve in the composite force being drawn up by the Department of National Defence.
This business of writing off the militia of Canada completely shocks me. I wonder if these comprehensive studies in depth of the Minister of National Defence have embraced this absolute and worth-while masterpiece by Dr. Stanley of Kingston entitled: "Canada's Soldiers, 1604-1954," which gives the story of three and a half centuries of Canadian militiamen. We have a tremendous background of service to our country. The essential activity of the militia in the 18th and 19th centuries was matched again in the 20th. Why is this Minister of National Defence writing down the militia of Canada? Does he know anything about the history of our country and the history of the militia? In 1840 the militia of Upper Canada showed a strength of 248 battalions, of Lower Canada 178, all told about 230,000 men. That was mostly on paper; it was a muster which they had each year. This is what Dr. Stanley said about it in his book:
The great advantage of the old compulsory militia system was a purely moral one, the fact that It brought home to every adult male and many an adolescent youth the idea that he was by virtue of his citizenship a militiaman, to whom the country had the right to look for its defence in time of need.
What was true in 1840 is true today in 1963. Why should not everyone in this country be prepared to serve his country? What is wrong with our young men joining the militia and, as some of them do, maintain an interest in it for 20 or 30 years? It is good for them and for their country. We owe more to our country than just the ordinary civilian service, important as that is.
I say that the minister has overlooked the history of this country and has downgraded the militia, and he will destroy the morale of our militiamen. It is hard enough to keep it up; if you weaken the force it will be very hard to sustain morale. Under our regime we were attempting to enlarge the militia because the two ministers of national defence who preceded me had an understanding of the militia, and I supported them in everything they did or said about it. The present

minister does not appreciate the militia and he is ruining it. This is the annihilation of the militia of Canada. He is going to stand down, as somebody said this afternoon, four out of ten of the men serving. It means cutting out four out of ten regiments or battalions. This will have a shattering effect in community after community in Canada where people have gladly given this type of service.
Over and above that-and this is even more serious, as mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary North-the training of the militia in the last few years has been toward the question of survival. And let us be realistic and practical about it; much as we deplore war and do not want to see it, we still have to be ready for every type of emergency. We have, of course, to have our strike forces and our men ready and active in the field; and you have to have reserves behind them. But in this age of nuclear war you also have to do something about civil defence or survival operations. Let the minister answer this question: What is he going to do about the 265 columns which have been prepared for civil defence organized into 66 mobile groups? In this age, when the fear overhanging the people of the world is nuclear war launched by missiles against which there is no defence, all we can look forward to is proper survival operations afterwards, and for that we are dependent on the armed forces and on the militia. Because trained, disciplined bodies of men know how to act in time of emergency. We had that situation at the time of the flood in Winnipeg in 1950 when the city was in danger of being completely under water. The people called out were the militia. People from the militia took full charge. I worked for ten nights on the dikes under the command of a major from the militia. You have to have organization, men with training to conduct operations of that nature. There are always events happening in Canada where military organization is essential to assist civilians who are ready, willing and anxious to assist but need to have some direction and some organization so that their efforts are not wasted.
This is what bothers me and it is why I asked the Prime Minister today, who has the overriding responsibility for the protection of the people of Canada-the emergency measures organization, civil defence and survival operations all come under the Prime Minister of the country, and he gets assistance from the Minister of National Defence-
Not any longer.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The minister says not any longer; there has been a shift of that to someone else. But that does not absolve the

Prime Minister from the primary responsibility. He is the person to look to, if this is what is going to happen. Has the Prime Minister agreed to this reduction in the militia? Has he agreed to cutting this organization almost in half, when its main duty in the last few years has been connected with survival operations? This is why I am so concerned over this matter. I think the militia, together with the reserve for the navy and the air force, is essential to assist the service in time of war. But we are faced with other possibilities and we must be ready for them. Unless there are trained, organized bodies of men, what are we to do? It does not matter how much training we may have had as individuals; we are just a group of civilians, a crowd, a mob, unless there are disciplined men who are able to take charge, give instructions and direct operations.
Why has the Minister of National Defence slaughtered the militia? What is he going to save? About $15 million. It is a worthy objective, to effect economies, but let us have the economies in the right place. None of us can foresee the future and we do not know exactly the nature of the holocaust which would occur in the event of a nuclear war. But we have some idea from experiences in the second world war and later, and as sensible people we have to make some provision. We are responsible for the younger generation of this country and for the children, and nothing can be done unless there is an organization. We spent many hours and days when we were the government of this country, trying to work out planned emergency measures. It is not easy, but an organization was gradually being built up. I realize there is not a great deal of public interest in many of the cities of this country with regard to this matter. But that does not absolve the government or the Minister of National Defence from taking action. It does not matter what the degree of public interest may be. There is a job to be done and it rests with the Minister of National Defence to find a means of carrying it out. Having worked this organization up to a fairly competent level the minister now proposes to cut it down and destroy it.
This is not good enough for the Canadian people and this is the most serious accusation I am making against the Prime Minister of this country and the Minister of National Defence. In their avid desire to save money here and some money there, they have forgotten the safety of the Canadian people. I should like the minister tonight to tell us he intends to review this program, to consult with his colleagues and with the Prime Minister and, perhaps, withhold this proposed 28902-5-355
Supply-National Defence destruction of the survival operations program for this country. I am quite prepared to pause at this moment and await an answer from the Minister of National Defence with regard to this matter.

I hope to be able to answer some of the questions which have been raised by hon. gentlemen and then, perhaps, we might pass item one and go on to the detailed items upon which some of the other questions which members of the committee may have in their minds can be answered.
At the outset, I should like to explain the absence of the associate minister this evening. He has gone to Montreal to address the 50th anniversary dinner of the C.O.T.C. of the University of Montreal. In recognition of the brilliant service of thousands of officers who have graduated from that university to serve in our armed forces throughout the years we agreed it was right for the associate minister to fulfil that engagement. May I join in congratulations to the University of Montreal contingent?
I regret the hon. member for Villeneuve is not here but perhaps I might reply briefly to a question he raised in respect to Mr. J. A. Lavoie and his mining claim on lands at Senneterre. The property involved in these claims comprises the lands which form R.C.A.F. station Senneterre. These lands together with other properties required for defence purposes were made available to the Department of National Defence by arrangement with Mr. Duplessis, former premier of Quebec. As required, this department advised Mr. Duplessis of the land requirement at Senneterre on August 10 and on August 11, 1950. However, the provincial department of lands and forests were unaware of the recording of D.N.D. requirements and on 25 October 1950 issued a mining licence. Later, when Mr. Duplessis was informed of the double interest in the lands, he expressed the view that no difficulty would be experienced by D.N.D. as conflict would be obviated by the operation of the requirement that the mining licensee must have consent of the proprietor to go on the land.
It is interesting to observe that the subject lands had been explored and prospected for over 30 years with no active interest by any prospector until the date following D.N.D.'s survey. Further, the application for a mining licence covered precisely the land that had been delineated by D.N.D. as the site for station Senneterre, and following a reduction of the defence department's requirement for land, a similar reduction was requested in the extent of the mining licence properties.
Since 1952, Mr. Lavoie has made repeated representations to the department through

Supply-National Defence each succeeding member of parliament and through the offices of solicitors. In each instance the department has set out its position and invited Mr. Lavoie to come forward with a reasonable and practical exploratory program which could be authorized or, alternatively, to present his claim to the court for determination of its validity. Mr. Lavoie refuses or is unable to do either.
The hon. member for Vancouver East read into the record yesterday some figures with respect to NATO. I expect there was a misunderstanding involved in them and, consequently, I should like to take this opportunity to correct the record. The hon. member referred to the costs of the brigade and the air division, comprising approximately 6,500 servicemen each, as being from $350 million to $465 million in each of the last five years. The cost figures used by the member appear to be those tabled in this house but I wish to point out that they include the cost of the ships and aircraft assigned to the supreme allied commander, the expenditures for mutual aid including contributions to infrastructure and NATO budgets, as well as the costs of the brigade and the air division.
The hon. member for Calgary North wished to have some further information with reference to the closing down of R.C.A.F. station, Calgary. I regret he is not here at this moment, but I may say that the flying field at this station, is a small one, built during the second world war, which cannot be used by the Tudor jet trainer to be introduced in 1964 in place of the Harvards. It would therefore be necessary to spend several millions of dollars on a major runway reconstruction project to continue the use of this field and the inherent facilities associated with it.
As the amount of repair and overhaul business available from R.C.A.F. operations in Canada has been substantially reduced with the discontinuance of NATO aircrew training and the reduction in the number of aircraft in the air defence system, it would be uneconomic to spend large sums on this airfield to maintain a repair facility at this location. These repairs can be undertaken at considerably less overhead cost by other arrangements.

Would the minister permit me to ask a question? It has to do with Pen-hold. The hon. gentleman's colleague, in reply to the Leader of the Opposition, said the decision as far as Penhold was concerned was final. At page 3204 of Hansard the minister gave the impression that before a decision of this nature was made the matter would be referred to the defence committee. Was the matter referred to the defence committee and were witnesses called before his colleague

made the statement today that the decision as far as Penhold is concerned is final and that ends it?
I would have to check the reference the hon. member has made because I am sure I gave no undertaking I would refer the matter to the defence committee.
I wonder whether the minister would allow me to put it on the record?
You can send it over and I will take a look at it later.
If you really want it on the record now is the time to put on the record.
After I have finished you can put it on the record.
May I ask the minister a question?

Would the hon. member mind waiting until we get down to the details and I have the officials in front of me? I can then answer these questions in greater detail.
The hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) asked if we would permit former members of the naval reserve to use naval facilities if there is no expense to the crown. The question arises whether in fact this can be done within the premise as he has stated it. Presumably in order to use facilities, equipment would be required. If equipment is required certainly there would be maintenance costs involved. If maintenance is involved there are costs to the crown. However, this is an interesting suggestion and we will certainly take it under advisement and see if there is any possibility that it could be done within the terms of reference suggested.
The hon. member for Pontiac-Temisca-mingue chastened me for saying first of all that the situation with respect to the air division in Europe is not satisfactory and then not doing something about it. He says I have a responsibility to settle it and to settle it immediately. I intend to do something about it, Mr. Chairman. However, there are two considerations. First of all there is the defence committee report which I suspect may have something to say about the air division and the roles it undertakes in the defence of Europe. Second, any change in configuration in the air division requires consultation with our NATO allies. Under these circumstances it is just not possible for me to make an announcement at this time, even if that were advisable.
He also raised the question of the possible use of nuclear weapons and he gave the impression, which he said he had gleaned from his tour, that these weapons might be used

by a brigade commander and presumably without any prior political authorization. This impression must be corrected at once because it is not in accordance with the facts. I am surprised that after all that has been said about the control of the use of atomic weapons some members still seem to be in doubt about the conditions under which military plans for their use are determined. I am sure it is realized by now that American weapons which will be available for Canadian forces remain the property of the American government and their ownership is never relinquished by that government.
American law provides that only the President of the United States can release atomic weapons to the American forces or to forces of other countries which have agreed to use them in support of NATO. This decision at the highest political level is a necessary first decision before any weapons can be used.
Once this decision has been taken to release the weapons the decision to use them in NATO is made at the highest level by the supreme allied commander, Europe. This decision is conveyed downward in the case of the Canadian brigade through the northern army group to the brigade commander, and the decision to release is conveyed downward from the senior American commander in Europe through a unique American communications system to the American custodial party, who retain custody of the weapons until they receive the release authority from the President of the United States.
Is the President of the United States the only political authority whose consent must be secured by the chief commander of NATO?

He is the only political authority who can release the weapons for use. After he has released them, whether or not they are used depends upon other considerations and the national forces who are part of-
Are the member nations to be consulted?

Yes, they are. If I may finish the statement perhaps we could come back to that later. Before SACEUR would authorize the use of atomic weapons by forces under his command-I think this is the answer to the hon. member's question-he would require to obtain national agreement from the governments of the forces which would be ordered to use the weapons. It can be seen therefore that the impression that Canadian commanders at brigade or lower levels would on their own authority use atomic weapons just is not so. Any such false impression must have been gathered through misunderstanding of the situation.
