Supply-National Defence
The hon. member for Simcoe North-I regret that he too is not here-raised the question of cadets for the army, navy and air force. In respect of cadets there are no reductions contemplated. However, with regard to the university naval training detachment, the C.O.T.C. and the U.R.T.P. reductions are contemplated. These will be of the order of approximately 50 per cent and the saving will be of the order of $1,400,000 annually. Discussions will be undertaken with the universities as to how this can best be carried out.
A question was raised in respect of search and rescue. Those activities at present carried out at Torbay will be undertaken by the unit at Summerside. This will result in providing adequate service at a considerably reduced cost. The same hon. gentleman asked why the frigates were cancelled before new programs were announced. As I explained earlier, it was necessary to give notice to end uncertainty in respect of a major program. It would have been unfair to a large number of people to have withheld this information once a decision had been taken. No doubt if it had been withheld an outcry would have taken place.
As already announced, we are doing our best to determine our future requirements to the end that new ships can be laid down just as quickly as possible and in order that we can have the best possible equipment for our armed forces. I agree with the hon. member that the emphasis at this moment should be on research in order that we can be sure of just what future requirements are.
He mentioned the NATO antisubmarine warfare research unit and I should like to say a few additional words about that. The SACLANT antisubmarine warfare research centre at La Spezia, Italy, is a NATO research establishment with a scientific staff drawn from NATO countries. This laboratory conducts research in fields of antisubmarine importance, in particular in applied physics, oceanography and operational research. Currently Canada is supplying on loan from the defence research board the leader for the operational research program. In addition, Canada is providing the chairman for the scientific committee of national representatives which advises on the research program to be pursued by this laboratory.
While talking about research I have an announcement which gives me great pleasure. I am sure hon. members will share my pleasure on reading a statement concerning the Alouette by E. M. Cortright, deputy director of the office of space science of the national aeronautics and space administration,

Supply-National Defence published in the special annual NASA issue of the magazine, Missiles and Rockets, November 25, 1963.
The statement reads:
Alouette, the Canadian swept frequency ionospheric top-sounder, has had the best test and flight record of any free world scientific satellite. After well over a year of orbital operation the system is working perfectly and has not even employed any of its redundant systems.
At this stage in the experiment, even though only a small fraction of the available data has been analysed, it is clear that a major advance in our knowledge of electron density distributions in the ionosphere has been achieved.
For your further information, the following is an operation summary for Alouette as of local noon, December 4, 1963:
Number of orbits around the earth 5,888
Number of miles travelled,	169 million
Number of commands executed	15,250
Miles of magnetic tape recordings	3,170
Requirement for spare equipments none
It sounds better than the Bobcat.

You are right.
Now, I should like to deal with some of the major criticisms of my statement. The hon. member for Calgary North said I was irresponsible in proposing the changes I announced yesterday. I do not agree with this judgment.
Oh, oh.
That is the most surprising statement of the session.

On the contrary, I think I would have been irresponsible if I had not undertaken these changes at this time. As a matter of fact, I think some of them might have been implemented several years ago.
Let us put this matter in perspective. Approximately since 1959 the Department of National Defence has had a serious problem. Insufficient money has been available to carry out all of its tasks. Under these circumstances, there were three alternatives available. The first was to get more money from the treasury.
Oh, oh.

I see one of my hon. friends, an ex-minister of finance, chuckling at that suggestion. The second one was to defer procurement and development programs. The third was to effect economies and to get a balance of forces, to provide an acceptable division of expenditures between operation and maintenance and capital programs. For national reasons, more money has not been available. There have been, as hon. members know, a series of very substantial deficits. The present Minister of Finance has stated that we will have a substantial deficit this

year, and I think it is no secret we will have another substantial deficit next year.
Carrying on your tradition.

We are carrying on your tradition. Under the circumstances, it seems unrealistic to expect larger sums of money to be available for defence in the immediate future.
Now, during those years, the option that has been chosen has been the deferment of programs. As a result, we now have an accumulation, a backlog, of about $400 million worth of equipment. If this policy were continued for a few more years, we would have no equipment for our armed forces at all. We would have the best housed, best dressed and best fed but most poorly equipped force in the western world. This is obviously an untenable position. A responsible minister has no real alternative but to reverse this trend. Only in this way can we have not only the best trained but also the best equipped force in the world.
Particular exception has been taken to the reduction in the militia. I am not a historian as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre is. My knowledge of the militia back to 1600 is probably not as thorough as his. I do know, however, the historic part it has played in the recent history of this country, and particularly in the first and second world wars. I do admit that in the first and second world wars, without the non-permanent active militia it would have been impossible to mobilize as we did. It was, in fact, the mobilization basis for two world wars. The situation in 1963, however, is not identical with the situation in 1939. As a matter of fact, it is about a world apart.
Our main activity now is the deterrence of war, the deterrence first of all of nuclear war, second, of a major non-nuclear war, right down through the scale to sub-limital war, insurrection and so on. Through this whole spectrum of deterrence, the greatest weapon available is forces in being. The chances of a long major war comparable to world war II, although it is a possibility, is extremely remote. Consequently, mobilization potential of the type relied on in two world wars now has a much lower priority than forces in being. The choice before us, then, is expenditure on equipment for troops in the front line versus other expenditures such as the militia.
This is the choice. In the present situation, we have a brigade group in Europe in the front line exposed to a well armoured, well equipped enemy force, without adequate equipment. We have two reserve brigades in Canada that are equipped with training

scales only. This decision taken in 1959 seems to me to be untenable. The choice, then, simply is an expenditure on the militia or on proper equipment tor our front line troops.
Will $15 million do it?

No, but it would help. This $15 million would buy a lot of M-113 APC carriers. No one likes to make a decision of this nature because it is tough. Nevertheless, hard decisions have to be made. If there is any one element which seems to be lacking amongst some people in this country at the moment it is a sense of realism. If we are going to be realistic, we have to make hard decisions. Everyone applauds them in theory, but not so much in practice. We are now considering the militia on the basis of what real part it would play in a mobilization potential, and with a priority in the scale of priorities which can be applied against modern strategy.
We are also mindful of its potential role in national survival. I think it is a real consideration because notwithstanding the remote possibility of a thermonuclear holocaust, there is at least a mathematical possibility, and this risk cannot be completely ignored. It is our plan to retain sufficient strength to cope with this requirement. It will not require 265 columns, as my hon. friend has suggested. This figure was based on a target system which was completely and utterly unrealistic in present circumstances.
Finally I may say that in respect to the R.C.A.F. reserve units, they too are allied with the militia units in this survival task, and in the reorganization that will take place the target system will be taken into consideration, as will other factors. Unfortunately at present a great number of our columns are in target areas and this is a difficult problem to solve, but I am sure it will be tackled realistically by the gentleman we will ask to assist us in this task.
Finally, the official opposition critic has scolded me for not giving a statement on policy at this time. I suppose his objection, however, is nothing like as severe as it would have been if I had announced the policy now. It is not that I have not been considering policy, because I have, morning, noon and night. It is true that studies have been undertaken, studies in depth and studies in breadth as well. The matter has been given a great deal of thought and I, Mr. Chairman, along with other members of the committee do have some thoughts on this subject.
However, I have been impressed by the work of the special committee on defence. They have been diligent in their work. They have laboured in their efforts to acquaint themselves with the complexities of defence
Supply-National Defence problems and policies based on modem strategy, the differences of opinion in this important fundamental field, and where perhaps a Canadian contribution might fit into the picture. This debate has reflected the new and much higher level of understanding in respect to defence matters which has been acquired as a result of the deliberations of the committee.
I think it is well worth while, therefore, to await their report before making recommendations to the government. If any of the hon. gentlemen opposite do not agree with this point of view, I would hope that in the course of this debate they would indicate that they do not agree with it.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, may I say again how much I regret the period of re-adjustment and uncertainty. I doubly regret the problems posed to individuals and to families. In the broader context, however, these dislocations will pass in time. Meanwhile we will be able to fashion a policy which will not only lift morale to its highest peak but will also produce the maximum and most flexible Canadian contribution to the peace and security of the world.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the minister complete his answers by telling us how long the air division in Europe will be unarmed and not ready for immediate action?

I cannot answer that question precisely, Mr. Chairman, because as has been pointed out there are a number of factors which have to be taken into consideration, including the completion of storage facilities, the signing of the technical agreement, the state of readiness and training of the squadrons and so on.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Then will the minister admit his decision to disband the interceptors was militarily unsound?
It was not my decision; it was that of my predecessor.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I question the minister's statement with regard to that. He is now making an accusation. Are you meaning me as your predecessor, or the hon. member for Calgary North?
I was not specific.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You never are. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I will have to make this a question of privilege. The minister has made an accusation which he knows is untrue, and I ask him to withdraw that statement.

If it will please my hon. friend I will withdraw it, but may I say the decision, at least by inference, was taken some time ago because this was part of the phasing out

Supply-National Defence of the old interceptor squadrons, which was directly related to the phasing in of the new CF-104 squadrons, which has been going on for a year and a half.

Mr. Chairman, although I have a very bad cold and it is very difficult for me to talk, I would like to say a few things which I feel are very important about matters which should be brought to the attention of the Minister of National Defence at this time. Principal among them is the reduction in personnel of the army, navy and air force, which would also contain the special training at the Kitchener tender H.M.C.S.
For the past three or four years the previous government did much to improve the conditions of the militia and the Royal Canadian Navy reserves in Waterloo North. However the minister now threatens to tear down all the splendid progress made, especially by the Kitchener tender H.M.C.S.
For over 30 years the city of Kitchener has been trying to purchase the old post office building on Benton and King streets, for the purpose of widening the street at this important intersection, which has been a distinct hazard for traffic. This building has now been sold through crown assets corporation to the city of Kitchener.
In order to bring about this successful purchase the former government leased property on Victoria street, so that the Twelfth Royal Canadian Army Medical Corps and the Royal Canadian Reserve could be moved from the old post office building to this new site.
Owing to the cost of housing the Scotch Fusiliers of Canada in the Dunker building, where they have resided for many years, it was decided by the Department of National Defence that this unit and the Twelfth Royal Canadian Army Medical Corps would be moved to the new armouries on Victoria street, and the Royal Canadian Navy reserve would be stationed in new quarters at the Kaya building on Weber street, which has been done.
Through the fine efforts of such men as Commodores Piercey, Kirkpatrick, and others, the Kitchener tender has produced the highest standard of training at the lowest cost per trainee in Canada. After much hard work by this unit they recently moved into these new quarters and are greatly concerned as to the intentions of the Minister of National Defence in regard to his remarks on page 5457 of yesterday's Hansard, that the tender at Kitchener would also be closed.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to read a telegram I received from the former officers of the Kitchener tender which explains their great concern in the announcement made by the minister.

Kitchener tender has been housed recently in a new building leased for five years. This unit has produced the highest standard of training at the lowest cost per trainee in Canada. Other than parade pay the only item to be saved by closing this unit is the pay of one writer. Furthermore, it is considered that the spirit of the ship's company is such that the unit could maintain its present strength if parade pay were discontinued. It is urged that the Kitchener tender be permitted to continue training during the tenure of its lease and to increase its complement to the training capacity of its new quarters in order to lower further the per capita cost of training R.C.N.R. personnel.
I sincerely hope the minister will give his very serious consideration to the Kitchener tender being continued in Kitchener.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kootenay West.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman; I have been sitting here since eleven o'clock this morning.
Since world war I.

My colleagues behind are saying "Since world war I". My remarks this evening could possibly be properly described as a speechette, because I do not wish to delay the estimates longer than necessary. However, I am interested in this subject and I do want to have the opportunity to express my view briefly. I regret I was unable to be here yesterday, owing to my attendance in the veterans affairs committee in the afternoon, and in the evening I spent two hours in the external affairs committee listening to the superbly phrased ambiguities of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I was interested in listening to the minister's reply to the various speeches that have been made. I noticed that he overlooked what I considered to be one or two of the better ones, but he may have something to say about them later.
These delayed estimates and the circumstances of the present time provide an opportunity, in my opinion, for this parliament and for the government to reassess our defence posture in a rapidly changing world. I use the word "posture" because I understand it was a word used very frequently by the defence committee when they were overseas, and I want to use language that is current nowadays. During the last 15 years we have spent millions of dollars in an effort to keep in step with our powerful allies and to meet, as various ministers of national defence have informed us, our commitments. However, the records of this house-and anybody who reads the records carefully, commencing with the establishment of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the speeches in this house on that subject, will confirm this-show that we have been repeatedly

misinformed as to the results that would flow from these massive expenditures and as to the future developments as the result of these expenditures in the political, military and economic fields.
Anyone reading the back history of these debates realizes how all governments were going into the future without much knowledge of what that future would be. We must make certain allowances for the fact that we are living in a very uncertain world, but these are facts. The minister's tale, shall I say, that was told this evening again amply demonstrates that fact. I remember that just a few years ago when the minister was in the opposition he was a famous anti-nuclear weapon exponent. He has changed his views somewhat in that respect. I also remember his telling us of the magnificent progress being made with the development of the Bobcat. My colleague from Port Arthur was quite interested in and enthusiastic about that subject. We believed what we were told. Now we are told it is being scrapped after spending some $7J million on it, and we are purchasing a similar type of vehicle from the United States.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, I want to be fair as I usually am, or try to be-except under conditions of stress-and congratulate the minister on this first attempt to reduce the expenditures by cutting out some of the duplication and the waste that has occurred in his department, waste and duplication that has cost the taxpayers, the Canadian people, so dearly throughout the years. This is a limited approach, but we congratulate him for having the courage to do this, because our knowledge of military people is that you meet with great resistance when you start to cut down the budget of any of our forces. I remember-and I have quoted it repeatedy- that distinguished minister of national defence, who now occupies a high position in British Columbia, saying on one occasion that in all his lengthy military experience he had never known an admiral, a general or an air marshal who did not ask for far more than he required. I have always approached these estimates having that in the back of my mind, and I have quoted the former minister throughout the years. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think all of us give the minister credit for grasping a rather nasty stinging nettle when it comes to dealing with the reduction of defence expenditures, and we wish him well in all he undertakes in that direction from now on.
It is obvious that the government, faced with unexpected expenditures in connection with old age security, old age assistance, blind pensions and disabled persons allowances, began to look around to see where they could
Supply*-National Defence save some money in some department to make up for these unexpected expenditures, and to see where they could recover some of this expense. In my opinion the government correctly focused its attention on the department that offers the greatest opportunity for saving the funds necessary for socially constructive programs. We congratulate the government for that approach, and the minister for his limited economy program in this respect.
Our expenditures on defence began to rise rapidly with the formation of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. At that time we were told that while NATO, as it is called, was basically a military alliance, great benefits were expected to flow from article 2 of this treaty, which provides for co-operation in economic, cultural and other fields. I remember the present Prime Minister making a considerable to-do about article 2 of the NATO treaty. It was the sugar coating, shall
1	say, that sweetened the treaty when it was presented to parliament at that time and attracted the support of many members of parliament who were somewhat dubious as to what this treaty would mean in the days ahead.
What has been the result as far as article
2	is concerned? The result has been nil. Only last evening in the external affairs committee I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs if he could mention one concrete achievement under article 2. If you read the minutes of the meeting last evening you will see that the minister was unable to mention one concrete achievement. He did mention the benefits of people getting together, even though they did not accomplish anything, and discussing trade, cultural activities and things of that sort-making a social event out of it. But he was unable to mention one concrete achievement. Of course, there was nothing done, although we had the committee of the Three Wise Men, of which our Prime Minister was a member. They made recommendations, but there was nothing done with respect to the recommendations of the Three Wise Men, because as many of us suspected even in the early days, persons engaged in a military alliance and that type of operation- and I do not blame them; they specialize in one field-generals, and so on, as far as I am concerned are not usually experts on trade, cultural and other activities of that kind.
The next step was the rearmament of Germany. This was one method that would help us keep Germany on our side, we were told; otherwise the militaristic elements in Germany might get out of control. By bringing Germany into the North Atlantic Treaty

Supply-National Defence Organization we did something to support the democratic element in Germany, we were informed, and a rearmed Germany would not be permitted atomic weapons or ships or submarines above a certain size. However, all these promises have been forgotten as German demands increase with the growing German economic and military strength. This has been noticed by a good many people in Canada. Our contribution to NATO has cost the Canadian people, I think, including all the infrastructure, logistic costs and things of that sort, and buildings and transportation, approximately $400 million a year. That is a very heavy expenditure. We are told that our presence is still required for the sake of maintaining the morale of our allies. However, there is a growing dissatisfaction with this continued expenditure under present circumstances. The Canadian people know that from a military point of view the European nations can provide the same forces at one quarter the cost. This is illustrated by articles in a number of periodicals and military journals. This is, in the first instance, a wasteful way of approaching defence, from our point of view.
This dissatisfaction with our defence expenditures is not confined to members of this party. A day or two ago, according to the press, a member of the Liberal party in the Senate complained of these wasteful expenditures over the years in NATO and a member of the Progressive Conservative party suggested economies would be made by bringing our brigade home and keeping it in Canada. Not that he was suggesting that we should withdraw from NATO, but he was suggesting economies would be made by returning our brigade and other forces to Canada.
This dissatisfaction is found amongst other members of this house. The minister knows there are members on the Liberal side who are quite critical of our expenditures with respect of NATO under present circum-tances, and there are members on the official opposition side who are also critical. Anyone who has been on committees or had conversations with members of the house knows that there is a growing dissatisfaction with the value we are receiving for this type of expenditure. I know from letters and conversations I have had in the country that there are also s'-pporters of all parties in the house who are beginning to question the value of these expenditures and urging that consideration be given for the use of the same funds to greater advantage in other directions.
In my opinion now is the time to reassess our defence posture. The present situation provides the government with an excellent opportunity to review the whole program.

People of all nations realize that war is international suicide. We can have nothing to do with the multiplication of nuclear weapons. We have the two giants with enough to destroy one another in a few hours. We can have nothing to do with that role. But we can do something effectively in other fields.
In regard to this theory, that war is international suicide, I want to quote briefly from a book entitled "Defence or Retaliation" by Schmidt. I have not read the book fully but I have read passages and on page 5 I find this paragraph:
Public opinion must recognize that we are going to live less and less under the protection of H-bomb deterrence. Many military men and politicians believe that this exposure can be remedied by means of tactical nuclear weapons, but at best this proposition is not even half true. Many have yet to learn that in the event of a collision in Europe our peoples would be destroyed by tactical nuclear weapons every bit as efficiently as by strategic bombs, and that, furthermore, the fact of their existence scarcely reduces the risk of the outbreak of war at all. If Liddell Hart, one of Europe's most respected writers on strategy, can say: "These governments will be unworthy of their trust unless they tackle the problem of developing a non-suicidal form of defence and providing the minimum military strength required for it"-
The writer of the book, I understand, is the military critic of the social democratic party in Germany and the book is recognized as very well written and is accepted as an authority by many persons who understand something about this very complicated subject.
The fact is that the cold war as the way of deciding who shall have world leadership and who shall not is out of date. I think that is recognized by all who have given the subject serious consideration. It has been superseded by the emergence on the world stage in the last 15 years of over a score of new nations in Asia and Africa which neither support the east nor the west at this time. True, they have as yet little power. They are undeveloped and in many cases poverty stricken. But they are developing. They have already won considerable world influence and influence in the United Nations, and it is their future support of either the east or the west that, in my opinion, in the long run is going to determine the question of world leadership.
I think we all recognize that there still is, and will be for a long time yet, a contest between western and communist values, but in my opinion that contest from now on, in these balance of terror circumstances, will be decided not by cold war tactics but by the values that win or lose the loyalty and support of the new and presently uncommitted nations. Canada is in a very good position to exercise influence far beyond her

military potential under these circumstances which offer us such a good opportunity.
What would this amount to in practice, Mr. Chairman? Economically it would mean our diverting that part of our military expenditure now required to keep our forces in Europe into uses such as social construction at home, and secondly as expenditures of foreign aid for the underdeveloped countries. It could also be diverted into manpower, as mentioned by one of my colleagues who is affectionately referred to by some of the ladies who sit in the gallery of the house and others as the Bertrand Russell of the House of Commons, namely the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands. I thought he made an excellent speech yesterday on this question, but the minister did not even make reference to his suggestions. I thought he made an excellent suggestion regarding the transposition of the use of manpower, taking advantage of the military training, the youth and knowledge of discipline of these men so as to utilize them in the field of assisting the underdeveloped countries. From a military point of view it would mean that we use our reduced establishment for home defence and civil defence and the protection of our population to the best advantage under the circumstances. Second, we would provide for the necessary air and sea patrols around our coast, and third we would provide for the maintenance of a highly trained mobile force with the necessary transport for use when required or called upon by the United Nations.
Politically, Mr. Chairman, what would this mean? It would mean a revamping of our foreign policy; a policy which would emphasize that the basic world problem is not the cold war-which we are inclined to overemphasize at this time-with an increase in nuclear weapons. We require a policy which underlines that the issue today is the future relationship between the rich and the poor nations and the need for some leadership on our part. In my opinion such policy takes time to develop; even some of the Liberal members agree with that. The only difference is that they were about 10 years behind us in their thinking, but you could see that subconsciously they were leaning in our direction, although the tempo of thought was somewhat slower. Such a policy is realistic from a Canadian point of view and provides Canada with the opportunity to set an example to the many nations who look to us for leadership in blazing new pathways to peace, which will gradually recognize the fact that the cold war is not an issue as far as we are concerned. It is the association with these underdeveloped nations
Supply-National Defence and giving leadership to these nations that we could welcome.
Later on in the session I look forward to hearing the minister's statement on defence policy. I urge him to make a short step in the right direction. He has shown courage in clipping the wings of some of these wasters and I do hope that after listening to some of our arguments he will take another step in the direction we propose.

It is always worth while to put things in their proper perspective. Taking the total amount of the cuts made in the military budget and dividing it into $1.6 billions which are, roughly, spent on defence, it amounts to about 4 per cent. Is that what the figure comes out at?
Close enough for argumentative purposes.

Close enough for our purposes. In other words the minister is attempting to cut the budget by 4 per cent. Well, it is a move in the right direction, but I think the newspaper articles and the publicity which has appeared have distorted this matter out of its proper proportion. I know these cuts have hit us worse in Alberta than elsewhere and we are not happy about them. I want to say to those who are smiling over there, and who seem to be getting some pleasure out of it, that if they had been hit as badly as we have in Alberta they would be smiling out of the other corner of their mouths.
The minister said McCall flying field would be closed. May I ask him what is to follow the closing down of this field in Calgary? Is it to be sold? I understand it is to be sold. These are matters which the minister ought to have at his fingertips. He must have known when he gave the order to close that airfield what would follow and what would be done with it. Is he going to put it under the auctioneer's hammer? Will he get the Minister of Agriculture to auction it off? Perhaps he should get the Minister of Agriculture to auction it, because he does not spend much time in the house.

There may be a certain amount of negotiation required. The department may wish to continue to use some of the buildings. It could be that another department of government has an interest there. I have heard that the city of Calgary is interested. We will probably negotiate with the interested parties to see what the best solution might be.
Is there any thought of adding to the length of any of the runways at McCall field?

I do not think so, Mr. Chairman.

Supply-National Defence

I turn, now, to one other point, my last, because I do not wish to delay the passage of these estimates. It has to do with the contract which was signed with the United States in connection with the acquisition of atomic warheads. That contract, I understand, was completed last August or October. May I say to the hon. member who is sitting beside the minister that I should like to have the minister's attention. I am about to ask some serious questions. This means a contract has been signed and licenses have been issued by the United States government. In other words, the deal has been buttoned up and it is just a question of getting the warheads. Am I right in that? I think the Canadian people have a right to know these things.
Would the hon. gentleman mind telling me which agreement in particular he was referring to?

Under the McMahon act, the United States atomic energy act, it is provided that a licence signed by the President or some high official in the United States government must be obtained and that the acceptance of nuclear warheads is subject to certain conditions. The President reserves the right to pull the trigger. Let us look at this situation in another way. Have the military authorities completed the signing of that declaration with the authorities in Washington?

I am not as familiar with the act mentioned by the hon. member as I might be, but I do know that the two steps which are required to take in connection with our North American defence arrangements, the Voodoo and the Bomarc, have been taken. The first was the general agreement which was signed in August, as was stated earlier this evening, and then there was the technical agreement which I believe was signed in October. These steps have been taken and all the technical requirements necessary to meet the provisions of the McMahon act are included in those two agreements.

In other words, it is all buttoned up. Now, where does Canada stand, as far as its sovereignty is concerned, in the event of an atomic war? The people of Canada are asking about this and they are looking to the minister to give them this information. Where does our sovereignty rest, now that these declarations have been signed and nuclear warheads have been taken from the United States?
As far as the use of the weapons system is concerned, our sovereignty remains with us.
I did not get that last.
Sovereignty remains with us in respect to the use of the weapons system.

All right. In other words, what the minister is saying is this. Let us approach it from another direction. The late President Kennedy sent a man to go around to the various NATO countries to obtain agreement on setting up committees on some kind of joint action before nuclear weapons were to be used, so that he as president would not have to shoulder the entire responsibility for making the decision. Those negotiations have been going on for some time. Could the minister tell the committee what progress has been made and where we stand with respect to that joint declaration, should we be faced with entering a nuclear war?

I think answers to most of the hon. gentleman's questions are included in reports of the special committee on defence. Since he is so interested in this subject perhaps he would find it worth while to read those reports and get the full background of information which is available in them.

I know about that. It is all well and good for the minister to try to evade the issue, but the people of Canada are looking to him for a clear statement as to where our sovereignty lies in the present circumstances.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to give an example to show where our sovereignty stands and I hope this will satisfy the hon. gentleman because-
That is what I am asking for.

-at first I thought he was quite familiar with the McMahon act, but now there appears to be some area of misunderstanding. The following statement applies to the Bomarc system. First, custody: The exercise of custody is a United States air force responsibility. This includes control over access to the nuclear warheads and related classified materials.
Base security: The security of all base facilities, consistent with the custodial responsibility of the United States air force detachment commander, is assigned to the R.C.A.F. squadron commander. All security guards on the base are R.C.A.F. The United States air force have the only custodial personnel and control access to U.S.A.F. owned weapons or non-releasable materials.
Storage: The storage functions of the warheads will be performed jointly under the direction of the United States air force personnel. The storage requirement is in fact very small because the warheads will normally be mated to the missiles.

Maintenance: All maintenance functions on the warheads are the sole responsibility of United States personnel. Other maintenance responsibilities, that is, on missiles, launchers or shelters, are either an R.C.A.F. or joint responsibility.
Safety: The development, observance and enforcement of safety standards and procedures is a joint responsibility. Compliance with applicable Canadian laws and regulations on the one hand and United States nuclear safety rules on the other, is an absolute requirement.
Inspections: After all preliminary inspections have been completed and the warheads have been delivered further inspections will be carried out at prescribed intervals. As a matter of convenience, United States air force standards and procedures for these inspections are being adopted. However, any additional Canadian requirement can be included. Actual inspections will be conducted on a joint basis.
Authorization for use: In general terms the policy is that Bomarcs may be fired only when authorized by both governments and then only in accordance with procedures established by the commander in chief, NORAD, and approved by the appropriate Canadian and United States authorities. Specifically, in the Bomarc control circuitry at the SAGE direction centre there are two locked switches, both of which must be turned "on" before a Bomarc can be launched. The keys to these two switches are held at all times by a designated Canadian officer and a designated United States officer respectively.
Actions that must have been taken before the Bomarc can be fired are: First, the commander in chief, NORAD, must have been notified that the President of the United States has authorized the release of weapons from United States custody for use by Canadian forces assigned to NORAD. Second, the commander in chief, NORAD, must also have received authorization from the Prime Minister or his authorized representative to release weapon carriers for use by Canadian forces assigned to NORAD. Third, the United States custodial officer on duty in the SAGE direction centre must have received properly authenticated evidence that United States governmental release has been given. He would thereupon unlock the United States release switch.
Fourth, the designated Canadian officer on duty in the SAGE direction centre must also have received properly authenticated evidence that Canadian governmental release has been given. He would thereupon unlock the second release switch.
Supply-National Defence
Fifth, at this point the weapon would be available for firing but still would not be fired until the SAGE sector commander had authorized the senior weapons director to commence using the Bomarcs against hostile targets.
So you can see that once the supreme political authorities have given authorization, a considerable sequence of events must occur before the weapon can be used. A number of people are involved and certain preconditions must exist. Then the two keys, one American and one Canadian, must be turned before a missile can be fired. This procedure, with its many checks and doublechecks, is designed to prevent missile firing by accident or malice or without the consent of both governments.
Is there any estimate of the time interval between the decision of the political authorities of both governments and the actual firing?
None that I could give, and it would depend on a number of circumstances, including the proximity of the hostile aircraft.
I thank the minister for having taken the time to give us these details. It is spelled out in the agreement between the two nations, is it, that the leaders of both governments must decide?
It is spelled out in the procedures.
Is that binding on both nations?
Yes, it is.
That is what we want to know. I want to thank the minister for having answered my questions and I shall turn the floor back to the chairman so that we can get on with the estimates.

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two matters I should like to bring before the committee this evening in relation to the remarks the minister made yesterday and I also have one or two questions I should like to ask him. I had intended that my remarks would be mostly of a constituency nature in relation to the announcement of the withdrawal of all armed forces from Fort Churchill. However, keeping in mind the unjustified attack which I felt was made on the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria yesterday merely for coming to the defence of his own constituency, I suppose I should make a few remarks on the general aspects of national defence.
I feel there is probably no better time than the closing days of this first session of the twenty sixth parliament to mention one or two of the issues which were current during

Supply-National Defence the last federal general election. While it is not my intention to rehash those issues I believe this would be a good time to put a few remarks with regard to them on the record. First of all, I am sure all Canadians realize by this time that the Liberal party perpetrated the greatest hoax that has ever been perpetrated in a general election when they created the myth that the former government had made certain commitments in regard to the acquisition of nuclear warheads. I feel that possibly the issue they raised in that regard in the campaign resulted in some of them being returned to the House of Commons. However, I also believe that as a result those Canadians who supported them must have expected that as soon as they took over the reins of office they would produce the evidence to show that the statements they had made were correct. But we all know what we have seen. Instead of producing any evidence the present government has built a sort of airtight capsule around what they say was the evidence of commitments. They set up a defence committee, but it was made quite apparent that the terms of reference of that committee would not include this question of commitment. In fact, there was a request made for copies of correspondence relating to these commitments, and some of the men who are sitting on the treasury benches made it quite clear that the correspondence concerning these commitments was regarded as classified and could not be given to the House of Commons. I believe I am justified in assuming that the people who supported these candidates are now wondering, if this information was so classified, how in heaven's name it was that practically every Liberal candidate in Canada seemed to know this commitment had been made. I am bringing this to the attention of the committee merely because during my own campaign I mentioned to my constituents that I thought the day was not too far removed when these charges would be proven to be the myth that they are.
There is one other minor issue of much the same nature that came up during the campaign. A great deal was made of it, and in fact some newspapers in Canada carried headlines relating to the charge made by the present Minister of National Defence to the effect that the former prime minister had given out confidential or classified information during a speech at Prince Albert. As I say, I am bringing this up now because headlines were created. It was not long before the former prime minister proved that this was not the case. The information he had given out at this meeting had been carried in


publications in North America many months before. Here, we have a situation in which charges are being made that classified information was given out, and those charges are being made by a man who is now the Minister of National Defence. This person should be the last one to charge anyone with giving out classified information. As I say, it was a false charge, but if one turns to page 3425 of Hansard for February 4, 1963, he finds the present minister, then the hon. member for Trinity, when discussing some aspects of a trip the NATO delegation made to Europe, using these words:
We were interviewed by the supreme allied commander of allied forces in Europe. We were briefed by Admiral Smeeton. deputy commander of the Atlantic fleet, by General Calmel deputy chief of staff of supreme allied headquarters.. .A number of questions have been asked as to what our commitments to NATO are. I realize that this information is presumably classified, but I could never understand why it was, so I am going to take the responsibility tonight of saying what they are.
Then, he went on to state the information which apparently was given to the NATO delegation. If one can judge by the words the minister used, it was classified information.

I wonder if the hon. member would just let me interrupt for a moment to correct that impression? I had been aware of the commitments from the time I was associate minister, and as a minister you are able to classify or declassify certain information. It was on that basis I took the responsibility for making these commitments known, as I believed they were known to everyone in the world, practically, except the Canadian people, and I thought it was time they were allowed to be in on that information. Since then, they have been referred to publicly in the special committee on defence.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I say, with regard to that, the minister as a minister is not entitled to disclose classified information which has been classified by NATO headquarters? We were given information of that nature in Paris just a few weeks ago, but we are not at liberty to disclose it.

That is my point, Mr. Chairman; it was not information which I had received over there. It was information which, in fact, had been available to me for many years and which I thought should be given to the public.

I noted carefully the remarks of the minister at this time, Mr. Chairman, and I am merely putting this on the record because at that time we were led to believe this was information which should not have been given to the public. I am particularly concerned about the minister's remarks at that

time. He said he realized that this information was presumably classified, but he could never understand why it was. If you were to look up the word "presumably" I believe it would indicate he believed it to be classified.
Be that as it may, I felt I should like to get these two points on the record during these closing days of the first session of the twenty sixth parliament because I firmly believe these were two misrepresentations during the last election.
I should like to deal very briefly with the announcement which the minister made yesterday concerning the withdrawal of armed personnel from Fort Churchill. First of all, I should like to tell the minister it is my understanding that the people of Manitoba have been completely shocked by this news and for very good reasons. I noticed that the minister stated that the government was making this announcement at this time in order to give maximum notice to the personnel and allow for readjustment. This is a very worthy objective. I do not intend to indicate that any announcement was made previously outside of this house in relation to the closing of Fort Churchill, but I do feel it was common knowledge in the town of Churchill for many months, I believe as far back as October 14, that this might happen. At that time, as a result of numerous telephone calls and telegrams from Churchill concerning the rumour, I inquired of the minister who told me at that time that they had plans for the withdrawal of forces. However, quite a number of people must have known about it. I am wondering why it was not possible, if the government wished to give maximum notice to the people, to make this announcement in October instead of leaving it until now.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and I wish to thank the committee for allowing me to continue. Returning to the very surprising announcement of the withdrawal of army personnel from Fort Churchill I wish to say I am sure all the people at Churchill, and the people of Manitoba in general, would be very appreciative if a reconsideration were made. There are several points which I am going to bring out.
The hon. member for Calgary North brought out the point of the value that Churchill has been in relation to Arctic training, and I believe it could also be used for training in survival for R.C.A.F. and other personnel.
Due to the geographical makeup of our country I suggest that if we are going to develop it in the way it should be developed, we must decentralize in many ways. It is often very difficult to get industry to decentralize; but in regard to national defence this is something where the government alone has the power, and I feel the obligation, to decentralize as much as possible and assist in the development of the country.
At the townsite of Churchill, as members of the treasury benches probably know, the population have made their homes there entirely as a result of federal government establishments. For instance, the armed forces have the only hospital within several hundred miles. Therefore they have the only doctors and nurses in that area. I am mightily concerned for the health needs of the people of that area if the camp at Fort Churchill is closed, and possibly the hospital along with it. There are many other reasons for taking a second look at this. It may be that relatively the same work which is carried out at Churchill may continue to be carried out in some other more populated area of Canada. Therefore if this is going to be the case I think reconsideration should be given to the army camp at Churchill.
The minister mentioned that the rocket range would continue to operate. I wonder, could he enlighten the committee as to what type of agreement Canada has with the United States government in relation to the maintenance of that rocket base, in regard to the length of contract, and in general how long does the government feel this rocket range will continue to operate? With regard to the minister's announcement that this withdrawal would take place in 1964, my information from Churchill is to the effect that the withdrawal has been under way for some time and some 60 army personnel have been withdrawn and not replaced. Therefore I suppose

the withdrawal took place some time prior to the announcement the minister made in the house.
I would also like to know the intention of the government with relation to the operation of the marine terminal at Churchill, which was built at a cost of some $7 million. The instructions for the construction of this marine terminal were given by a former Liberal government and I would be interested to know whether it can be turned over to other government departments; in other words, will this marine terminal continue to be used? I was very pleased to hear the minister announce this evening that cadet units would not be affected by this announcement. I am wondering whether he would consider it possible if cuts are made in certain departments of the army, to allow these cadet units, such as the naval, air force and army cadets, to have greater use of armouries throughout the country.
The minister also said something about air search and rescue, I believe, in Prince Edward Island. I would be very interested to learn from him whether it is intended to curtail R.C.A.F. air search and rescue to any extent in western Canada. I do not think this question has yet been raised. If I can get answers from the minister to those questions, Mr. Chairman, and an assurance that some reconsideration will be given to the matter of the withdrawal of all army personnel from Churchill, I would greatly appreciate it and I am sure the people of Manitoba would also.

With respect to the rocket range, Mr. Chairman, it is anticipated that it will be kept open during the term of the agreement, which I think extends to 1965. It is likely that it will be continued beyond that, but possibly by a civilian agency, and this is something that will be subject to negotiation.

How did that get in there?

My reason for asking for these figures is that I understand the minister said the present strength of the militia
Supply-National Defence is somewhere in the neighbourhood of 51,000 men and the intention is to cut it down to

down by 20,000 men. Our concern is, first of all, as to where this cut-back is going to take place. Will it take place in these centres, or in the rural areas? I am also concerned about the relationship of the militia to the civil defence role. That role has changed. The minister also said he had two choices to make, with which I do not agree. He said, first of all, he had the choice of cutting down the militia or giving our first-line troops adequate weapons. If this is what he bases his cut-back on, I would say it is a false premise, because there are many other choices. It is not necessary to go into them at the present time because I doubt very much if this discussion will be over by eleven o'clock tonight. We are concerned with the role of the militia. The determination will be made by a commission of militiamen which will be put together for that purpose. They will take into account the various factors, including the role of the militia, and particularly civil survival and how this could best be carried out, and all of the other considerations. Mr. Chairman, I was waiting for the hon. member for Lotbiniere to make his speech. I understand he had a little homily to make about the soldiers of the Queen, and I was ready to prevent his having a go. My original plans have gone by the board in view of the late hour. I wanted to talk about two specific matters. I suppose I spent too much time on kitchen fatigue during the war to ever feel I should rise to a sort of

Supply-National Defence summit to approach defence problems from the heights from which the Minister of National Defence approaches them. I was going to confine my remarks to two things, the Bobcat and the educational program of the Department of National Defence. Instead of making a speech I will just ask the minister some questions.
I want to know how we could have such a dunderhead, clotted-up, stupid line of development with relation to the Bobcat. I use those adjectives of invective because I cannot conceive how any Department of National Defence or any Department of Defence Production with any integrity or any ability could manage to botch a program the way this program has been botched. You can go back through the years 1959, 1960 and before, and little statements were made, "We need another $1 million for the Bobcat", "We need another $600,000 for the Bobcat", "We need another $200,000 for the Bobcat development". Obviously either the army did not give a damn about that Bobcat, or the government did not give a damn about it, or Canadian Car and Foundry did not. The reason I am a little incensed about this is that our community at the lakehead was "suckered" on this deal: That is the word, "suckered". We were told four years ago that in 18 months the development program would be through and our factory would be considered as the place where the thing would go into production.
The Bobcat became a joke a long time ago in our community. We were under no illusions that anything was ever going to come of it. But the joke still exists. The minister has to give us some satisfactory explanation. He almost stood up here as though he was a hero when talking about cutting out the Bobcat. God, some hero. He has arrived well after the last act curtain has come down. How about it? How about knowing, Mr. Chairman, what is the real story on this ridiculous situation? I can remember that when Mr. Pearkes was the minister of national defence I went to knock at his door to speak to him about an important problem in my constituency. I went in. He was walking up and down. He said, "Fisher, I am just bogged down with problems-the damned Bobcat, the Bomarc, and so on. What do you want to see me about?" I said, "I have some ladies putting out washing on Monday mornings near the armouries at Port Arthur, and they want them to burn hard coal". I always remember his reaction. He said, "That's the kind of problem I like to deal with". And, by jove, they started burning hard coal. I wish some of these brains we have in the department had done something about the Bobcat. What a pitiful tale it has

been throughout the years. I hear someone say it has not got a tail, but I want the t-a-l-e from the minister now.
It is a long, sad tale. To reduce it to one sentence it is: Two successive governments, treasury board, changes in ownership and problems of private management as well.

Reduced to one sentence it is still not very satisfactory. What do we get out of all that money spent? What conclusions are we to draw about the military which can conceive a program like this and fumble it along? I want to ask the minister whether the army really felt any urgency about having that particular carrier. That is a direct question.

Yes, I would say categorically the army did have a feeling toward it and I think it still does. I think they realize now the only solution is the one we have taken. The concept was excellent. The failure was in the execution, and rather than point the finger at any one group it has to be summed up the way I summed it up in that sentence. It fell to a series of misfortunes.
The hon. member asked what lessons can be learned. One of the great lessons which can be learned from this experiment is that when you have a good idea, if the people concerned can push it through for all they are worth until it is completed in that way, there is some chance for success. But to string it out and procrastinate and spread the development over a longer period, for whatever reason, it almost inevitably winds up the way the Avro Arrow wound up or the Bobcat wound up. That is the lesson which has been learned.
Part of the problem is the system. The decision-making system is too slow and cumbersome; too many committees, too many reviews, some by people who do not have direct responsibility. A lesson can be learned in that respect too, I can assure my hon. friend. So far as possible we will push any developmental work which we undertake so as to get production started before the people who take away the same idea from us overtake us in their decision-making process and beat us to the finished product.

Why should not some heads roll over this? A few years ago heads were threatening to roll over a five minute broadcast in the morning on the C.B.C. Here millions of dollars has been wasted. We have had this cumbersome procedure. Surely someone is responsible. Surely some minister, some politician, some senior administrative

officer is responsible for this haywire situation. Where was the great defence research board establishment during this time? I have gone through the estimates and seen the details of the big salaries paid these scientists. They have a library full of classified material. They put out a beautiful magazine called 'The Canadian Army" and you get the impression our army is swimming in experts on almost every phase of modern gadgetry in war. Yet the minister says this is an unfortunate thing and shows a weakness. At least the Avro people got the thing in the air and it looked good. It makes a nice model on the mantle. I do not know why there has been no investigation, instead of running off to find some horses who are on the payroll at Camp Petawawa. We have spent millions of dollars and swaggered and blustered about our own Canadian vehicle, and look at the lamentable result. What a travesty of defence. I am glad I stayed mostly on kitchen fatigue, if that is the kind of thing our military men come up with. What an outfit.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Do not condemn them all. That is a generalization.
I know it is, but the hon. member has to admit it is a pretty ridiculous situation in regard to the Bobcat.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Of course it is.

The hon. member and I were of the same regiment and he remembers we wound up with a vehicle not designed for us, and it turned out very well. It was something thrown off by the Americans called the Stag-hound armoured car. The Canadian forces got it by luck and it turned out quite well. The minister has not given us any satisfaction in his announcement regarding the very relevant criticisms and analyses made by the Glassco commission of education establishments in the Department of National Defence. I am referring to the millions of dollars spent in the education of dependants overseas and in particular colleges. Tonight he comes along with a statement which flies in the face of what the Glassco commission says, and what is obvious from the statistics in relation to the cost of training an officer. He is going to cut down on the university training program for officers.
I think you have the two programs confused.
Is the minister cutting down on Royal Roads and on C.M.R. and R.M.C.?

No. There are two training programs at universities, the C.O.T.C. and also the R.O.T.P. It is the C.O.T.C. we are cutting back on.
Supply-National Defence

As long as it is not the R.O.T.P.
I think the minister should explain why he has not done anything about these educational costs and why he has gone in the face of the information on Royal Roads. One of the things which interests me is that in 1959 I had a letter from a person on the staff of Royal Roads giving exactly the same information and reaching the same conclusions. The Glassco commission reported that this junior college at Royal Roads is in effect redundant, and not only that but that it could never really be anything but a gross misconception of the university function because it is a junior college built up of a staff pushing for Ph.D's. The staff is very well qualified academically, yet does not live in an environment where they can exercise skill.
Eleven o'clock.

The hon. member says eleven o'clock. I want to ask the minister whether he would give us a fuller explanation as to why he did not accept the Glassco commission recommendations that something should be done, if necessary putting some of the responsibility for the cost on the parents. Second, how could he not move on the position of the high cost of the officer educated through the Royal Roads-C.M.R.-R.M.C. system, when the Glassco commission suggested that the R.O.T.P. produces as good an officer or as comparable an officer and much more cheaply?

This is a broad and comprehensive question and I should like to give time and thought to preparing a statement with regard to it. I should like to take the time between now and the presentation of next year's estimates, for which I shall be taking full responsibility, to prepare such a statement answering the hon. member in detail.

I was given returns to two questions relating to the ability of French speaking as opposed to English speaking students. I have forgotten the numbers of the questions. I am not satisfied from these returns that the French speaking students are getting a fair deal. In brief, I think their failure rate is too high. Attrition from other causes is too high. I am still staggered by the fact that though, in the main, English speaking students at C.M.R. outnumber the French speaking students I should like the minister, when he is conducting this review and trying to develop an approach to the educational commitments of the department, to consider, if we are making an effort to have French

Supply-National Defence speaking officers, whether it is not necessary for us to get better results than we have been getting. If necessary, we must spend a lot more time and effort in doing so. I would prefer to spend more money in this field than to carry on with Royal Roads out in British Columbia, which in a sense, appears to be an unnecessary adjunct to the military college at Kingston.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the acting leader of the house what the business will be for Monday?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
On Monday, the first item of government business will be the resolution respecting the representation commissioner. If it passes and the bill is introduced, it is not proposed to proceed with the bill until the following Monday. The second item will be the resolution regarding finances of the C.N.R. and if it passes it is not proposed to proceed with the bill until the following week. The third item will be the bill respecting the emergency gold mining assistance. The fourth item will be the bill respecting the small businesses loans. The fifth item will be the bill respecting the Canadian world exhibition. The sixth item will be the bill regarding old age, blind persons and disability assistance. The seventh item will be the bill respecting the auditors of the C.N.R. The eighth item will be the bill respecting the currency, mint and exchange fund.
The same business will be continued on Tuesday in this order and, if it is completed, other items of legislation announced by the Prime Minister will be taken after consultation with representatives of the opposition.

It being eight minutes after eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.
